teile.einleitung: An electrical conductor is a material that carries electric current well. This includes above all metals such as copper and aluminium. The opposite are insulators such as plastic or glass, which do not let current through.
wichtigste: Conductors are materials that carry electric current well.
The best conductors are metals such as silver, copper, gold and aluminium.
In metals there are freely moving electrons that carry the current.
Materials that do not conduct electricity are called insulators.
A cable consists of a conducting copper wire and an insulating covering.
Water with dissolved salts and the human body also conduct electricity.
Semiconductors such as silicon are the basis for computer chips.

abschnitte.text: Electric **current** is a movement of electrically charged particles. A **conductor** is a substance in which such particles can move easily. In metals these are the **electrons**, which move freely between the atoms. If you apply a voltage, they flow in one direction. This is how electricity gets from the socket to the lamp, for example.

**Silver** conducts best of all metals, but it is expensive. That is why **copper**, which conducts almost as well, is usually used for cables. For large overhead power lines, aluminium is often used because it is light. Gold does not rust and is therefore used for fine contacts in mobile phones and computers. Graphite, the material in pencils, also conducts electricity.

Substances that do not let current through are called **insulators**. These include plastic, rubber, glass, porcelain, dry wood and air. They protect us from electric current. That is why cables are covered with plastic and plugs have a plastic grip. On electricity pylons, insulators of glass or ceramic hold the lines in place.

The **human body** also conducts electricity, because it contains a lot of salty water. Current from a socket can therefore be life-threatening. Electrical devices should never be near a bath. In Switzerland the voltage at a socket is 230 volts. On the railway, the overhead line even carries electricity at 15,000 volts, which is why you must never climb on railway wagons.

Between conductors and insulators lie the **semiconductors**, for example silicon. Their conductivity can be controlled deliberately. Computer chips, light-emitting diodes and solar cells are built from them. Some substances conduct electricity at very low temperatures with no loss at all. These **superconductors** are used, for example, in the magnets at CERN near Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: The movement of electrically charged particles through a substance.
A material that does not conduct electricity, for example plastic.
A material whose conductivity can be controlled, such as silicon.
Tiny, negatively charged particles that carry the current in metals.

gewusst: Pure water hardly conducts electricity; only dissolved salts and minerals make it a conductor.
Birds can sit on a power line without danger, because the current cannot flow through their bodies into the ground.

teile.einleitung: Daniel Bernoulli was a mathematician and physicist from the famous Bernoulli family of scholars in Basel. He studied how liquids and gases flow and, in doing so, discovered the law named after him. His ideas still explain why a spray bottle works or why two sheets of paper move towards each other when you blow between them.
wichtigste: Daniel Bernoulli was born in Groningen in 1700 and died in Basel in 1782.
He came from the Bernoulli family of Basel, which produced several important mathematicians.
From 1725 he worked for a few years at the Academy of Sciences in St Petersburg.
In 1738 he published his famous book “Hydrodynamica”.
Put simply, Bernoulli's law says: the faster something flows, the lower the pressure.
He explained the pressure of a gas by the impacts of many tiny particles.
In 1760 he used statistics to calculate the benefit of vaccination against smallpox.

abschnitte.text: Daniel Bernoulli was born in **1700** in **Groningen** in the Netherlands, where his father Johann Bernoulli was a professor at the time. The family came from **Basel** and soon returned there. His uncle Jakob and his father were already famous mathematicians. Daniel studied medicine, but was mainly interested in mathematics and physics.

From **1725** Daniel Bernoulli worked at the newly founded Academy of Sciences in **St Petersburg** in Russia. There he also met the Basel mathematician Leonhard Euler, who became his friend. In 1733 he returned to Basel and at first taught **anatomy and botany** at the university. Later he became professor of physiology and finally of physics.

In 1738 his book **“Hydrodynamica”** about flowing liquids appeared. It contains the basic idea of **Bernoulli's law**: the faster a liquid or gas flows, the lower the pressure. That is why, if you blow between two sheets of paper hanging close together, they move towards each other. The law also helps to understand how water flows in pipes and how air flows around aircraft wings.

Daniel Bernoulli had a bold idea: a gas consists of a huge number of tiny particles that are constantly flying around. When these particles hit a wall, **gas pressure** is created. With this he laid a foundation stone of the **kinetic theory of gases**. It was only about a hundred years later that this idea was generally accepted.

In the 18th century **smallpox** was a feared disease from which many people died. In 1760 Bernoulli used **statistics** to calculate how many years of life an early vaccination would save on average. His calculation showed that vaccination was worth it. This makes him a pioneer of the mathematical study of diseases.

Daniel Bernoulli won a prize of the Paris Academy of Sciences ten times, a great success for a researcher of his time. He also worked on probability, vibrating strings and shipbuilding. The **Bernoulli principle** is explained today in physics books all over the world. In Basel, a street and a university building still remind people of the famous Bernoulli family.

begriffe.erklaerung: The movement of a liquid or gas in one direction.
How strongly something pushes on a surface, for example air on a wall.
The study of how liquids move and which forces act on them.
Mathematics that collects and analyses lots of data in order to draw conclusions.

gewusst: In 1734 Daniel shared a prize of the Paris Academy with his father Johann, who was so annoyed about it that he is said to have thrown him out of the house.
As a medical student, Daniel Bernoulli wrote his doctoral thesis on breathing.

teile.einleitung: Fermentation is the transformation of foods or other substances by tiny living things such as bacteria, yeasts and moulds. Without it there would be no cheese, no yoghurt, no airy bread and no sauerkraut. People have used this method for thousands of years, often without knowing how it works.
wichtigste: Fermentation is the transformation of substances by microorganisms.
Cheese, yoghurt, sauerkraut, bread and soy sauce are fermented foods.
Propionic acid bacteria make the holes in Emmental cheese.
Grape juice becomes wine through fermentation, and alcohol becomes vinegar with acetic acid bacteria.
In the 19th century Louis Pasteur showed that living microorganisms cause fermentation.
Kimchi from Korea is fermented vegetables.
Kombucha is made from sweetened tea with bacteria and yeasts.

abschnitte.text: In **fermentation**, **microorganisms** turn sugar and other substances into new substances. These are living things so small that you can only see them under a microscope. Usually this happens wholly or partly without oxygen. In the process, lactic acid, carbon dioxide, alcohol or acetic acid are formed, for example. These substances change the taste, the smell and the keeping quality of a food.

In yoghurt and cheese, **lactic acid bacteria** turn the milk sugar into lactic acid. This makes the milk thick and sour and helps it keep longer. In **Emmental** cheese, propionic acid bacteria also work and produce carbon dioxide. The gas collects in the cheese and forms the famous holes. Switzerland is known for its many fermented cheeses such as Gruyère, Appenzeller or Sbrinz.

In bread dough, **yeast** turns the sugar into carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise. During baking the gas escapes and the airy holes remain in the bread. Yeasts turn grape juice into wine, and apple juice becomes cider. If alcohol comes into contact with air, **acetic acid bacteria** can turn it into vinegar. Kombucha is a drink made from sweetened tea, fermented by bacteria and yeasts together.

**Sauerkraut** is finely cut white cabbage that ferments with salt in pots. In a similar way, **kimchi** is made in Korea from Chinese cabbage, radish and hot spices. **Soy sauce** has long been made in Asia from soya beans, grain and salt with the help of moulds. Fermented vegetables used to be important for keeping vitamins through the winter. Sailors therefore took sauerkraut with them on long voyages.

For a long time nobody knew why grape juice turns into wine or milk turns sour. Around 1860 the French chemist **Louis Pasteur** showed that living microorganisms cause fermentation. He also found out how to kill unwanted germs by heating. This process is named after him, **pasteurisation**, and is still used for milk today. His research laid the foundation of microbiology.

Today fermentation is also used in large factories, in **biotechnology**. In huge steel tanks, microorganisms produce medicines such as insulin, vitamins or enzymes for detergents. Citric acid for drinks is also usually made by fermentation with moulds. In biogas plants, bacteria break down slurry and green waste and produce gas for electricity and heat. So fermentation is not only cooking but also modern technology.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny living thing such as a bacterium or a yeast that you can only see under a microscope.
A single-celled fungus that turns sugar into carbon dioxide and alcohol.
Bacteria that turn sugar into lactic acid, for example in yoghurt and sauerkraut.
Brief heating to kill harmful germs in food.

gewusst: A single gram of yoghurt can contain many millions of living bacteria.
The holes in Emmental cheese can grow as big as a walnut.
Chocolate also gets its flavour because the cocoa beans ferment for a few days after harvesting.

teile.einleitung: A double-blind study is an especially reliable way of testing medicines and treatments. In it, neither the participants nor the experts treating them know who is getting the real medicine and who is getting a dummy. This way, expectations and hopes cannot distort the result.
wichtigste: In a double-blind study, neither the participants nor the experts treating them know who receives which treatment.
The double blinding is meant to stop expectations from influencing the result.
If only the participants do not know their group, it is called a single-blind study.
In a triple-blind study, the people analysing the data are also blinded.
Often a comparison group receives a placebo, a dummy medicine without an active ingredient.
In a medical emergency, the blinding may be lifted for an individual person.
Double-blind studies are regarded as the gold standard for testing new medicines.

abschnitte.text: In a **double-blind study**, the participants are usually divided at random into two groups. One group receives the new medicine, the other a **placebo** or a proven treatment. “Double-blind” means that neither the participants nor the doctors know who is in which group. Only at the end of the study is the secret revealed.

People sometimes feel better just because they believe they are getting an effective medicine; this is the **placebo effect**. On the other hand, some people feel side effects because they expect them; this is called the **nocebo effect**. Experts too may observe differently without realising it if they know who is getting the real medicine. **Blinding** rules out these influences.

In a **single-blind** study, only the participants do not know their group. In a double-blind study, the experts giving the treatment are also kept in the dark. In a **triple-blind** study, the people who analyse the data do not know either. The more people involved are blinded, the less expectations can distort the result.

The placebo must look, smell and taste exactly the same as the real medicine. If a tablet is being compared with an injection, everyone gets **a tablet and an injection**, one of them being a placebo. In operations, the real procedure is sometimes compared with a **sham operation**. But such studies are controversial and need especially good reasons.

In a **medical emergency**, the blinding may be lifted for an individual person so that they get the right treatment. Every study must first be checked by an **ethics committee**. In Switzerland, Swissmedic also checks studies with new medicines before these are approved. Taking part is always voluntary.

As early as 1784, a commission in Paris that included Benjamin Franklin had experiments carried out with blindfolds to test a doubtful healing method. In the 20th century the double-blind study became the **gold standard** in medicine. The principle is also known from everyday life, for example in a **blind tasting** of chocolate. If you do not know the brand, you judge only by the taste.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dummy medicine without an active ingredient, used for comparison.
A measure in which those involved do not know who receives which treatment.
When someone feels symptoms just because they expect them.
The best and most reliable method, against which others are measured.

gewusst: Placebos can work even when people know they are getting a placebo.
Even the colour of a tablet can influence how strongly people feel its effect.

teile.einleitung: The foehn is a warm, dry wind that falls down from the mountains and blows especially often in the Alps. When it blows, it often turns mild all of a sudden, the sky is clear and the mountains look close enough to touch. For many Swiss valleys it is so typical that it has even been called “the oldest citizen of Uri”.
wichtigste: The foehn is a warm, dry wind that falls down the lee side of a mountain range.
When it blows from the south across the Alps it is called the south foehn, and from the north into Ticino the north foehn.
Sinking dry air warms up by about 1 degree per 100 metres.
In foehn conditions you often see a wall of cloud over the main Alpine ridge, the foehn wall.
In a south foehn it often rains in Ticino, because the air builds up against the Alps.
Because the foehn fans fires strongly, strict bans on fires used to apply in foehn valleys.
The name foehn comes from the Latin word favonius.

abschnitte.text: A **foehn** is a warm, dry wind that falls into the valley on the side of a mountain range away from the wind. This side is called the **lee**, and the side the wind hits is called the windward side. There are foehn winds in many mountain ranges of the world, but the Alps are especially known for them. In Switzerland it blows often in spring and in autumn. The name comes from the Latin **favonius**, the Romans' name for a mild west wind.

In a **south foehn**, damp air flows from the Mediterranean against the Alps and has to rise. As it does so it cools, the water vapour forms clouds, and in Ticino it often rains or snows heavily. Because heat is released as the clouds form, the air cools as it rises only about half as much as dry air would. On the northern side the now dry air falls down and warms up by about **1 degree per 100 metres**. So it arrives in the Reuss valley or the Rhine valley much warmer than it started on the southern side.

In foehn conditions, a thick wall of cloud often hangs over the main Alpine ridge, the **foehn wall**. Over the foreland the clouds dissolve and a cloud-free zone appears, the **foehn window**. You often see smooth, lens-shaped clouds that look like UFOs, which are called foehn fish. The air is very dry and clear, so the mountains look especially close. When the wind blows the other way, from the north into Ticino, it is called the **north foehn**, and then it is sunny and windy on the southern side of the Alps.

The foehn blows especially strongly in valleys running from south to north. Well-known **foehn valleys** are the Reuss valley in Uri with Altdorf, the Hasli valley, the Glarus region and the St Gallen Rhine valley. In Altdorf the foehn sometimes reaches storm force, and the temperature can rise sharply in a short time. Because the foehn melts a lot of snow in spring, it is also called the **snow eater**. In autumn it helps grapes and maize to ripen in some areas.

The warm, dry wind fans fires strongly. In 1861 a large part of the town of **Glarus** burned down during a foehn storm. In foehn valleys, strict **bans on fires** used to apply, and men walked through the villages as a foehn watch to spot sparks. Some people also feel the foehn in their own bodies and complain of headaches or tiredness. This sensitivity to the foehn is not fully explained scientifically, however.

abschnitte.titel: From a wind to a hairdryer
abschnitte.text: In German the electric **hairdryer** is often called a Föhn. The name comes from a brand that named it after the warm wind at the beginning of the 20th century. In Switzerland people often simply say “Föhn” or “Haartrockner”. Here too, warm, dry air blows, just as with the real foehn. In this way an Alpine wind became an everyday object in almost every bathroom.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wind that blows down from a mountain range into the valley.
The side of a mountain that faces away from the wind.
The side of a mountain that the wind hits.
A wall of cloud that hangs over the main Alpine ridge in foehn conditions.

gewusst: In a strong foehn it can be warmer in Altdorf in winter than in Ticino.
In foehn conditions you can sometimes see mountains from the Swiss Plateau that are more than 100 kilometres away.
There are foehn winds in other mountain ranges too; in North America a similar wind is called the Chinook.

teile.einleitung: Carl Linnaeus was a Swedish naturalist who brought order to the variety of living things. He invented a system in which every plant and animal species gets a unique name made of two words. Researchers all over the world still use this system today.
wichtigste: Carl Linnaeus lived in Sweden from 1707 to 1778.
His most famous work is called Systema Naturae; the first edition appeared in 1735.
In his system a scientific species name consists of two words.
The first word names the genus, for example Canis for the wolf, Canis lupus.
Linnaeus gave humans the name Homo sapiens.
In 1758 he correctly placed whales among the mammals.
In 1732 he went on a research expedition to Lapland.

abschnitte.text: Carl Linnaeus was born in 1707 in Råshult in southern Sweden, the son of a pastor. Even as a child he loved plants; his father had a large garden. He studied medicine and later became a professor at **Uppsala University**. In 1761 he was made a nobleman and from then on called himself **Carl von Linné**.

In 1732 the young Linnaeus travelled to **Lapland** in the far north. On this journey he covered long distances, partly on foot and partly by boat. He described unknown plants and animals and observed the life of the **Sami**, the indigenous people of Lapland. His notes were later published as a book.

In 1735 the first edition of his work **Systema Naturae** appeared; at that time it was only a few pages long. In it Linnaeus divided nature into three kingdoms: animals, plants and stones. Within the kingdoms he arranged living things into levels such as class, order, genus and species. In the famous 10th edition of 1758 he placed **whales** among the mammals and not among the fish.

Before Linnaeus, plants often had long Latin descriptions as names. Linnaeus established **binomial nomenclature**: every name consists of the **genus** and a second word for the species. The wolf is called Canis lupus, and the dog belongs to the same genus Canis. Linnaeus called humans **Homo sapiens**, which means wise human.

Linnaeus had the idea of a **flower clock**, in which flowers that open and close at fixed times of day show the time. His favourite flower was the delicate **twinflower**, which bears his name: Linnaea borealis. Many of his students travelled around the world as his “apostles” and collected plants. One of them, Daniel Solander, sailed with James Cook to the South Seas.

Zoologists officially start their naming with the 10th edition of Systema Naturae from **1758**, botanists with his work Species Plantarum from 1753. Even today every newly discovered species gets a two-part name according to Linnaeus's rules. In London the **Linnean Society** bears his name and looks after his collections. Linnaeus has also appeared on Swedish banknotes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of closely related species, for example all dog-like animals of the genus Canis.
The smallest basic unit in the system of living things, such as the wolf.
Naming every species with two Latin words.
The science of classifying living things.

gewusst: Even during his lifetime Linnaeus was called the “prince of botanists”.
The name Mammalia for the mammals comes from Linnaeus.
Linnaeus gave a scientific name to more than 10,000 plant and animal species.

teile.einleitung: The idea of a flat Earth says that the Earth is a disc and not a sphere. But more than 2,000 years ago Greek scholars already knew that the Earth is round. Today, photos from space and countless observations clearly show its spherical shape.
wichtigste: The Earth is a sphere that is slightly flattened at the poles.
Aristotle recognised the spherical shape from the round shadow of the Earth during lunar eclipses.
A ship that sails away disappears over the horizon from the bottom upwards.
Scholars in the Middle Ages knew that the Earth is a sphere.
Before Columbus's voyage in 1492, the argument was about the size of the Earth, not its shape.
Magellan's expedition was the first to sail all the way around the Earth, from 1519 to 1522.
The circumference of the Earth at the equator is about 40,000 kilometres.

abschnitte.text: **Flat Earth** means the idea that the Earth is a flat disc. In very early times some cultures pictured the world like that, such as the ancient Babylonians. From about 500 BC, however, the idea of a **spherical shape** became accepted among Greek scholars. Today we know precisely that the Earth is a sphere, slightly flattened at the poles. The diameter at the equator is only about 43 kilometres greater than from pole to pole.

Around 350 BC **Aristotle** gave several pieces of evidence for a round Earth. During a **lunar eclipse** the Earth casts a shadow on the Moon, and this shadow is always round. You also see different stars in the south than in the north, which is only possible on a sphere. When a ship sails away, the hull disappears first and the tip of the mast last behind the **horizon**. Around 240 BC Eratosthenes even calculated the circumference of the Earth.

abschnitte.titel: The myth about the Middle Ages
abschnitte.text: You often hear that people in the Middle Ages believed in a disc, but that is not true. The scholars of the Middle Ages, such as the monk Bede or Thomas Aquinas, knew about the spherical shape. At ceremonies, kings held an **orb** in their hand, a sphere as a symbol of the world. Before **Columbus's** voyage in 1492, the only argument was about how big the Earth is. Columbus greatly underestimated its size and believed he would soon reach Asia.

In 1519 a fleet under **Ferdinand Magellan** set out from Spain to sail west to the Spice Islands. Magellan himself died in the Philippines in 1521. But in 1522 the ship Victoria returned under Juan Sebastián Elcano with only 18 men of the original crew. This completed the first **circumnavigation of the world**, which showed that you can sail right around the Earth. Today aircraft fly around the world in less than two days.

Since space travel began, the Earth can be seen from outside. Famous photos are “Earthrise” from 1968, taken by Apollo 8, and **“Blue Marble”** from 1972. Astronauts on the **ISS** see the curved surface of the Earth from about 400 kilometres up. The **time zones** also show the spherical shape: when it is midday in Zurich, it is still early morning in New York, because the sun lights only half of the turning globe. Navigation systems such as GPS only work because satellites orbit the sphere.

The false belief that people in the Middle Ages thought the Earth was a disc only spread in the 19th century, partly through a biography of Columbus by the American Washington Irving. Today there are again people on the internet who claim that the Earth is flat. Their claims can be disproved with simple observations. Experts call this a **conspiracy theory**. The subject is therefore a good example of how to test claims against evidence.

begriffe.erklaerung: The line where the sky and the land or sea seem to meet.
When the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon and casts its shadow on the Moon.
A voyage by ship right around the whole Earth.
A claim that something is being kept secret, although the evidence is against it.

gewusst: Because of the flattening, the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point furthest from the centre of the Earth, not Mount Everest.
The circumference of the Earth over the two poles is about 67 kilometres shorter than the circumference at the equator.
Sailors in the ancient world already used the spherical shape to navigate by the stars.

teile.einleitung: The Encyclopédie was a huge French encyclopedia that began to appear in 1751. Edited by Denis Diderot and Jean-Baptiste le Rond d'Alembert, it set out to collect all the knowledge of its time and make it available to everyone. It is regarded as one of the most important works of the Enlightenment.
wichtigste: The Encyclopédie was edited by Diderot and d'Alembert.
The first volume appeared in 1751.
With its text and plate volumes it comprised 28 volumes in all.
Its aim was to make the knowledge of the time available to everyone.
It belongs to the intellectual movement of the Enlightenment.
The plate volumes showed workshops, tools and machines in especially great detail.
In 1759 the Encyclopédie was banned in France.
In Yverdon a separate, revised version in 58 volumes appeared from 1770 to 1780.

abschnitte.text: Its full title, translated, was “Encyclopedia, or a Systematic Dictionary of the Sciences, Arts, and Crafts”. The work was created in **Paris** and was originally only meant to be a translation of an English encyclopedia. Under **Denis Diderot** and **Jean-Baptiste le Rond d'Alembert** it became a completely new and much larger work. The first volume appeared in 1751 and the last in 1772. With 17 volumes of text and 11 volumes of plates, it comprised 28 volumes in all and more than 70,000 articles.

The Encyclopédie belongs to the **Enlightenment**, a movement of the 18th century. Its supporters wanted people to think for themselves and to rely on reason and observation rather than mere obedience. The encyclopedia was meant to make the **knowledge of the time** available to everyone, not just to scholars and nobles. Well-known thinkers such as Voltaire, Rousseau and Montesquieu wrote articles. Louis de Jaucourt was especially hard-working and wrote thousands of articles.

What was new was that the Encyclopédie also took **crafts** seriously. Diderot visited workshops and had craftspeople explain to him how they worked. In the **plate volumes**, detailed copperplate engravings showed workshops, tools and machines. You can see, for example, how paper, glass or needles were made. Today these pictures are a valuable source for understanding life in the 18th century.

Many articles carefully criticised the church and the power of the king. So the Encyclopédie had powerful opponents. In 1759 it was **banned** in France, and the Pope also put it on the list of forbidden books. D'Alembert withdrew, but Diderot carried on working in secret. The remaining volumes of text appeared later as a set with a false place of printing.

The work had a great effect in Switzerland too. In **Yverdon** in the canton of Vaud, the Italian-born scholar Fortunato Bartolomeo De Felice published his own revised version from 1770 to 1780. It comprised 58 volumes and was less critical of the church than the Paris original. For that reason it was read especially in Protestant areas. Yverdon was thus an important place for books and ideas of the Enlightenment.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large reference work that collects knowledge from many fields.
A movement in the 18th century that relied on reason and independent thinking.
A picture cut into a copper plate and then printed on paper.
The control or banning of books and opinions by those in power.

gewusst: Diderot worked on the Encyclopédie for more than 20 years, and in 1749, two years before the first volume, he spent several months in prison because of a critical piece of writing.
An article by d'Alembert about the city of Geneva caused a great dispute there, partly because he suggested the city should have a theatre.

teile.einleitung: The fossil record is the whole collection of all the fossils found on Earth. It is like a gigantic but incomplete history book of life. From it, researchers read which living things lived when and how they changed over millions of years.
wichtigste: Fossils are remains or traces of living things that lived a very long time ago.
Deeper layers of rock usually contain older fossils, because those layers were deposited first.
The fossil record has gaps, because only very few living things become fossils.
Transitional forms such as Archaeopteryx and Tiktaalik show how new animal groups arose.
Index fossils help to determine the age of layers of rock.
With radiometric dating, the age of rocks is measured in years.
About 540 million years ago, many animal groups appeared in the Cambrian explosion.

abschnitte.text: A **fossil** is a petrified remain of a living thing, for example a bone, a shell or the impression of a leaf. Footprints or feeding marks can also be preserved, and these are called **trace fossils**. All the known finds together form the **fossil record**. It ranges from tiny traces of bacteria to the skeletons of giant dinosaurs.

Rock is often deposited in **layers**, like sheets in a pile of paper. The lowest layers were deposited first and are therefore usually the oldest. This principle was already described in the 17th century by the Danish scientist Nicolaus Steno. Certain fossils occur only in layers from a short span of time, and these are called **index fossils**. Good examples are ammonites and trilobites.

To determine the exact age, **radiometric dating** is used. In it you measure how much of a radioactive substance in the rock has already decayed. Because this decay happens very evenly, it works like a clock. In this way we now know that the Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.

**Archaeopteryx** was found in limestone quarries in Bavaria. It had feathers like a bird but teeth, claws and a long tail like a dinosaur. The first skeleton became known in 1861, shortly after Charles Darwin published his book on the origin of species in 1859. **Tiktaalik** from the north of Canada lived about 375 million years ago and shows the change from fish to land animals.

Most dead living things are eaten or rot away before they can petrify. Only if a body is quickly covered by mud or sand can a fossil form. Soft animals such as jellyfish or worms are especially rarely preserved. That is why the fossil record has **gaps**, and every new find can close one.

A famous site is **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino, which has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003. Fish and marine reptiles from the Triassic, about 240 million years old, were found there. In the Jura and in the Alps, ammonites and sea urchins are also often found. They show that the area of today's Switzerland was once covered by a **sea**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A petrified remain or a trace of a living thing from prehistoric times.
A fossil that occurred only at a particular time and so reveals the age of a layer.
A living thing that has features of two different animal groups.
A time about 540 million years ago in which many new animal groups suddenly appeared.

gewusst: Only a little more than a dozen finds of Archaeopteryx are known today.
Some trace fossils are petrified dinosaur footprints, and such tracks have been discovered in the Swiss Alps and in the Jura too.
Researchers estimate that far less than one per cent of all the species that ever lived are known as fossils.

teile.einleitung: In a chemical reaction, substances turn into new substances with different properties. This happens all around us all the time, for example when cooking, when things rust or when a fire burns. Even in our bodies, countless chemical reactions take place every second.
wichtigste: In a chemical reaction, substances turn into new substances.
The starting substances are called reactants, the new substances products.
The atoms are kept; they are just rearranged.
Typical signs are a change of colour, gas bubbles, heat or light.
Examples are burning, rusting, baking and digestion.
Many reactions first need a trigger, for example a spark.
Chemists describe reactions with chemical equations.

abschnitte.text: In a **chemical reaction**, substances form that did not exist before. The substances at the start are called **reactants**, the new substances **products**. Bonds between atoms are broken and new ones are formed. The atoms themselves do not disappear; they just rearrange themselves. This is different from melting ice, because water stays water.

You can often spot a reaction by a **change of colour**, for example when iron rusts brown. Sometimes gas bubbles form, for example when you mix baking powder with vinegar. Many reactions give off heat or light, like a burning match. A solid substance or a new smell can also appear. Some reactions happen so slowly that you hardly notice them.

When **burning**, wood reacts with the oxygen in the air to form carbon dioxide, water and ash. When you bake a cake, the eggs, flour and sugar change because of the heat. In our bodies, digestion breaks food down into smaller building blocks. In **photosynthesis**, plants make sugar from water and carbon dioxide. A cut apple turning brown is also a chemical reaction.

In the 18th century the French chemist **Antoine Lavoisier** showed something important by weighing very precisely. In a reaction, the mass at the end is the same as at the start. This is called the **law of conservation of mass**. When wood burns it seems to disappear, but the substances escape into the air as gases. In a closed container the weight would stay the same.

Chemists write reactions down using formulas. One example is the reaction of hydrogen with oxygen to form water. It is written as 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O. The reactants are on the left, the products on the right, and the arrow shows the direction. There must be the same number of atoms of each kind on both sides.

Many reactions do not start by themselves; they need **activation energy**. A match only lights when you strike it on the rough strip. Heat speeds up most reactions and cold slows them down, which is why food keeps longer in the fridge. A **catalyst** is a substance that makes a reaction faster without being used up itself. In the body, enzymes do this job.

begriffe.erklaerung: A starting substance that is used up in a reaction.
A new substance that is formed in a reaction.
The energy needed for a reaction to start.
A substance that speeds up a reaction and is not used up in it.

gewusst: The fireworks on Swiss National Day on 1 August glow in many colours because different metal salts give off coloured light in the reactions.
In every cell of your body, thousands of chemical reactions take place at the same time every second.

teile.einleitung: CERN is the largest research centre for particle physics in the world. It lies near Geneva, right on the border between Switzerland and France. There, thousands of researchers study what the world is made of at the very smallest scale.
wichtigste: CERN is a European organisation for nuclear research based in Geneva.
It was founded in 1954, and Switzerland was part of it from the start.
The largest particle accelerator, the LHC, is a ring 27 kilometres long.
The LHC lies about 100 metres underground and reaches into France.
In 2012 the Higgs particle was detected at CERN.
The World Wide Web was invented at CERN in 1989.
Researchers from more than 100 countries work together at CERN.

abschnitte.text: The name **CERN** comes from the French “Conseil européen pour la recherche nucléaire”. The organisation was founded in 1954 by twelve European countries, including Switzerland. It was meant to bring researchers from Europe back together after the Second World War. Today more than 20 countries are members. The site lies in **Meyrin** near Geneva and stretches across the border into France.

The most important machine is the **Large Hadron Collider**, or LHC for short. It is a ring-shaped tunnel 27 kilometres round and lies about 100 metres below the ground. Inside it, tiny particles called **protons** are accelerated to almost the speed of light. Powerful magnets keep them on their circular path, and for this the magnets are cooled to almost minus 271 degrees Celsius. The LHC started operating in 2008.

In the LHC, particles coming from opposite directions are made to crash into each other. These **collisions** create new particles for tiny moments. Huge measuring devices, the **detectors**, record everything. The ATLAS detector is about as tall as a seven-storey building. Computers all over the world analyse the enormous amounts of data.

On 4 July 2012, CERN announced the detection of the **Higgs particle**. This particle explains why other particles have mass. The physicists Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize for it in 2013. **Antimatter** is also produced and studied at CERN. As early as the 1980s, important particles such as the W and Z bosons were discovered here.

In 1989 the British computer scientist **Tim Berners-Lee** proposed a system for sharing documents at CERN. This became the **World Wide Web** with web pages and links. The world's first website went online at CERN in 1991. CERN made the technology freely available in 1993 so that everyone could use it at no cost. Without this invention, the internet as we know it would not exist.

CERN is one of the most important research sites in Switzerland. Visitors can see an exhibition in the new Science Gateway visitor centre. The wooden building called the **Globe** is a well-known landmark in front of the site. Many school classes from Switzerland visit CERN every year. CERN is also a big employer for Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of the very smallest building blocks of matter.
A machine that makes tiny particles extremely fast.
A positively charged particle in the nucleus of an atom.
A particle detected in 2012 that explains why things have mass.
A measuring device that records particles and their tracks.

gewusst: The protons in the LHC whizz around the 27 kilometre ring more than 11,000 times in one second.
The computer that ran the first website had a note on it asking people not to switch it off.

teile.einleitung: First aid is the first set of measures with which you help an injured or suddenly ill person until experts arrive. It includes calling for help, calming the person down and knowing some simple techniques. Anyone can give first aid, including children.
wichtigste: At an accident you first pay attention to your own safety.
The ambulance emergency number in Switzerland is 144.
The air rescue service Rega can be reached on 1414.
The number 112 works throughout Europe and also in Switzerland.
In cases of poisoning, Tox Info Suisse helps on the number 145.
An unconscious person who is breathing normally is placed in the recovery position.
Small burns are cooled at once with cool water.

abschnitte.text: Before you help, you look around carefully and pay attention to your **own safety**. On a road, for example, you put up a warning triangle or stay at the edge. Then you think about what has happened and who needs help. Only after that do you act, call for help and look after the injured person.

For an ambulance you dial **144**, for the police 117 and for the fire brigade 118. Rega with its rescue helicopters can be reached on 1414. The European emergency number 112 also works in Switzerland. In cases of poisoning, **Tox Info Suisse** gives advice on 145 around the clock.

On the phone you say calmly **where** something has happened, what has happened and how many people are injured. You only hang up when the person taking the emergency call says so. After that you stay with the injured person, talk to them and comfort them. Just listening and staying there helps many people a great deal.

If a person does not react, you check whether they are breathing normally. If they are breathing, you place them in the **recovery position** so that the airways stay clear. You cover them up and watch their breathing until help arrives. If they are not breathing, you start **chest compressions** and, if possible, have someone fetch a defibrillator.

A small **burn** is cooled for about ten to twenty minutes with cool, but not ice-cold, water. With a nosebleed you bend the head slightly forward and press the nostrils together. Tipping the head back is wrong, because the blood then runs into the throat. Small grazes are rinsed clean and covered with a plaster.

In Switzerland everyone has to attend a **first aid course** to get a learner driving licence. Courses are offered, for example, by Samaritan associations and the Swiss Red Cross. There are also special courses for children in which you practise in a playful way. If you practise regularly, you stay calmer in an emergency.

begriffe.erklaerung: A telephone number on which you get help straight away.
A position in which an unconscious person lies safely on their side and can breathe freely.
A device that can use an electric shock to bring a fluttering heart back into the right rhythm.
Rhythmic pressing on the chest so that the blood keeps flowing.

gewusst: Modern defibrillators speak and explain step by step what you should do.
The emergency numbers 144, 117, 118 and 112 can be called on a mobile phone even without credit.
In Switzerland you can even be committing an offence if you do nothing although you could help.

teile.einleitung: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make food from sunlight. In doing so they give off oxygen, which people and animals need to breathe. Without photosynthesis there would be hardly any life on Earth.
wichtigste: In photosynthesis, plants turn sunlight into energy for growing.
For this they need light, water and carbon dioxide from the air.
From these they make sugar, their nutrient.
As a by-product, plants give off oxygen.
Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts, above all in the leaves.
The green pigment chlorophyll captures the sunlight.
Algae and some bacteria also carry out photosynthesis.

abschnitte.text: The word photosynthesis means roughly “putting together with light”. Plants take in water through their roots and **carbon dioxide** through tiny openings in their leaves. With the energy of sunlight they build **glucose** from them. In the process oxygen is formed, which the plant gives off into the air.

Photosynthesis takes place in small components of plant cells, the **chloroplasts**. They contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**, which captures the light. That is why leaves are green. The gases get in and out through tiny pores on the underside of the leaf.

Put simply, you can write: water plus carbon dioxide gives, with light, sugar plus oxygen. From six particles of carbon dioxide and six particles of water, one particle of **glucose** and six particles of oxygen are formed. The plant uses the sugar as energy or builds starch and wood from it. In this way a whole tree is made from air and water.

Almost all food on Earth goes back to photosynthesis. Animals eat plants, and people eat plants and animals. Photosynthesis also provides the **oxygen** in the air. A large part of it is produced by tiny algae in the sea, known as **phytoplankton**.

In the 17th century Jan Baptist van Helmont showed that a tree does not simply grow out of soil. In 1771 Joseph Priestley discovered that a plant can “improve” used-up air again. A little later Jan Ingenhousz found that plants need **light** for this. In the 20th century researchers worked out the individual chemical steps precisely.

begriffe.erklaerung: The green pigment of plants that captures sunlight.
A tiny part of a plant cell in which photosynthesis takes place.
A gas in the air that plants take in and people breathe out.
A sugar that plants make as energy.

gewusst: In autumn the chlorophyll is broken down, which is why yellow and red colours appear in the leaves.
The oxygen you are breathing in right now comes from the photosynthesis of plants and algae.
Coal and oil are the remains of living things that stored the energy of the sun millions of years ago.

teile.einleitung: DNA is the carrier of genetic information in the cells of all living things. It is like a huge set of building instructions that decides what a living thing looks like and how it works. Its shape is a twisted rope ladder, the double helix.
wichtigste: DNA is short for deoxyribonucleic acid; in German it is also called DNS.
It is the carrier of genetic information in cells.
DNA has the shape of a twisted rope ladder, the double helix.
James Watson and Francis Crick described this structure in 1953.
The building instructions are written with four building blocks: A, T, G and C.
A section of DNA with a particular instruction is called a gene.
Friedrich Miescher from Basel discovered DNA as early as 1869.

abschnitte.text: **DNA** stands for **deoxyribonucleic acid**. It is found in the nucleus of almost every cell of humans, animals and plants. It stores how a living thing is built, for example what colour its eyes are. DNA is passed on from parents to their children. That is why children often look like their parents.

DNA looks like a rope ladder that is twisted around itself. This shape is called a **double helix**. The rungs of the ladder are made of the four **bases** adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine. A always fits with T and G always with C. The order of these letters is the code for the genetic information.

In 1869 the Basel doctor **Friedrich Miescher**, working in Tübingen, found a new substance in cell nuclei. He called it nuclein; today it is called DNA. In 1953 **James Watson** and **Francis Crick** in Cambridge described the double helix. An X-ray image by the researcher Rosalind Franklin was important for this. Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962.

A person's DNA consists of about three billion base pairs. If you unrolled the DNA of a single cell, it would be about two metres long. But it is so thin and so tightly coiled that it fits into a tiny cell nucleus. Humans have about 20,000 **genes**. In 2003 the human genetic material was almost completely decoded for the first time in the **Human Genome Project**.

With DNA tests the police can link traces at a crime scene to a person. You can also find out who is related to whom. In medicine, DNA helps to detect inherited diseases and to develop new treatments. Researchers study DNA from old bones to learn more about Neanderthals. With genetic engineering, DNA can even be changed in a targeted way.

begriffe.erklaerung: The instructions that decide how a living thing is built and that are inherited.
The shape of DNA, like a twisted rope ladder.
One of the four building blocks A, T, G and C that make up the DNA code.
A section of DNA with the instructions for a particular feature.

gewusst: The DNA of all of a person's cells laid end to end would stretch from the Earth to the Sun and back many times.
Humans and chimpanzees share about 98 per cent of their DNA.

teile.einleitung: The endosymbiotic theory explains where important parts of our cells come from. It says that mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria that were taken in by a larger cell and went on living inside it. Out of this cooperation came the complex cells of plants, animals and fungi.
wichtigste: The biologist Lynn Margulis made the theory well known from 1967.
As early as 1905 the Russian botanist Konstantin Mereschkowski suggested that chloroplasts descend from symbionts.
Chloroplasts descend from cyanobacteria.
According to current knowledge, mitochondria descend from alphaproteobacteria.
Mitochondria have their own ring-shaped DNA, like bacteria.
New chloroplasts only form by the division of existing plastids.
When a cell takes in an alga that already has chloroplasts, this is called secondary endosymbiosis.

abschnitte.text: The cells of animals, plants and fungi contain small components called **organelles**. Two of them are special: the **mitochondria**, the power stations of the cell, and the **chloroplasts**, in which plants carry out photosynthesis. According to the endosymbiotic theory, these organelles used to be independent bacteria. A larger cell took them in but did not digest them. Instead the two lived together and both gained from it.

Living together for mutual benefit is called **symbiosis**. If one partner lives inside the other, it is called **endosymbiosis**. The bacterium that was taken in got protection and nutrients. In return the host cell got plenty of energy, or, with chloroplasts, sugar from sunlight. Over time the bacteria handed many of their genes over to the cell nucleus and could no longer live on their own.

Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own **ring-shaped DNA**, just like bacteria. They have their own **70S ribosomes**, which resemble the ribosomes of bacteria and are smaller than the cell's other ribosomes. They are surrounded by two envelopes, which fits with having been taken in. New chloroplasts and mitochondria only form by the division of existing ones; the cell cannot build them from scratch. Comparisons of genes show that chloroplasts descend from **cyanobacteria** and mitochondria from alphaproteobacteria.

As early as 1905 the Russian botanist **Konstantin Mereschkowski** suggested that chloroplasts descend from symbionts. For a long time this idea was hardly noticed or even laughed at. In 1967 the US biologist **Lynn Margulis** published an article that put the theory on a new footing. Her work was at first rejected by many scientific journals. Only when the DNA of the organelles could be studied did the theory become accepted, and today it is regarded as well supported.

The taking in of cyanobacteria by a cell is called **primary endosymbiosis**. From it came green algae, red algae and later land plants. Some cells later took in a whole alga that already had chloroplasts of its own; this is **secondary endosymbiosis**. Diatoms and the eyespot flagellate came about in this way, for example. These events were a very long time ago, with the taking in of mitochondria probably well over a billion years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small component in a cell with a particular job.
The power station of the cell, which gets energy from food.
A green organelle in which plants make sugar from sunlight.
Two living things living together in a way that benefits both.

gewusst: In each of your cells, often hundreds to thousands of mitochondria are at work, which were once bacteria.
There is a sea slug that takes chloroplasts from the algae it eats into its body and lets them carry on photosynthesis for a while.

teile.einleitung: In fact-checking you examine whether a claim is really true. Journalists do this, but anyone can learn it. It is especially important on the internet, where pictures and reports spread at lightning speed.
wichtigste: Fact-checking examines whether a claim is true.
With quotations you look for the original source.
With a reverse image search you can find out where a photo first appeared.
In lateral reading you check in other tabs what others write about a website.
The metadata of a photo file can reveal the time it was taken and the camera.
If two things increase at the same time, that does not mean one causes the other.
Before sharing, you should read more than just the headline.

abschnitte.text: In **fact-checking** you examine a statement step by step. You ask: who is claiming this, where does the information come from, and is there evidence? Many newspapers and news agencies have their own fact-checking teams. They check, for example, statements by politicians, pictures or viral videos.

A supposed quotation from a famous person should be traced back to the **original source**. Often it turns out that it has been shortened, changed or completely made up. With figures too it is worth looking at the original study. Reliable articles name their sources so that you can check them.

With a **reverse image search** you can find out where and when a photo first appeared on the internet. In this way you can tell whether an old picture is being passed off as a new one. The **metadata** of a photo file sometimes gives the time it was taken and the camera model. With pictures created by artificial intelligence, you look out for odd details such as hands, writing or shadows.

When you come across an unknown website, you do not only read on the site itself. In **lateral reading** you open other tabs and look at what others write about this website. In this way you find out who is behind it and whether the site is considered reliable. Professionals do this very quickly and so fall for deception less often.

If a risk rises from 1 to 2 cases per 10,000 people, “twice as high” sounds dramatic. In absolute terms, though, the risk has risen by only 0.01 percentage points. A **correlation** is also not proof of cause and effect. In summer, ice cream sales and swimming accidents rise at the same time, because both have a common cause, the heat.

Before sharing, read more than just the **headline**, because headlines can shorten or exaggerate. Check the date, because old reports often reappear. Be especially careful with reports that make you angry or afraid. And if you are unsure, better not share the report.

begriffe.erklaerung: The origin of a piece of information, for example a study or an original video.
A search in which you enter a picture instead of a word.
Hidden extra information in a file, such as the date and the camera.
Two things change at the same time, without one necessarily causing the other.

gewusst: Professionals often check an unknown website within a few minutes, because they immediately look at what others write about it.
Some photos shared as pictures of a current storm are in fact many years old.
Many social networks automatically delete metadata when photos are uploaded.

teile.einleitung: The Dunning-Kruger effect describes how people who are not very good at something often greatly overestimate their own ability. It is named after the two US psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger. The effect shows why it is so hard to see your own mistakes.
wichtigste: According to the Dunning-Kruger effect, people with little competence often overestimate their ability.
Justin Kruger and David Dunning published their well-known study in 1999.
According to the researchers, the weaker participants lack metacognition, that is, thinking about their own thinking.
A bank robber who believed lemon juice made him invisible inspired the research.
The best participants usually slightly underestimated their rank.
Dunning and Kruger received the Ig Nobel Prize in 2000.
Critics say that part of the effect comes from regression to the mean.

abschnitte.text: The **Dunning-Kruger effect** is a thinking bias. People with little knowledge in a field often think they are better than they are. The reason: to notice that you are doing something wrong, you need exactly the knowledge you are missing. Someone who does not know the rules of spelling, for example, also does not see their own mistakes. The ability to check your own thinking is called **metacognition**.

In 1995 a man in Pittsburgh in the USA robbed two banks without hiding his face. He had rubbed lemon juice on his face because he believed it made him invisible to security cameras. After all, lemon juice does work as **invisible ink**. Of course he was recognised on the camera images and quickly arrested. The psychologist David Dunning read about this and wondered how someone can be so convinced of something false.

Justin Kruger and David Dunning worked at **Cornell University** in the US state of New York. They had students take tests on humour, logical thinking and grammar. Afterwards everyone had to estimate how well they had done compared with the others. The weakest were in fact far behind, but on average placed themselves at about the 60th **percentile**, that is, in the better half. The best, on the other hand, slightly underestimated their rank, because they thought the others found the tasks just as easy.

In 2000 Dunning and Kruger received the **Ig Nobel Prize**, a fun prize for research that first makes you laugh and then makes you think. In science, however, the effect is also disputed. One statistical objection is **regression to the mean**: someone who does very badly can hardly misjudge themselves in any direction but upwards. Besides, most people generally think they are a bit better than average. So the effect is probably smaller than many people on the internet claim.

abschnitte.titel: What you can learn from it
abschnitte.text: The well-known curve with the “peak of overconfidence”, by the way, does not come from the original study but from the internet. All the same, there is a useful lesson in the effect. If you are learning something new, you should ask others for feedback. The more you know about a field, the better you see what you do not yet know. So doubting yourself is sometimes a sign that you have already learned a lot.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thinking about your own thinking and your own ability.
A rank from 1 to 100: someone in the 60th percentile is better than 60 per cent of the others.
A typical mistake that our brain often makes when judging things.
Extreme measurements are usually closer to the average the next time.

gewusst: Charles Darwin already wrote, in effect, that ignorance more often produces confidence than knowledge does.
The Ig Nobel Prize is awarded every year at Harvard University, often by real Nobel laureates.

teile.einleitung: A shape memory alloy is a metal that “remembers” its original shape. If you bend it and then warm it up, it springs back into its old shape by itself. The best-known example is Nitinol, made of nickel and titanium.
wichtigste: Shape memory alloys take on their original shape again when warmed.
The best-known one is Nitinol, a mixture of nickel and titanium.
The ending “NOL” stands for Naval Ordnance Laboratory, a research laboratory of the US Navy.
Behind it lies a change between two crystal structures, martensite and austenite.
Superelastic alloys can be bent a great deal and spring back by themselves.
In medicine they are used to make stents and wires for braces.
Flexible spectacle frames are also often made of such alloys.

abschnitte.text: An **alloy** is a mixture of several metals, just as brass is made of copper and zinc. Shape memory alloys are special alloys that can “remember” a shape. First you give them a shape at a high temperature, for example a spiral. If you later bend the metal straight while it is cold and then warm it, it returns to the stored spiral shape.

In a metal the atoms are arranged in a regular lattice, which is called the **crystal structure**. In shape memory alloys there are two structures: the cold, soft **martensite** and the warm, firmer **austenite**. In martensite the layers of atoms can easily shift against each other without the lattice breaking. On warming, the metal changes into austenite, and the atoms return to their old places.

Some alloys are set up so that they are already austenite at room temperature. If you bend them, the pressure briefly turns them into martensite, and when you let go they spring back at once. This property is called **superelasticity**. A wire of Nitinol can therefore be bent about ten times further than an ordinary steel wire without being permanently deformed.

In medicine, **stents** made of Nitinol are important: these are fine mesh tubes that keep narrowed blood vessels open. They are pushed into the vessel folded up, and there they unfold through the warmth of the body. In braces, superelastic wires pull the teeth gently and evenly into the right position. In everyday life you find such alloys in spectacle frames that can be bent without breaking.

The shape memory effect had already been observed in individual alloys before. At the beginning of the 1960s the researcher William Buehler discovered the properties of nickel-titanium at the **Naval Ordnance Laboratory** of the US Navy. From this came the name **Nitinol**: Ni for nickel, Ti for titanium and NOL for the laboratory. Today alloys of copper, zinc and aluminium are also used as shape memory metals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of two or more metals
A shape memory alloy made of nickel and titanium
The cold, easily deformed crystal structure
The warm crystal structure that the metal returns to on warming
A small mesh tube that keeps a narrow blood vessel open

gewusst: A bent Nitinol wire can straighten itself again in an instant in hot water.
Shape memory metals can produce great forces as they spring back and are therefore also used as small drives.
A Nitinol stent is set up so that it unfolds exactly at body temperature.

teile.einleitung: A research team is a group of people who want to find out something new together. Today almost all great discoveries are made in teams in which experts from different fields work together. A school class can be a small research team too.
wichtigste: In a research team, several people work on the same question.
Together you achieve more, because each member brings their own knowledge and skills.
What matters is listening, clear tasks and a fair division of work.
If members have different ideas, the team tests both with experiments.
Famous teams were, for example, Marie and Pierre Curie or Auguste Piccard with his assistant.
At CERN near Geneva, thousands of researchers from all over the world work together.
At ETH Zurich and other universities many teams do research.

abschnitte.text: A **research team** is a group that wants to answer a scientific question together. Usually there is a leader who keeps an overview. The other members take on parts of the work, for example measurements, calculations or writing a report. Teams can consist of two people or of thousands of people on several continents.

In a good team people **listen to each other** and take other ideas seriously. Every member gets a clear **task**, so that nothing is done twice. If there are two different ideas, both are tested with experiments instead of being argued about. At the end everyone brings their results together and discusses what they have learned.

The physicist **Marie Curie** and her husband Pierre Curie studied radioactive substances together in Paris. In 1898 they discovered the chemical elements polonium and radium. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 together with Henri Becquerel. In 1931 the Swiss **Auguste Piccard** was the first to rise into the **stratosphere** in a gas balloon with his assistant Paul Kipfer.

**CERN** is a large European research centre near Geneva, founded in 1954. There the particle accelerator **LHC** lies in a tunnel about 27 kilometres long under the border between Switzerland and France. Thousands of people from many countries work on individual experiments. The World Wide Web was also invented at CERN in 1989.

abschnitte.titel: Many experts for one space probe
abschnitte.text: Anyone building a **space probe** needs quite different experts. Engineers design the craft, physicists calculate the flight path and computer scientists write the programs. Chemists, geologists and technicians are often involved too. Such projects last many years and only succeed if everyone **works together** closely.

abschnitte.titel: Research in Switzerland and in class
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland many teams do research at universities such as **ETH Zurich**, EPFL in Lausanne or at the cantonal universities. At school too you can form a class research team. One child measures, one writes things down, one takes photos and one presents the results. In this way you learn how real **science** works.

begriffe.erklaerung: An idea that you want to test with an experiment.
Each team member takes on a particular part of the work.
A layer of the atmosphere about 10 to 50 kilometres above the ground.
A huge machine that makes tiny particles very fast and lets them crash into each other.

gewusst: Some scientific articles from CERN have several thousand authors.
Marie Curie is the only person to have received Nobel Prizes in two different natural sciences, physics and chemistry.
Auguste Piccard's grandson Bertrand Piccard was one of the first to circle the Earth in a balloon without landing, with a team, in 1999.

teile.einleitung: Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist. In 1869 he drew up the first comprehensive periodic table of the elements, a table that arranges all the chemical elements. He even predicted elements that nobody knew about at the time.
wichtigste: Dmitri Ivanovich Mendeleev lived from 1834 to 1907.
He was born in Tobolsk in Siberia.
In 1869 he published his periodic table of the elements.
He arranged the elements by their atomic mass and their properties.
In his table he left gaps for elements that were still unknown.
Elements such as gallium and germanium were later discovered exactly as he had predicted.
The element mendelevium is named after him.

abschnitte.text: **Dmitri Mendeleev** was born in Tobolsk in Siberia in 1834. He was the youngest of many brothers and sisters. After his father's death, his mother moved with him to St Petersburg so that he could study. There he later became professor of **chemistry**. He died in St Petersburg in 1907.

In the middle of the 19th century about 60 **chemical elements** were known. Mendeleev looked for a way to order them so that he could explain them better to his students. He wrote down the elements with their properties and sorted them by their **atomic mass**. He noticed that similar properties repeated at regular intervals. In 1869 he published his table based on this.

Where no known element fitted, Mendeleev simply left a **gap**. He claimed that elements were missing there that would still be discovered. He even predicted how heavy they would be and how they would behave. Gallium was discovered in 1875, scandium in 1879 and germanium in 1886. Their properties matched his predictions astonishingly well.

Today's **periodic table** contains 118 elements. They are arranged by the number of their protons, the so-called atomic number. The rows are called **periods** and the columns groups. Elements in the same group behave in a similar way chemically, such as the noble gases in the last column. A table like this hangs on the wall in almost every chemistry classroom.

At about the same time as Mendeleev, the German chemist Lothar Meyer developed a similar table. But Mendeleev is usually named as the father of the periodic table, above all because of his predictions. The artificial element with atomic number 101 is called **mendelevium** in his honour. A crater on the Moon also bears his name. The UN declared 2019, 150 years after his table, the International Year of the Periodic Table.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic substance made of only one kind of atom, for example gold or oxygen.
A table in which all the chemical elements are arranged.
How heavy an atom of an element is.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, by which the elements are sorted today.

gewusst: There is a legend that Mendeleev saw the arrangement of the elements in a dream.
Mendeleev is said to have sorted the elements using cards, rather like in a card game.

teile.einleitung: The candela is the unit of measurement for luminous intensity, in other words how strongly a light source shines in a particular direction. It is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units. Its name comes from the Latin word for candle.
wichtigste: Luminous intensity is measured in candelas.
The Latin word “candela” means candle.
A candle flame has a luminous intensity of roughly 1 candela.
The unit symbol of the candela is cd.
The candela is the SI base unit that takes into account how sensitive the human eye is.
Its definition uses green light.
Related units are the lumen for the amount of light and the lux for how brightly a surface is lit.

abschnitte.text: The **candela** measures **luminous intensity**, that is, how brightly a light source shines in a particular direction. Its symbol is **cd**. The name comes from the Latin word for candle. An ordinary candle flame really does shine with about one candela.

The candela is one of the seven **SI base units**, together with the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and mole. All other units can be derived from these base units. The candela is the only one that has to do with the human eye. It takes into account how sensitive our eyes are to different colours.

Our eyes are most sensitive to **green light**. That is why the definition of the candela uses green light with a precisely fixed frequency. Red or blue light with the same energy looks less bright to us. So the candela does not simply measure energy, but brightness as we perceive it.

Besides the candela there are two related units. The **lumen** tells you how much light a lamp gives off in total; you can find it on the packaging of LED bulbs, for example. The **lux** measures how brightly a surface is lit, such as a school desk. For comfortable reading, a desk needs a lot more lux than a corridor.

In the past, light was compared with real candles, but candles never burn exactly the same. So different countries had different candle units, for example the Hefner candle in Germany. Around the middle of the 20th century, countries agreed internationally on the candela. Since then its definition has been made more precise several times.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly a light source shines in a particular direction.
Unit for the total amount of light a lamp gives off.
Unit for how brightly a surface is lit.
Internationally agreed units of measurement that are used almost everywhere in the world.

gewusst: A powerful lighthouse can reach a luminous intensity of many hundreds of thousands of candelas.
The brightness of mobile phone and computer screens is often given in candelas per square metre.
The candela is the only SI base unit that is based on human perception.

teile.einleitung: Epidemiology is the science that studies how often diseases occur, who they affect and why. It counts the sick, compares groups and looks for causes. In this way it helps to prevent diseases and to keep whole populations healthy.
wichtigste: Epidemiology studies the spread and the causes of diseases in the population.
John Snow, who traced a source of cholera in London in 1854, is regarded as its founder.
Incidence measures the new cases in a particular period.
Prevalence says how many people are ill at a particular time.
Case fatality says what share of those who fall ill die of a disease.
Cohort studies follow groups of people over many years.
In Switzerland the Federal Office of Public Health monitors the spread of infectious diseases.

abschnitte.text: The word **epidemiology** comes from Greek and means roughly “the study of what comes upon the people”. While a doctor treats an individual person, epidemiologists look at whole groups. They ask, for example: how many people have flu, at what age, in what place? They study not only infectious diseases but also heart disease, allergies or accidents. Their most important tool is numbers and **statistics**.

In 1854 hundreds of people in the London district of Soho died of **cholera** within a few days. At the time many people believed that bad air caused the disease. The doctor **John Snow** marked the deaths on a street map and saw that they clustered around a water pump in Broad Street. He had the pump handle removed, and the number of new cases fell. For this, Snow is regarded as the founder of modern epidemiology.

**Incidence** counts the new cases in a period. If 30 out of 10,000 people in a town fall ill in one year, that is 300 cases per 100,000 people. **Prevalence** says what share of the population is ill at a particular time. **Case fatality** says how many of those who fall ill die of the disease. A disease that occurs with a steady, similar frequency in a region is called endemic; if it suddenly spreads strongly, it is called an epidemic, or, worldwide, a pandemic.

In a **cohort study**, a group of people is followed over years and it is recorded who newly falls ill. If, for example, 1,000 smokers are compared with 1,000 non-smokers and 40 fall ill against 10, the **relative risk** is 4. In this way the Britons Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill showed around 1950 that smoking causes lung cancer. Researchers have to watch out for **confounders**, that is, hidden factors that create an apparent link. Someone who buys lighters more often, for example, does not have a higher cancer risk because of the lighters but because they smoke.

In Switzerland, doctors and laboratories must report certain infectious diseases to the **Federal Office of Public Health**. In this way it is noticed early when, for example, measles or flu are spreading. During the Covid-19 pandemic from 2020, epidemiological figures were in the news every day. Well-known research centres are the universities of Bern, Zurich, Basel, Geneva and Lausanne. The Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute in Allschwil near Basel studies diseases such as malaria worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of new cases of a disease in a particular period.
The share of people who are ill at a particular time.
When a disease suddenly occurs much more often in a region than usual.
A hidden disturbing factor that can create a false link.
A group of people that a study follows over a longer time.

gewusst: John Snow's map with the cholera deaths is regarded as one of the most famous maps in the history of science.
In London today there is a replica of the old pump without a handle at the spot.
The Framingham study in the USA has been following the residents of a small town and their descendants since 1948.

teile.einleitung: The kingfisher is a small bird with a brilliant blue back and an orange belly that lives by streams, rivers and lakes. It dives into the water at lightning speed to catch small fish. Its beak is so well shaped that it inspired engineers in Japan to build a better high-speed train.
wichtigste: The kingfisher has a brilliant blue back.
It eats mainly small fish.
It dives into the water almost without a splash.
In Switzerland you can watch it by streams, rivers and lakes.
It makes its nest in a tunnel in an earth bank.
A Japanese high-speed train was given a nose modelled on the kingfisher's beak.
The train with the new nose no longer made a loud tunnel boom and used less electricity.

abschnitte.text: The **kingfisher** is about as big as a sparrow, but looks stocky because of its large head and short tail. Its back shines **blue** to turquoise, and its belly is orange-red. The blue does not come from pigment but from tiny structures in the feathers that bend the light. Its long, pointed beak looks like a dagger. Because of its colours it is also called a “flying jewel”.

The kingfisher lives by slow-flowing, clear **streams, rivers and lakes**. In Switzerland you see it mainly on the Swiss Plateau, for example on the Aare, the Reuss or the Rhine. It needs clear water so that it can see the fish. It also needs branches above the water from which it can hunt. In very cold winters, when the waters freeze over, it can hardly find food, and many kingfishers die.

The kingfisher eats mainly **small fish**, and also water insects and tadpoles. It sits still on a branch and watches the water. When it sees a fish, it plunges in head first and enters the water **almost without a splash**. With the fish in its beak it flies back to the branch and knocks it against the wood. Then it swallows it head first.

The kingfisher does not build its nest in trees but in a **tunnel in a steep earth bank**, usually right by the water. With their beaks the parents dig a tunnel that is often half a metre long or more. At the end there is a small chamber in which the female lays several white eggs. The young are fed with fish until they can fly. Because many rivers have been straightened, such natural steep banks are often missing today.

In Japan the **Shinkansen** high-speed train used to enter tunnels at high speed. In doing so it pushed the air ahead of it, and on leaving the tunnel there was a loud **boom**. The engineer Eiji Nakatsu, a birdwatcher, thought of the kingfisher, which moves from water to air without a splash. The train was given a long nose modelled on the kingfisher's beak. The new train was quieter and faster and used less electricity, an example of **biomimetics**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technology that copies solutions from nature.
A colour created by tiny structures instead of by pigment.
A steep bank of earth or sand by a river or lake.
Hunting in which an animal waits quietly and then strikes at lightning speed.

gewusst: The kingfisher can hover on the spot in flight above the water, rather like a helicopter.
The German name Eisvogel probably does not come from the word for ice but from an old word for shining or shimmering.

teile.einleitung: Daniel Kahneman was an Israeli-American psychologist who studied how people make decisions and why they often make thinking errors in the process. Although he was a psychologist, he received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002. His book about fast and slow thinking became a bestseller around the world.
wichtigste: Daniel Kahneman lived from 1934 to 2024.
He received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002.
With Amos Tversky he developed prospect theory in 1979.
Loss aversion means that losses hurt more than gains of the same size give pleasure.
In his 2011 book “Thinking, Fast and Slow” he describes two systems of thinking.
System 1 works quickly, automatically and intuitively; System 2 works slowly and deliberately.
With Olivier Sibony and Cass Sunstein he wrote the book “Noise”.

abschnitte.text: Daniel Kahneman was born in **Tel Aviv** in 1934 and grew up in Paris. As a Jewish child he survived the German occupation there during the Second World War. Later he studied psychology in Jerusalem and in the USA. Among other places he taught at **Princeton University**, and he died in March 2024.
