abschnitte.text: **DNA** is a long molecule that looks like a twisted rope ladder, called a double helix. The rungs of the ladder are made of four building blocks, the **bases** adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine. Adenine always fits with thymine and guanine always with cytosine. Because the pairs firmly belong together, you can read the matching opposite strand from one strand. The cell uses exactly this in **replication**, when it doubles its DNA.

Replication begins at particular places, the **origins of replication**. There the enzyme **helicase** opens the double helix by separating the base pairs from each other. This creates a Y-shaped point, the replication fork. Because the DNA in front of the fork becomes more and more twisted, other enzymes relax it again, in bacteria for example **DNA gyrase**. Bacteria such as Escherichia coli usually have only one starting point; in humans there are tens of thousands.

**DNA polymerase** reads the old strand and attaches matching building blocks, the nucleotides, to the new strand. But it cannot start from nothing; it can only add on to an existing 3' end. That is why an enzyme called primase first lays down a short starting piece, the **primer**. The polymerase works in only one direction, so one strand is copied in one go, the leading strand. The other one, the lagging strand, is made in short pieces, the **Okazaki fragments**, which **DNA ligase** glues together at the end.

DNA polymerase has a built-in correction function called **3' to 5' exonuclease activity**. If it inserts a wrong building block, it notices, removes it straight away and puts in the right one. Together with other repair systems, this leaves only about one mistake per billion copied building blocks. That is roughly as if you copied out a thousand thick books by hand and made only a single typing error. If a mistake does remain, it is called a **mutation**.

James Watson and Francis Crick described the double helix in 1953 and already suspected how it is copied. In 1958 Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl proved with a famous experiment that replication is **semi-conservative**. They first grew bacteria in heavy nitrogen and then in light nitrogen, and were able to separate the DNA by weight. Arthur Kornberg discovered the first DNA polymerase in 1956 and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1959. Elizabeth Blackburn, Carol Greider and Jack Szostak received the Nobel Prize in 2009 for discovering **telomerase**.

At the ends of the chromosomes there are protective caps, the **telomeres**. Because the polymerase cannot copy the very end of the lagging strand, the telomeres get a little shorter with each cell division. When they are too short, the cell stops dividing, which is linked to ageing. The enzyme **telomerase** lengthens the ends again, above all in stem cells and in many cancer cells. That is why telomerase is very interesting for cancer research.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single building block of DNA, made of sugar, phosphate and a base.
A protein that does a particular chemical job in the cell, like a small tool.
A short starting piece to which DNA polymerase can attach new building blocks.
A short piece of DNA that forms on the lagging strand and is later joined to others.
Half kept: each new DNA contains one old strand and one newly built strand.

gewusst: If you unrolled the DNA from a single human cell, it would be about two metres long.
Okazaki fragments are named after the Japanese research couple Reiji and Tsuneko Okazaki.
A gut bacterium can copy all its genetic material in less than an hour.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Federal Institute of Metrology, or METAS for short, is Switzerland's national institute for precise measures and measurements. It makes sure that a metre, a kilogram or a second is the same everywhere in Switzerland. It also provides the country's official time with atomic clocks.
wichtigste: METAS stands for the Swiss Federal Institute of Metrology.
It is located in Wabern near Bern.
Metrology means the science of measuring.
With its atomic clocks, METAS provides the official time of Switzerland.
Scales in shops must be calibrated regularly so that nobody is cheated.
With a Kibble balance, METAS can determine the kilogram using a constant of nature.
Since 2013 METAS has been a public institution.

abschnitte.text: The word **metrology** comes from Greek and means the science of measuring. It is not to be confused with meteorology, the study of the weather. Measuring means comparing a quantity with a fixed unit, for example a length with the metre. For this to work, everyone has to use the same units. Worldwide, the **International System of Units**, abbreviated SI, applies for this.

METAS is located in **Wabern** in the municipality of Köniz near Bern. Since 2013 it has been an independent public institution of the federal government. Physicists, engineers and technicians work here in laboratories where temperature and vibrations are carefully controlled. They keep the national standards, which are the most precise reference measures in Switzerland. Companies, hospitals and laboratories can have their measuring devices checked there.

METAS runs several **atomic clocks**, which measure time extremely precisely. They use the regular vibrations of atoms, for example of caesium. Their signals produce the official time of Switzerland. This time is compared with institutes all over the world and feeds into international world time. Computers, station clocks and mobile phone networks need such precise time.

When you buy cheese in a shop, you pay by weight. That is why scales in shops must be **calibrated** regularly, so that customers are not cheated. Petrol pumps at filling stations, water meters, electricity meters and police radar devices are also checked. Many of these checks are carried out by cantonal inspectors, and METAS sets the rules for them. So you can rely on a kilo of apples in Geneva being the same as in St Gallen.

In the past the kilogram was defined by a metal cylinder near Paris, the **prototype kilogram**. Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined using a constant of nature, the Planck constant. To determine it this way, you need an especially precise balance, the **Kibble balance**. It compares the weight of an object with an electromagnetic force. METAS has developed its own Kibble balance and is therefore one of only a few institutes worldwide that can do this.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of precise measuring.
To have a measuring device officially checked to see whether it measures correctly.
A very precise clock that uses the vibrations of atoms to keep time.
An especially precise reference measure for a unit.

gewusst: A good atomic clock is out by less than one second in many millions of years.
In 1875 Switzerland was one of the countries that signed the international Metre Convention.

teile.einleitung: Felix Bloch was a physicist from Zurich who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1952. He developed methods of nuclear magnetic resonance, on which magnetic resonance imaging in hospitals is based today. He was also the first Director-General of CERN in Geneva.
wichtigste: Felix Bloch was born in Zurich in 1905.
In 1928 he took his doctorate in Leipzig as Werner Heisenberg's first doctoral student.
After emigrating he did research at Stanford University in the USA.
In 1952 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for new methods of nuclear magnetic resonance.
He shared the Nobel Prize with the US physicist Edward Purcell.
In 1954 he became the first Director-General of CERN in Geneva.
The Bloch theorem and the Bloch wall bear his name.

abschnitte.text: **Felix Bloch** was born on 23 October 1905 in Zurich. He studied at ETH Zurich, first engineering and then physics. In 1928 he took his doctorate in Leipzig as the first doctoral student of **Werner Heisenberg**, one of the founders of quantum mechanics. Bloch died in Zurich in 1983.

Bloch came from a Jewish family. When the Nazis came to power in Germany in 1933, he left the country. In 1934 he went to **Stanford University** in California, where he did research for most of his life. Later he also became an American citizen.

In a magnetic field, atomic nuclei behave like tiny spinning tops. In 1946 Bloch and Edward Purcell independently found methods for measuring this behaviour precisely. This **nuclear magnetic resonance** shows which atoms and building blocks a substance consists of. For this both received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics jointly in 1952.

From nuclear magnetic resonance, **magnetic resonance imaging**, or MRI, was later developed. With it, precise pictures of the inside of the body can be made without X-rays. Today there is an MRI scanner in almost every larger hospital. In chemistry the method helps to work out the structure of molecules.

As a young researcher, Bloch described how **electron waves** travel in a regular crystal lattice. This Bloch theorem is still a foundation of solid-state physics and helps to explain why some substances conduct electricity. The **Bloch wall** is named after him and is the transition zone between two magnetic areas. Many terms in physics therefore bear his name.

In 1954 Bloch became the first **Director-General of CERN** in Geneva. CERN had only just been founded so that European countries could do particle physics together. Bloch stayed only about a year and then returned to Stanford University. He is regarded as one of the most important Swiss physicists of the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: A famous prize for outstanding achievements in science, literature and peace.
A method in which the behaviour of atomic nuclei in a magnetic field is measured.
A method that uses magnets and radio waves to make pictures of the inside of the body.
A person writing a doctoral thesis in order to gain a doctorate.

gewusst: CERN, which Bloch led as its first Director-General, now runs the largest particle accelerator in the world.
Without Bloch's research there would probably be no MRI scans, which are carried out in hospitals every day.
Bloch and Purcell discovered their measuring methods almost at the same time but independently, at two different universities.

teile.einleitung: A university of applied sciences is a higher education institution where studies are especially close to practice. In Switzerland it combines teaching with applied research, often together with companies. Many students come to a university of applied sciences after an apprenticeship with a vocational baccalaureate.
wichtigste: Universities of applied sciences offer practice-oriented teaching and applied research.
The typical route is through an apprenticeship and a vocational baccalaureate.
With an academic baccalaureate you usually also need a year of experience of the world of work.
Universities of applied sciences award bachelor's and master's degrees.
Doctorates are only available in cooperation with universities (as of 2025).
The first Swiss universities of applied sciences started at the end of the 1990s.
The HES-SO in western Switzerland has schools in seven cantons.

abschnitte.titel: What is a university of applied sciences?
abschnitte.text: A **university of applied sciences** is a higher education institution with a strong link to practice. You learn theory there but apply it straight away in projects, placements and laboratories. In German-speaking countries these schools are called Fachhochschulen. In Germany they are now often called universities of applied sciences too.

The basis was a federal law on universities of applied sciences from 1995. At the end of the 1990s the first Swiss universities of applied sciences began operating. They grew out of earlier higher technical colleges, such as engineering schools and schools for business or design. Today, together with universities and **universities of teacher education**, they form part of Switzerland's higher education landscape.

abschnitte.titel: Universities of applied sciences in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: The large public ones include the Bern University of Applied Sciences, the University of Applied Sciences and Arts Northwestern Switzerland and the Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts. In the canton of Zurich there are the ZHAW and the Zurich University of the Arts, among others. In Ticino there is SUPSI. The **HES-SO** in western Switzerland has schools in seven cantons.

The typical route is through an **apprenticeship** with a **vocational baccalaureate**. Someone who has trained as an electronics technician, for example, can then study electrical engineering. With an academic baccalaureate you usually also need at least one year of experience of the world of work. For art, music or health subjects there is often an entrance examination too.

You can study engineering, computer science, business, architecture, social work, health, design, music and much more. After usually three years of full-time study you receive a **bachelor's degree**, and after that you can do a **master's**. Swiss universities of applied sciences may not award their own doctorates (as of 2025). However, a doctorate is possible in cooperation with a university.

Universities of applied sciences very often do research together with **companies** and public institutions. The work deals with concrete problems, for example new machines, better care in hospitals or saving energy in buildings. Students often take part in such projects. In this way new knowledge quickly reaches practice.

begriffe.erklaerung: A qualification taken alongside an apprenticeship that opens the way to a university of applied sciences.
The first higher education qualification, usually after three years of study.
A further higher education qualification after the bachelor's.
Research that aims to solve a concrete problem from practice.

gewusst: In Switzerland you can go from an apprenticeship through a university of applied sciences all the way to a master's degree.
Musicians, actors and designers also study at universities of applied sciences in Switzerland.
Many final projects at universities of applied sciences are carried out for a company.

teile.einleitung: An experiment is a planned test with which researchers check an idea. Instead of just guessing, they put a question to nature and look carefully at what happens. Experiments are the most important tool of the natural sciences.
wichtigste: Researchers carry out experiments to check an idea with a planned test.
The idea you want to test is called a hypothesis.
In a good experiment you change only one thing and keep everything else the same.
A control group serves as a comparison; nothing is changed for it.
Results are measured and written down precisely.
An experiment must be repeatable so that others can check the result.
An experiment that disproves the idea also brings new knowledge.

abschnitte.text: An experiment is a test under controlled conditions. You begin with a question, for example: do beans grow in the dark? Then you put forward a **hypothesis**, that is, a reasoned idea. With the experiment you check whether this idea is right or not.

First you put forward a question and a hypothesis. Then you plan the test and decide what you will measure. Then you carry out the test and write all the **observations** in a record. At the end you analyse the results and draw a conclusion.

In a fair experiment you change only one single quantity, the **variable**. If you want to know whether light makes plants grow, you put one plant in the light and an identical one in the dark. Both get the same amount of water and the same soil. The plant with no change is called the **control group**.

A single result may be down to chance. That is why researchers repeat an experiment several times. Other experts all over the world should be able to repeat the test and get the same result. This **reproducibility** makes science reliable.

Around 1600 Galileo Galilei used balls on inclined planes to study how things fall. Gregor Mendel crossed peas for years and so found the rules of inheritance. Today huge experiments run at **CERN** near Geneva, in which tiny particles crash into each other. Children can also experiment in the kitchen, for example with vinegar and baking powder.

With experiments the rule is: safety first. At school you wear **safety glasses** for chemistry experiments. You only experiment with fire, electricity or unknown substances together with an adult. You never eat or drink anything that is being used for an experiment.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reasoned idea that you check with an experiment.
The quantity you deliberately change or measure in an experiment.
A part of the test in which you change nothing, so that you can compare.
A precise written note of what you did and observed.

gewusst: The word experiment comes from the Latin experimentum and means test or trial.
The largest particle accelerator in the world at CERN has a ring about 27 kilometres round.
Many important discoveries, such as penicillin, came about through an experiment that went differently from planned.

teile.einleitung: Daniel Peter was a Swiss businessman from the canton of Vaud who was the first to make milk chocolate successfully. Thanks to his invention, Switzerland became a world-famous chocolate country. His company is now part of the Nestlé group.
wichtigste: Daniel Peter lived from 1836 to 1919 and worked in Vevey on Lake Geneva.
Before he made chocolate, he was a candle maker.
He married the daughter of the chocolate maker François-Louis Cailler.
For a long time it was difficult to combine milk with chocolate, because the water in the milk spoiled the mixture.
Using condensed milk, he made the first successful milk chocolate.
His neighbour Henri Nestlé helped him with his knowledge of milk products.
He sold his milk chocolate under the name “Gala Peter”.
In 1929 the company of Peter, Cailler and Kohler became part of Nestlé.

abschnitte.text: Daniel Peter was born in **1836** in **Moudon** in the canton of Vaud and died in Vevey in 1919. As a young man he worked as a **candle maker**. But paraffin lamps gradually replaced candles, and business became harder. He married Fanny Cailler, the daughter of the chocolate pioneer **François-Louis Cailler**, and turned to chocolate.

In the past there was only dark chocolate, which people often enjoyed as a drink. Many tried to mix in milk so that the chocolate would taste milder. But fresh milk contains a lot of **water**, and that made the chocolate mixture go mouldy or lumpy. Daniel Peter worked on this problem for many years.

The breakthrough came with **condensed milk**, that is, thickened milk with little water. His neighbour in **Vevey**, the businessman **Henri Nestlé**, knew a great deal about milk products and supported him. In 1875 Peter succeeded in making a first milk chocolate, which he then went on improving. In 1887 he launched the brand **“Gala Peter”**; the Greek word gala means milk.

Peter founded his chocolate company in Vevey in 1867. Later he joined forces with the company of Jean-Jacques Kohler, and in 1911 also with Cailler, which created Peter, Cailler, Kohler. In **1929** this company became part of **Nestlé**. The Cailler brand is still made today in Broc in the canton of Fribourg.

Milk chocolate became a huge export success and made **Swiss chocolate** famous worldwide. In 1879 Rodolphe Lindt in Bern invented **conching**, which makes chocolate melt especially smoothly. Together with pioneers such as Cailler, Suchard and Tobler, this created a strong chocolate industry. Today people in Switzerland eat a particularly large amount of chocolate per person.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thickened milk from which a large part of the water has been removed.
Chocolate made from cocoa, sugar and milk, which is lighter and milder than dark chocolate.
Stirring and warming the chocolate mixture for a long time so that it becomes fine and smooth.
Someone who founds and runs their own company.

gewusst: It took Daniel Peter about eight years before his milk chocolate really worked.
The name “Gala” comes from Greek and simply means milk.

teile.einleitung: The Jungfraujoch research station is one of the highest research stations in Europe. It lies in the Bernese Oberland in the middle of the Alps, between the peaks of the Jungfrau and the Mönch. Up here, experts from all over the world study the air, the weather and the sky.
wichtigste: The Jungfraujoch is a glaciated saddle between the Jungfrau and the Mönch in the Bernese Alps.
The weather observatory with the silver dome is called the Sphinx and lies at more than 3,500 metres.
Researchers there mainly measure the make-up of the air and the weather.
The air at this altitude is very clean, because cities and factories are far away.
You reach the Jungfraujoch with the Jungfrau Railway, which runs mostly through a tunnel.
The Great Aletsch Glacier, the longest glacier in the Alps, begins at the Jungfraujoch.
Even in high summer there is snow and ice up there.

abschnitte.text: The Jungfraujoch lies at about 3,460 metres above sea level on the border between the cantons of **Bern** and **Valais**. To the left and right, the peaks of the Jungfrau and the Mönch rise into the sky. On the southern side the eternal ice spreads out, because this is where the **Great Aletsch Glacier** begins. Because it lies so high, the snow never melts completely, even in summer.

The research station itself was built into the rock at the beginning of the 1930s. A little higher up, the **Sphinx Observatory** with its striking dome sits on a rocky peak. It lies at more than 3,500 metres and can be reached by a lift through the mountain. In the rooms of the **High Altitude Research Station** there are laboratories, instruments and even bedrooms for the researchers.

On the Jungfraujoch the **air** is studied round the clock. Instruments determine, for example, how much carbon dioxide and other **greenhouse gases** are in the atmosphere. Tiny particles of dust, known as **aerosols**, are also measured, for example desert dust from the Sahara. These long series of measurements help to understand climate change better. The station is therefore part of a worldwide network of measuring stations.

You get up there with the **Jungfrau Railway**, which starts at Kleine Scheidegg. It runs through a long tunnel inside the Eiger and the Mönch. The railway opened in 1912 and was a technical sensation at the time. Jungfraujoch station is regarded as the highest railway station in Europe, which is why the place is also called **Top of Europe**.

Around the Jungfraujoch lies an enormous landscape of rock, firn and ice. The area is part of the **UNESCO World Heritage Site** Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch. The Aletsch Glacier is more than 20 kilometres long and one of the best-known stretches of ice in the world. Here researchers also observe how much the **glaciers** are shrinking because of warming.

On the Jungfraujoch, experts from many countries work together. Besides air and weather, **cosmic radiation** and the sun were also studied here in the past. Because the measurements have been running for decades, they are especially valuable. In this way you can see exactly how the **atmosphere** changes over a long time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building with instruments for observing the sky, the weather or the air.
A dip or pass between two mountain peaks.
A gas in the air that holds heat, for example carbon dioxide.
Tiny particles of dust, soot or droplets floating in the air.

gewusst: The air on the Jungfraujoch is so clean that even the smallest amounts of substances from far-off countries can be detected there.
The Jungfrau Railway runs almost the whole way through a tunnel inside the mountain, with windows in the north face of the Eiger on the way.
When Sahara dust blows over the Alps, it sometimes colours the snow around the station reddish.

teile.einleitung: At an inventors' competition, children, young people or adults show their own inventions. A jury judges how new, useful and well made an idea is. Anyone who takes part learns to tinker, to try things out and not to give up.
wichtigste: An invention is something new that did not exist before.
At an inventors' competition, a new idea matters most.
A first trial model of an invention is called a prototype.
A jury decides who wins the competition.
With a patent you can protect an invention in Switzerland for at most 20 years.
A big international inventions fair takes place in Geneva every year.
If a prototype does not work, you improve it and try again.

abschnitte.text: An **inventors' competition** is a competition in which inventions are presented and judged. An **invention** is something new that solves a problem or makes something easier. It can be a device, a tool, a game or an idea for protecting the environment. What matters is that the idea does not yet exist in that form. Many competitions have their own categories for children and young people.

It starts with a problem from everyday life, for example a school bag that always falls over. In an **inventor's notebook** you record ideas, sketches and experiments. Then you build a first model, the **prototype**, often out of cardboard, wood, Lego or with a 3D printer. If the prototype does not work straight away, you look for the fault, improve it and test again. Many famous inventions needed hundreds of attempts.

At the competition you present your invention at a stand or in a presentation. A **jury** of experts examines the projects. They look at whether the idea is new, whether it works and whether it is useful. A good explanation and clear documentation also count. There are often prizes, awards or contacts with companies that may develop the invention further.

In **Geneva** the International Exhibition of Inventions takes place every year, where inventors from many countries exhibit. For young people the foundation **Swiss Youth in Science** organises a national competition in which their own research and invention projects are awarded prizes. The best participants get to travel to international competitions. Many schools and municipalities also hold smaller inventors' days. Switzerland is regarded as a very inventive country, the home of the hook-and-loop fastener and the vegetable peeler, for example.

If you want to protect an invention from copycats, you can apply for a **patent**. In Switzerland the Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property in Bern is responsible for this. A patent protects an invention for at most 20 years; after that anyone may copy it. For this you have to describe the invention exactly, and it must really be new. Albert Einstein, by the way, worked as an examiner at the patent office in Bern from 1902 to 1909.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something new that did not exist before and that solves a problem.
A first trial model with which you test whether an idea works.
A protection right that forbids others to copy an invention without permission.
A group of experts who judge entries in a competition.

gewusst: The Swiss inventor George de Mestral invented the hook-and-loop fastener after burrs got stuck on his dog.
The Rex vegetable peeler was invented in Switzerland in 1947 and is still made almost unchanged today.
Thomas Edison is said to have remarked that he had not failed but had simply found many ways that do not work.

teile.einleitung: Friendship is a close, voluntary relationship between people who like and trust each other. Friends share joy and worries, help each other and like spending time together. Researchers have found that good friendships make people happy and even healthier.
wichtigste: In a good friendship you can trust each other.
Loyalty is an important feature of true friendship.
After a quarrel, good friends make up again.
A friend from nursery age is called a childhood friend.
The dog is known as “man's best friend”.
The UN International Day of Friendship is on 30 July.
You find new friends by speaking to others in a friendly way.

abschnitte.text: **Friendship** is a relationship you choose yourself, unlike your family. Friends like each other, spend time together and are there for one another. **Trust**, honesty and loyalty are important. More than 2,300 years ago the Greek philosopher Aristotle already thought about what makes a true friendship.

Small children often play with whoever happens to be there, for example in the sandpit. A **childhood friend** is a friend you have known since that time. At school age, shared interests and secrets become more important. Young people often look for friends they can talk to about everything.

Even in good friendships there are sometimes **quarrels**. What matters is listening to each other and saying your own opinion calmly. An apology can achieve a great deal. Good friends **make up** after a quarrel, and often the friendship is even stronger afterwards.

If you are looking for new friends, you can **speak to others in a friendly way** and ask questions. Shared hobbies in a sports club, at music school or in the scouts help a great deal. You do not have to find good friends straight away; friendship grows over time. If you are helpful and honest yourself, it is easier to become a good friend.

Many children make **friendship bracelets**, colourful knotted bands, and give them to each other. The UN has declared 30 July the **International Day of Friendship**. Animals can be friends too: the dog is often called “man's best friend”. Researchers have observed that animals such as chimpanzees, elephants and horses also form close bonds with particular members of their own kind.

begriffe.erklaerung: The feeling that you can rely on someone
Sticking by someone, even when things get difficult
Making peace again after a quarrel
A colourful knotted band that you give to friends

gewusst: Studies show that people with good friends are often healthier and live longer.
Many people have only a handful of really close friends, even if they have many acquaintances.
The English word friend is related to an old word for “to love”.

teile.einleitung: Electroencephalography, or EEG for short, is an examination in which the electrical activity of the brain is measured. Small electrodes are stuck onto the scalp and record tiny voltages. The traces show whether you are awake, asleep or whether the brain is working abnormally.
wichtigste: An EEG measures the electrical activity of the brain.
Hans Berger recorded the first EEG in a human being in 1924.
The electrodes are placed on the scalp.
When relaxed with the eyes closed, alpha waves typically appear.
In deep sleep, slow delta waves are typical.
The EEG is especially helpful in diagnosing epilepsy.
How fast brain waves oscillate is given in hertz.

abschnitte.text: Our brain consists of billions of **nerve cells** that communicate with electrical signals. When many nerve cells are active at the same time, tiny voltages arise that can be measured on the scalp. They are only a few millionths of a volt, so strong amplifiers are needed. The device records these voltages as wavy lines. This recording is called an **electroencephalogram**.

For a normal EEG, a cap is put on or **electrodes** are stuck onto the scalp. Usually there are about 20 electrodes, arranged according to a fixed scheme. To make sure the contact is good, a conducting gel is used. The examination does not hurt, because the device only measures and gives off no current. Sometimes you are asked to breathe deeply or to look into a flickering light.

How fast the waves oscillate is given in **hertz**, that is, oscillations per second. Someone lying awake and relaxed with their eyes closed typically shows **alpha waves** at about 8 to 13 hertz. During concentrated thinking, faster beta waves appear. In deep sleep, slow **delta waves** below 4 hertz are typical. In between there are theta waves, for example when falling asleep.

The EEG is especially important in diagnosing **epilepsy**. During an epileptic seizure, many nerve cells fire at the same time, which produces typical spikes in the EEG. In a **sleep laboratory**, the EEG is used to determine the sleep stages, for example in cases of sleep problems. Doctors also use it in intensive care and during operations. In research, people even use EEG signals to control computers without using their hands.

The German psychiatrist **Hans Berger** recorded the first EEG in a human being in Jena in 1924. However, he only published his results in 1929, because he himself was unsure for a long time. The alpha waves were at first called the Berger rhythm after him. At the beginning, many experts did not believe that brain currents could be measured. Today the EEG is standard equipment in every larger hospital.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small sensor that picks up electrical signals.
The unit for oscillations per second.
A condition in which seizures occur because of excessive nerve activity in the brain.
A cell that receives electrical signals and passes them on.

gewusst: The brain is very active during sleep too, and the EEG shows quite different wave patterns then.
When you open your eyes, the alpha waves usually disappear at once, because the brain is busy seeing.

teile.einleitung: Photolithography is a process for transferring tiny patterns onto a surface with light. It is the most important step in making computer chips. Without it there would be no smartphones, laptops or games consoles.
wichtigste: In photolithography a light-sensitive coating is exposed through a mask and then developed.
With a positive resist, the exposed places become soluble and are washed away.
After developing, the pattern is transferred into the layer beneath by etching.
Computer chips are usually made on round discs of silicon, the wafers.
The shorter the wavelength of the light, the finer the structures become.
The most modern machines use extreme ultraviolet with a wavelength of about 13.5 nanometres.
Work is done in cleanrooms, because even the smallest particles of dust would destroy the chips.

abschnitte.text: The word is made up of Greek parts and means roughly **writing on stone with light**. In photolithography, light draws a pattern into a thin layer of resist. This pattern serves as a template for conductor tracks and **transistors** on a chip. A modern processor contains billions of these tiny switches.

First a **wafer** of silicon is coated with a light-sensitive **photoresist**. Then light shines through a **mask**, which, like a stencil, lets light through only in certain places. With a positive resist, the exposed places become soluble in the developer and are removed; with a negative resist it is the other way round. After that the exposed material is etched away, and the remaining resist is removed. For one chip, these steps are often repeated several dozen times.

How finely you can expose depends above all on the **wavelength** of the light. For a long time people worked with ultraviolet light of 193 nanometres wavelength, often with water between the lens and the wafer. According to the **Rayleigh criterion**, this achieves structures of about 43 nanometres. For even finer patterns, **extreme ultraviolet** with a wavelength of only 13.5 nanometres is used today.

Exposure machines for extreme ultraviolet are as big as a bus and very expensive. The only maker of such machines is the company **ASML** from the Netherlands (as of 2026). Instead of lenses, these machines use especially smooth mirrors, because extreme ultraviolet is absorbed by glass. For research and one-off pieces there is also **electron beam lithography**, which works without a mask but is too slow for mass production.

Photolithography takes place in **cleanrooms** in which the air is constantly filtered. The air there is much cleaner than in an operating theatre. The staff wear protective suits, hoods and gloves so that no flakes of skin or hairs get onto the wafers. The light in the cleanroom is often yellow, because the photoresist does not react to yellow light.

**Lithography** as a printing process was invented at the end of the 18th century by Alois Senefelder, who printed from stone plates. The idea of transferring patterns with light was later taken up for electronics. Since the 1960s, **integrated circuits** have been made in this way. Since then the structures on chips have become thousands of times smaller.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin, round disc of silicon on which many chips are made at once.
A coating that changes when light falls on it.
A stencil that lets light through only in certain places.
The deliberate removal of material with chemicals or gases.
A millionth of a millimetre; a hair is about 80,000 nanometres thick.

gewusst: The finest structures on modern chips are a thousand times thinner than a human hair.
The extreme ultraviolet in the newest machines is created by a laser making tiny droplets of tin glow.
A single speck of dust on a wafer can make a whole chip useless.

teile.einleitung: Eratosthenes was a Greek scholar who lived in Egypt more than 2,200 years ago. Using only shadows, geometry and clever thinking, he worked out the circumference of the Earth astonishingly accurately. He also invented a simple method for finding prime numbers.
wichtigste: Eratosthenes lived from about 276 to 194 BC.
He was in charge of the famous Library of Alexandria.
He calculated the circumference of the Earth using the shadow of the midday sun in Alexandria and Syene.
Syene is now called Aswan and lies in the south of Egypt.
With the sieve of Eratosthenes you can find prime numbers.
He is regarded as the founder of geography and is said to have coined its name.
Critics called him “Beta”, because in many subjects he was considered the second best.

abschnitte.text: **Eratosthenes** was born around 276 BC in Cyrene, a Greek city in what is now Libya. He studied in Athens and was then brought to Alexandria by the Egyptian king. There he was in charge of the **Library of Alexandria**, the largest collection of books in the ancient world. He worked on mathematics, astronomy, geography, history and poetry. He died around 194 BC.

Eratosthenes heard that in **Syene**, today's **Aswan**, the sun stood exactly overhead at midday on the longest day of the year. Then objects cast no shadow, and sunlight reached the bottom of a well. In Alexandria, further north, a vertical stick cast a short **shadow** at the same time. From this he calculated that the angle between the cities was about one fiftieth of a whole circle. Because the distance between the cities was about 5,000 stadia, this gave a circumference of the Earth of 250,000 stadia.

A **stadion** was an old Greek unit of length whose exact length we do not know for certain today. Depending on the conversion, Eratosthenes arrived at about 39,000 to 46,000 kilometres. The true circumference at the equator is about 40,075 kilometres. For a measurement without modern instruments, that is a splendid result. His method also shows that the scholars of the ancient world had long known that the Earth is a **sphere**.

A **prime number** is a number that can only be divided by 1 and by itself. In the **sieve of Eratosthenes** you write down all the numbers and first cross out all the multiples of 2, then those of 3, then those of 5 and so on. What is left are the prime numbers. Between 1 and 20 there remain 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19, so eight prime numbers. School pupils still learn this method today.

Eratosthenes wrote a work describing the Earth and is said to have coined the word **geography** in it. He drew a world map with lines resembling lines of longitude and latitude. He also estimated the tilt of the Earth's axis and drew up a list of stars. Because he was very good in so many subjects but never the best in all of them, critics mockingly called him **“Beta”**, after the second letter of the Greek alphabet. Others called him “Pentathlos”, like an athlete in the pentathlon who is good at many things.

begriffe.erklaerung: The length of a line all the way around the Earth.
A number greater than 1 that can only be divided by 1 and by itself.
A Greek unit of length from ancient times, roughly as long as a running track in a stadium.
The science of the Earth, its countries, landscapes and peoples.

gewusst: There is a crater on the Moon named after Eratosthenes.
The word stadium for a sports ground comes from the old unit of length, because the running track in Olympia was one stadion long.
Eratosthenes' experiment can be repeated today by school classes measuring shadows at the same time in different places.

teile.einleitung: Ethnology is the science that studies and compares cultures and societies all over the world. It asks how people live together, celebrate, work, believe and communicate. In German-speaking countries it used to be called Völkerkunde.
wichtigste: Ethnology studies and compares cultures and societies.
In German-speaking countries it used to be called Völkerkunde.
Ethnography describes a culture, while ethnology compares and explains.
The emic perspective is the view of the people of a culture themselves.
The most important method is fieldwork, in which researchers live with the people for a long time.
In 1871 Edward Burnett Tylor defined culture as “that complex whole”.
The Museum der Kulturen in Basel has one of the most important ethnographic collections in Europe.

abschnitte.text: The word **ethnology** comes from the Greek ethnos, people, and logos, study. Ethnologists study how people live in different societies. This includes family and kinship, language, religion, economy, art and festivals. Today they study not only distant villages but also big cities, clubs or internet communities. In English-speaking countries people usually speak of **cultural anthropology** or social anthropology.

**Ethnography** describes a single culture as precisely as possible. Ethnology compares many such descriptions and looks for explanations. The difference between two points of view is important. The **emic perspective** is the view of the people of the culture themselves, while the etic perspective is the view from outside. Good research tries to see the world through other people's eyes, without taking one's own culture as the measure.

The most important method is **fieldwork**. Researchers often live for months with the people they are studying, learn their language and join in everyday life. This is called **participant observation**. The method became well known through Bronisław Malinowski, who did research on the Trobriand Islands in the Pacific during the First World War. The American Clifford Geertz later made **thick description** well known, which explains not only actions but also their meaning.

In 1871 the Briton **Edward Burnett Tylor** described culture as “that complex whole” that includes knowledge, belief, art, morals and custom. **Franz Boas**, who emigrated from Germany to the USA, is regarded as the founder of American cultural anthropology. He showed that no culture is “higher” or “lower” than another. In 1925 the Frenchman Marcel Mauss wrote the “Essai sur le don” about gifts and return gifts. He showed that giving creates relationships between people everywhere in the world.

In Switzerland you can study ethnology at the universities of Basel, Bern, Zurich, Fribourg and Neuchâtel, for example. The **Museum der Kulturen Basel** holds more than 340,000 objects from all over the world. The Musée d'ethnographie in Geneva and the ethnographic museum of the University of Zurich also show fascinating collections. Today museums also ask critical questions about how objects were acquired in colonial times. Some pieces are therefore being returned to their countries of origin.

begriffe.erklaerung: Everything people learn together and pass on: language, customs, beliefs, art and knowledge.
Research on the spot, in which you live with the people being studied.
From the point of view of the people who belong to a culture.
The attitude of taking one's own culture as the measure for all others.

gewusst: Swiss customs such as the carnival or the bringing down of cattle from the alpine pastures are also studied by ethnologists.
Franz Boas studied the languages and cultures of the Inuit and of the peoples of the northwest coast of America.
Many ethnologists keep a diary during their fieldwork, which later becomes an important source in itself.

teile.einleitung: Extremophiles are living things that grow best in places where most others would die. They live in boiling hot springs, in salty lakes, in ice or deep in the sea. Most of them are tiny bacteria or archaea.
wichtigste: Extremophiles grow best under extreme conditions.
Heat-loving organisms are called thermophilic, cold-loving ones psychrophilic.
Halophiles need high concentrations of salt.
Acidophiles thrive in strongly acidic surroundings.
Piezophiles grow best under very high pressure, for example in the deep sea.
Methanopyrus kandleri still grows at 122 °C.
An enzyme from Thermus aquaticus made PCR practical.

abschnitte.text: The word **extremophile** means “lover of the extreme”. It refers to living things that not only survive under extreme conditions but grow best there. Most are single-celled **archaea** or bacteria. Under normal conditions many of them grow badly or not at all.

**Thermophiles** love heat and live in hot springs or at deep-sea vents, the black smokers. The archaeon Methanopyrus kandleri holds a record: it still grows at 122 degrees Celsius. **Psychrophiles**, by contrast, grow best at very low temperatures, for example in polar ice or in glaciers. Their proteins are built so that they stay flexible even in the cold.

**Halophiles** need a great deal of salt and live in salt lakes such as the Dead Sea or in salt pans. Some turn the water pink or red. Acidophiles thrive in strongly acidic water, for example in the Rio Tinto in Spain. Piezophiles live in the deep sea, where the water pressure is hundreds of times higher than at the surface.

The bacterium **Deinococcus radiodurans** is known for its enormous resistance to radioactive radiation. It can survive a dose of radiation that would be a thousand times over lethal for humans. This is possible because it repairs damage to its genetic information very quickly. It also copes well with dryness.

A special enzyme comes from the heat-loving bacterium **Thermus aquaticus** from hot springs in Yellowstone National Park. This enzyme withstands high temperatures and made **PCR** practical, a method for copying DNA. PCR is used today for tests for diseases, in research and in forensics. Enzymes from extremophiles are also found in some detergents.

Extremophiles show how adaptable life is. That is why space researchers are also interested in them. If life is possible in ice, acid or heat, then perhaps it could also exist on Mars or on icy moons. This research is called **astrobiology**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Single-celled living things without a nucleus, which often live in extreme places.
A protein that speeds up chemical processes in the body.
A laboratory method with which tiny amounts of DNA are copied millions of times.
Salt-loving, that is, needing a lot of salt.

gewusst: Some salt lakes are a bright pink colour because of salt-loving microbes.
There are microbes that live in the rock deep below the sea floor.
Water bears are regarded as extremely tough, but they grow best under normal conditions and are therefore not true extremophiles.

teile.einleitung: In colour mixing, many new colours are made from just a few. Yellow and blue make green, and red and yellow make orange. But paints and coloured light mix in completely different ways, and that is exactly what makes the subject so exciting.
wichtigste: Yellow and blue make green, red and yellow make orange, and red and blue make violet.
White makes colours lighter, and black makes them darker.
If you mix all your paints, you usually get a dark brown.
If you mix coloured light, it always gets brighter; all the colours of light together give white.
Screens build up all their colours from red, green and blue.
Printers mix their colours from cyan, magenta, yellow and black.
The Swiss painter Johannes Itten developed a well-known colour wheel.

abschnitte.text: In a paint box you can mix many new colours from a few **primary colours**. Yellow and blue give green, red and yellow give orange, and red and blue give violet. These new colours are called **secondary colours**. If you add white, the colour becomes lighter; red becomes pink, for example, and blue becomes light blue. A little black, on the other hand, makes a colour darker.

Paints **absorb** part of the light and reflect only the rest. A yellow paint absorbs blue light, for example. The more colours you mix, the more light is absorbed and the darker the result. That is why the water in your jar usually ends up a dark brown or grey. This kind of mixing is called **subtractive colour mixing**, because light is taken away. Printers use cyan, magenta and yellow for this, plus black.

With coloured light it is the other way round: the more colours of light come together, the brighter it gets. This is called **additive colour mixing**. Red and green light together give yellow, and red, green and blue together give white. A mobile phone or television screen is made of tiny dots in exactly these three colours, the **pixels**. With a magnifying glass you can even make them out on some screens.

Around 1666 the English scientist **Isaac Newton** used a glass prism to show that white sunlight is made up of all the colours of the rainbow. It works the other way round too: a disc with all the colours of the rainbow looks almost white when it spins very fast. Our eyes can then no longer see the colours separately and mix them. This disc is called **Newton's colour disc**. A rainbow forms when raindrops split sunlight into its colours.

Even colours that look the same can be made up of several dyes. If you draw a dot with a black felt pen on a coffee filter and wet it, the water travels through the paper. As it does so, the colour separates into several coloured rings, for example blue, violet and yellow. This method is called **chromatography** and is also used in laboratories. In this way you can find out which substances are in a mixture.

The Swiss painter **Johannes Itten**, born in 1888 in the canton of Bern, taught at the famous Bauhaus in Germany. He developed a **colour wheel** with twelve segments that is still used in schools today. In it the primary colours yellow, red and blue are in the middle and the mixed colours all around. Colours opposite each other in the wheel are called **complementary colours**, for example red and green. Side by side they make each other glow especially strongly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A colour from which other colours can be mixed but which cannot itself be mixed.
Colours of light are added together, and the result gets brighter.
Paints take light away, and the result gets darker.
The colour exactly opposite in the colour wheel, such as blue and orange.
A tiny dot of the picture on a screen.

gewusst: Yellow on a screen contains no yellow light at all, only red and green.
Many animals see colours differently from us; bees, for example, see ultraviolet light.
Johannes Itten's colour wheel can be found in many Swiss classrooms.

teile.einleitung: In ice core drilling, long cylinders of ice are pulled out of glaciers and ice sheets. The ice is like an archive in which the climate of many thousands of years is stored. Researchers from Bern are among the most important experts in the world in this field.
wichtigste: An ice core is a long column of ice taken out of the ice with a hollow drill.
In Greenland the years can often be counted from visible layers of summer and winter snow.
Tiny air bubbles in the ice contain old air with earlier CO2 and methane levels.
The ratio of oxygen isotopes reveals the temperature of the past.
In 1966 the Greenland ice was drilled through to the bedrock for the first time at Camp Century.
The Bern physicist Hans Oeschger gave his name to the Dansgaard-Oeschger events.
Ice cores from the Antarctic reach back much further than those from Greenland.

abschnitte.text: In Greenland and in the Antarctic there are huge ice sheets kilometres thick. They formed because year after year snow fell and no longer melted. Under the weight above it, the snow was pressed into **firn** and finally into ice. In **ice core drilling**, a hollow drill cuts out a round column of ice, the **ice core**. Piece by piece it is brought to the surface, often in sections a few metres long.

The layers in the ice are like the growth rings of a tree, which is why in Greenland the **annual layers** can often be counted directly. As the snow was compressed, tiny **air bubbles** were trapped. They contain real air from the past, and you can measure in them how much CO2 and methane there was at the time. The Dane Willi Dansgaard used the ratio of **oxygen isotopes** as a thermometer of the past. Dust and volcanic ash in the ice also tell of storms and volcanic eruptions.

From the 1960s the physicist **Hans Oeschger** built up a laboratory at the University of Bern that is still one of the world's leading ones today. He developed methods for measuring the air from the bubbles very precisely. Together with Dansgaard, sudden climate jumps during the ice age were discovered in Greenland ice cores. Today these are called **Dansgaard-Oeschger events**. Researchers from Bern have taken part in almost all the major drilling projects.

The first drilling down to the bedrock in Greenland succeeded in 1966 at the American military base **Camp Century**. In the early 1990s the European project **GRIP** drilled to the bottom at the summit of the Greenland ice sheet, about 3,000 metres deep. The NEEM project was meant above all to capture the **Eemian warm period** about 120,000 years ago. Since the 2010s, EastGRIP has been studying a large ice stream in northeast Greenland. In the Antarctic, the EPICA project at Dome C produced ice that is about 800,000 years old.

In the Antarctic much less snow falls each year than in Greenland, so far older layers lie on top of each other there. Ice cores show that CO2 and temperature were closely linked in the past. They also show that there is clearly more CO2 in the air today than at any time in the last 800,000 years. This makes ice cores an important piece of evidence in **climate research**. The Beyond EPICA project is even looking in the Antarctic for ice that is more than a million years old.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge mass of ice, several kilometres thick, that covers a whole country.
Old, grainy snow that slowly turns into glacier ice.
A kind of atom of an element that is slightly heavier or lighter than others.
Something from nature in which information about the climate of earlier times is stored.

gewusst: Ice cores are stored in freezer rooms at about minus 20 degrees or colder so that they do not melt.
If you put a piece of very old ice in water, it crackles, because the old air escapes from the bubbles.
In ice cores you find traces of volcanic eruptions that can be dated precisely.

teile.einleitung: Fire is burning that produces light and heat. It has been with humankind for hundreds of thousands of years: for warmth, cooking and protection. But fire can also become dangerous if you are not careful.
wichtigste: Fire is a chemical reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen.
To burn, fire needs fuel, oxygen and enough heat.
These three conditions are called the fire triangle.
If one of the three conditions is missing, the fire goes out.
A flame consists of hot, glowing gases.
People have used fire for a very long time for cooking, warmth and forging.
In Switzerland you reach the fire brigade on the emergency number 118.

abschnitte.text: Fire is **burning**, that is, a chemical reaction. A fuel such as wood, paper or gas combines with the **oxygen** in the air. In the process, energy is released that we feel as heat and see as light. What remains is ash, smoke and gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour.

Fire needs three things at the same time: fuel, oxygen and heat. This is shown as the **fire triangle**. If you take one side away, the fire goes out. That is why a blanket smothers a flame, because no more oxygen gets to it, and water puts out a fire because it cools.

A flame consists of hot gases that glow. In a candle the inner part is darker and cooler, and the outer part is hottest. The yellow colour comes from tiny glowing particles of **soot**. A blue gas flame is especially hot, because the gas there burns very completely.

Early humans such as **Homo erectus** probably used fire several hundred thousand years ago. With fire they could cook meat, keep warm and keep wild animals away. Later, people learned to fire clay and melt metals with fire. Today burning takes place in heating systems, engines and power stations.

A fire can spread very quickly. **Smoke** is especially dangerous, because it contains poisonous gases. In Switzerland you call the fire brigade on the number **118** if there is a fire. Smoke alarms in the home give an early warning, and in an emergency you should go outside at once.

On 1 August, the national holiday, **bonfires** burn on hills and mountains all over Switzerland. In Zurich, at the Sechseläuten festival, the Böögg, a snowman made of cotton wool, is burned on a pile of wood. In summer, when it is dry, some cantons impose a **ban on fires** in the woods, so that forest fires do not start.

begriffe.erklaerung: A chemical reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen and gives off heat.
A gas in the air that fire and living things need.
Something that can burn, for example wood, coal or gas.
The temperature at which a substance begins to burn by itself.

gewusst: In space on the space station, candle flames are almost perfectly round and blue, because hot air does not rise there.
The temperature in a candle flame reaches about 1,400 degrees Celsius at its hottest point.
Diamonds are made of carbon and can burn at very high temperatures.

teile.einleitung: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in plants; it is also called leaf green. The plant needs it to make energy from sunlight. Without chlorophyll there would be no photosynthesis and therefore no oxygen to breathe.
wichtigste: Chlorophyll is the green pigment of plants and is also called leaf green.
It is found in tiny parts of plant cells, the chloroplasts.
Chlorophyll captures sunlight, especially red and blue light.
With this energy the plant makes sugar in photosynthesis.
As a by-product, this produces the oxygen we breathe.
Leaves look green because chlorophyll reflects green light.
In autumn the chlorophyll is broken down and yellow and red colours become visible.

abschnitte.text: The name **chlorophyll** comes from Greek and means “leaf green”. It is a pigment found in almost all plants, in algae and in some bacteria. In leaf cells it sits in small green grains, the **chloroplasts**. A single leaf cell can contain dozens of them. In the middle of a chlorophyll molecule there is an atom of the metal **magnesium**.

Sunlight is made up of many colours, as you can see in a rainbow. Chlorophyll mainly absorbs **red** and **blue** light. Green light, on the other hand, is reflected. That is why leaves, grass and forests look green to our eyes. The chlorophyll passes the light energy it has absorbed on to the plant.

With the light energy, the plant makes glucose in **photosynthesis**. To do this it takes in water from the soil and carbon dioxide from the air. From the sugar it builds wood, leaves, fruit and seeds. As a by-product, **oxygen** is produced, which gets into the air through tiny openings. In this way plants provide the basis for almost all life on Earth.

abschnitte.titel: Why leaves change colour in autumn
abschnitte.text: In autumn, deciduous trees get ready for winter. They break down the valuable chlorophyll and store its building blocks in the trunk and roots. Now the yellow and orange **carotenoids**, which were in the leaf all along, become visible. Some trees also make red pigments. That is why forests in Switzerland glow yellow, orange and red in autumn.

The German chemist **Richard Willstätter** studied the structure of chlorophyll in detail. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1915. He also worked at ETH Zurich. Today chlorophyll is used as a green food colouring, for example in sweets. Researchers are trying to copy photosynthesis in order to make fuel from sunlight.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny green grain in plant cells in which photosynthesis takes place.
The process in which plants use light to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide.
Yellow and orange pigments in plants, for example in carrots.
A substance that colours something because it absorbs certain colours of light.

gewusst: The red pigment in our blood is built very much like chlorophyll, but it has iron in the middle instead of magnesium.
Plants that sprout in the dark are a yellowish white, because without light they hardly make any chlorophyll.

teile.einleitung: A clinical thermometer is a small measuring device that shows the temperature of the body. With it you can tell whether someone has a fever and so might be ill. Today most clinical thermometers are digital and beep when they have finished measuring.
wichtigste: A clinical thermometer measures body temperature.
A healthy person is about 37 degrees warm.
From about 38 degrees, you speak of a fever.
Digital clinical thermometers usually beep when they are finished.
With a special thermometer you can measure quickly in the ear.
In the past many clinical thermometers contained the poisonous metal mercury.
After measuring you clean the thermometer so that no germs are passed on.

abschnitte.text: A **clinical thermometer** measures **body temperature** in degrees Celsius. A healthy person is about 37 degrees warm, and this varies a little over the day. From about 38 degrees, you speak of a fever. Fever is a defence reaction of the body, for example against viruses or bacteria.

Most clinical thermometers today are **digital**. A small sensor in the tip measures the warmth, and a display shows the number. When the thermometer has finished measuring, it usually beeps. You measure with it under the tongue or under the arm, for example.

With a special **infrared thermometer** you can measure in the ear in a few seconds. It measures the invisible heat radiation coming from the eardrum. Other devices measure at the forehead without touching the skin. Often you notice even without a thermometer that someone might have a fever, because their forehead feels hot.

In the past many clinical thermometers contained the poisonous metal **mercury**. It expanded when warm and rose up a thin glass tube. If the thermometer broke, poisonous vapours could be released. That is why such thermometers have not been sold in Switzerland and the EU for a long time.

As early as the 17th century the Italian doctor Santorio Santorio tried to measure body heat. The temperature scale we use today goes back to the Swede **Anders Celsius**. In the 19th century the German doctor Carl Wunderlich showed with countless measurements that about 37 degrees is normal. Since then, taking the temperature has been part of every medical examination.

abschnitte.titel: Tips when you have a fever
abschnitte.text: A child with a fever should **drink** plenty and rest. Light clothing and a thin blanket help to stop the body overheating. If the fever is very high, lasts a long time or the child feels very unwell, you call a doctor. After measuring you clean the thermometer so that no **germs** are passed on.

begriffe.erklaerung: How warm the inside of the body is.
A raised body temperature with which the body fights off illness.
Invisible heat radiation that all warm things give off.
A poisonous metal that is liquid at room temperature.

gewusst: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Body temperature is usually a little lower in the early morning than in the evening.
Fever is actually useful, because many germs multiply less well at higher temperatures.

teile.einleitung: Charles Darwin was an English naturalist. He developed the theory of evolution by natural selection and used it to explain how living things change over very long periods of time. His ideas are among the most important in the whole of biology.
wichtigste: Charles Darwin lived in England from 1809 to 1882.
From 1831 to 1836 he sailed around the world on the ship HMS Beagle.
On the Galápagos Islands he observed finches with different beaks.
He developed the theory of evolution by natural selection.
In 1859 his famous book “On the Origin of Species” was published.
Alfred Russel Wallace came to similar conclusions independently of him.
Darwin was buried in Westminster Abbey in London.

abschnitte.text: **Charles Darwin** was born on 12 February 1809 in Shrewsbury in England. His father was a doctor and wanted Charles to study medicine too. But Charles preferred collecting beetles and observing nature. Later he studied theology in Cambridge. There he met naturalists who encouraged his enthusiasm.

In 1831 the young Darwin was allowed to travel on the survey ship **HMS Beagle**. The voyage lasted almost five years and went all the way around the world. Darwin collected plants, animals, rocks and fossils in South America, Australia and on many islands. The **Galápagos Islands** in the Pacific were especially important. There he saw that finches and tortoises differed from island to island.

Darwin realised that living things of the same species differ slightly from one another. Those that are better adapted to their environment are more likely to survive and have more young. These features are passed on to the young. In this way species change over many generations. Darwin called this process **natural selection**, and it leads to **evolution**.

Darwin worked on his theory for more than 20 years before he published it. In 1858 he learned that **Alfred Russel Wallace** had come to similar ideas independently. Both presented their ideas together in 1858. In 1859 Darwin's book “On the Origin of Species” was published and sold out immediately. In 1871 it was followed by a book on **the descent of man**.

Darwin's ideas caused fierce debates, because many people believed that species never changed. Today the **theory of evolution** is the foundation of modern biology. It has been confirmed many times by fossil finds and by genetics. Darwin died on 19 April 1882 at his home in Kent. He was buried in **Westminster Abbey** in London.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change of living things over many generations.
The better adapted living things survive and reproduce more often.
A group of living things that can reproduce with one another.
Remains or traces of living things from earlier times that have turned to stone.

gewusst: The finches of the Galápagos Islands are now called Darwin's finches in honour of the scientist.
Darwin suffered from seasickness almost the whole time on the voyage of the Beagle.

teile.einleitung: The Declaration of Helsinki is a set of principles for medical research on people. The World Medical Association adopted it in 1964 in the Finnish capital, Helsinki. It is meant to make sure that people who take part in studies are protected and respected.
wichtigste: The Declaration of Helsinki was adopted by the World Medical Association in 1964.
It sets out the ethics of medical research on people.
The well-being of the individual research participant comes before the interests of science and society.
Participants must be well informed and agree voluntarily.
An independent ethics committee must check the research plan before the study begins.
Studies should be registered before the first person takes part, and negative results should also be published.
Since 1964 the declaration has been revised several times.

abschnitte.text: The **Declaration of Helsinki** is a kind of rulebook for doctors and researchers. It describes how new medicines and treatments may be tested on people without putting the participants at risk. It was adopted by the **World Medical Association**, an alliance of doctors' organisations from many countries. It is not a law, but many countries have included its principles in their laws.

After the Second World War it became known that during the Nazi era experiments had been carried out on people without their consent. As a result, the **Nuremberg Code** was drawn up in 1947 with the first rules for experiments on people. The World Medical Association built on this and adopted its own declaration in **Helsinki** in **1964**. Since then it has been revised several times so that it fits new questions in medicine.

At its centre is the **well-being of the individual participant**, which comes before the interests of science and society. Every person must be told in an understandable way about the aims, benefits and risks. Only then may they agree voluntarily; this is called **informed consent**. They may drop out again at any time without any disadvantage.

Before a study begins, an independent **ethics committee** must check the research plan. Every study should be entered in a public register before the first person takes part. In addition, **all results** should be published, including negative or unclear ones. That way nobody can show only the good results and hide the bad ones.

A **placebo** is a dummy medicine without an active ingredient, used to compare new medicines against. Its use is especially controversial when a proven treatment already exists. In that case, sick people in the placebo group would miss out on an effective treatment. The declaration therefore only allows placebos under strict conditions.

In Switzerland, the **Human Research Act** regulates research on people, and it is based on similar principles. Several cantonal and regional ethics committees here check numerous studies every year. No study involving people may begin without their approval. In this way patients in Switzerland also benefit from the protection the declaration demands.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thinking about what is right and wrong and how to act fairly.
A group of experts who check whether a study protects its participants.
Agreeing to a study after you have understood all the important information.
A dummy medicine without an active ingredient, used for comparison.

gewusst: The World Medical Association has its headquarters in Ferney-Voltaire in France, right on the border with Geneva.
Many scientific journals only publish studies that follow the Declaration of Helsinki.

teile.einleitung: The use of fire was one of the most important steps in human history. With fire, early humans could cook, keep warm and protect themselves from predators. The oldest reliable traces are about a million years old.
wichtigste: The oldest reliable traces of the use of fire are about 1 million years old.
Such traces were found in the Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa.
Cooked food was easier to digest.
Fire gave protection at night from predators and cold.
Stone Age people struck sparks with flint and pyrite.
Tinder fungus was used as tinder for making fire.
A place where fire burned regularly is called a hearth.

abschnitte.titel: What is the use of fire?
abschnitte.text: The **use of fire** means that people use, tend and later light fire deliberately. At the beginning they probably used fire that arose from lightning or bush fires. They kept the embers alive and carried them with them. Only much later did they learn to make fire themselves at any time.

In the **Wonderwerk Cave** in South Africa, burnt bones and plant ash about a million years old were found. At that time **Homo erectus** lived there, an ancestor of modern humans. There are also very old sites with traces of fire in Israel. Whether even older finds really come from humans is disputed among experts.

Cooked food was **easier to digest** and often less dangerous, because heat kills germs. People needed less time for chewing and got more energy from their food. Some researchers believe this even supported the growth of the brain. Meat and tough plants also became easier to eat through cooking.

At night, fire gave protection from **predators** and cold. In this way people could also move into cooler regions such as Europe. In the evening they gathered around the fire, told stories and shared food. In archaeology, a place where fire burned regularly is called a **hearth**.

Stone Age people struck sparks with **flint** and the mineral pyrite. They caught the sparks in dry **tinder**, such as tinder fungus, a fungus that grows on trees. Another method was fire drilling, in which you turn a wooden stick quickly in a board until embers form. Matches have only existed for about 200 years.

The man from the ice, **Ötzi**, lived about 5,300 years ago in the Alps. He was found in 1991 in a glacier on the border between Italy and Austria. In his equipment he had tinder fungus and other things for making fire. He also carried a container of birch bark in which he probably transported embers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Easily flammable material that starts to smoulder from just a spark.
A shiny, gold-coloured mineral that gives sparks when struck with flint.
An early kind of human that lived more than a million years ago.
A place where fire burned regularly in the past.

gewusst: Because of its shine, pyrite is also called fool's gold.
With fire, people also hardened wooden points and heated stones so that they were easier to work.
Humans are the only living creatures that can light a fire themselves.

teile.einleitung: A false report is a piece of news that is not true. Some come about by mistake, while others are spread deliberately to deceive people. A false story in a newspaper is sometimes called a canard, and today you often hear the term fake news.
wichtigste: A false report is a piece of news that is not true.
Deliberate false reports are often called fake news.
In German, the word for duck stands for a false report in a newspaper.
A hoax is a false report that is passed on as a warning.
A 2018 study by MIT showed that falsehoods spread faster on Twitter than the truth.
Satire exaggerates deliberately and recognisably.
In 1957 the BBC showed a spaghetti harvest on trees in Ticino as an April Fool's joke.

abschnitte.text: A **false report** is a piece of news that is not true. It can come about by mistake, for example through a translation error. But if it is spread deliberately in order to deceive, it is called **disinformation** or fake news. People who pass on falsehoods unknowingly often join in without noticing.

In German, a false newspaper story is called an “Ente”, a duck. Where exactly this expression comes from is not certain. A **hoax** is a false report that is passed on as a warning, such as “send this to all your friends”. Such chain messages often spread needless fear.

A large MIT study from 2018 examined reports on Twitter. It found that falsehoods spread faster and further than the truth. One reason is that false reports are often surprising and set off strong feelings. On top of that there are **social bots**, that is, automatically controlled accounts that share reports in huge numbers.

**Clickbait** is a sensational headline whose main purpose is to tempt people to click. The article behind it often does not deliver what the headline promises. **Satire**, by contrast, exaggerates deliberately in order to criticise something or make people laugh. It is not really a false report, but it is sometimes shared out of context and then taken as true.

On 1 April 1957 the British BBC showed a report about a **spaghetti harvest** on trees in Ticino. Many viewers believed the joke and asked how they could grow spaghetti trees themselves. In 1983 the German magazine Stern published supposed diaries of Adolf Hitler, which soon turned out to be forgeries. Such cases show that even large media organisations can be deceived.

Check who is spreading a report and whether reliable media are also reporting on it. Pay attention to the date, the source and exaggerated language. Pictures can be checked with a **reverse search**. And above all: think first, then share.

begriffe.erklaerung: Deliberately spread false reports that look like real news.
A false report, usually passed on as a warning or a chain message.
A sensational headline meant to tempt people to click.
A computer program that shares posts in social networks as if it were a person.
A form of humour that deliberately exaggerates in order to criticise something.

gewusst: The BBC's spaghetti joke is regarded as one of the most famous April Fool's jokes in the history of television.
False reports existed long before the internet, for example on leaflets and in newspapers.
The Collins dictionary team chose “fake news” as word of the year in 2017.

teile.einleitung: Fridtjof Nansen was a Norwegian polar explorer, scientist and diplomat. He was the first to cross Greenland on skis and deliberately let his ship Fram freeze into the pack ice of the Arctic Ocean. Later he helped millions of refugees and received the Nobel Peace Prize for it in 1922.
wichtigste: Fridtjof Nansen was born near Oslo in 1861 and died in 1930.
In 1888 he made the first crossing of Greenland on skis.
From 1893 he planned to freeze the Fram into the pack ice and drift across the Arctic Ocean with the ice.
He got the idea from wreckage of the Jeannette that had washed up on Greenland.
The Fram was built by Colin Archer, and its name means Forward.
In 1895 Nansen tried with Hjalmar Johansen to reach the North Pole with dog sledges and skis.
In 1922 he received the Nobel Peace Prize for his help for refugees and prisoners of war.

abschnitte.text: Fridtjof Nansen was born in 1861 near **Christiania**, today's Oslo. He was an athletic young man and an excellent skier. He studied zoology and did research on the nervous system of animals. Later he became professor of **oceanography**, the study of the sea.

In 1888 Nansen set out with five companions on a daring journey. They crossed the huge **inland ice** of Greenland from the east to the west coast on **skis**. Nobody had managed that before. The journey made Nansen famous and helped to make skiing known all over the world.

In 1884, wreckage of the ship **Jeannette**, which had sunk far away near Siberia, was found on the coast of Greenland. From this Nansen concluded that the ice drifts right across the Arctic Ocean. He had the ship **Fram** built, which means Forward in Norwegian. The shipbuilder **Colin Archer** gave it an especially round hull so that under pressure from the ice it would be pushed upwards instead of being crushed.

In 1893 the Fram sailed north and deliberately froze into the **pack ice**. It then drifted with the ice through the Arctic Ocean for years. In 1895 Nansen and Hjalmar **Johansen** left the ship to reach the North Pole with dog sledges and skis. They had to turn back but got further north than anyone before them. After spending a winter on Franz Josef Land, both returned home in 1896, and the Fram also came back safely the same year.

After the First World War, Nansen worked for people in need. On behalf of the **League of Nations** he helped to bring hundreds of thousands of prisoners of war home. For refugees without a nationality he created a special document, the **Nansen passport**. For this he received the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1922.
