The Fram later sailed with other explorers too, for example with **Roald Amundsen** to the Antarctic. Today the ship stands in the **Fram Museum** in Oslo. Visitors can go on board and see how cramped the explorers' lives were. In Norway, Nansen is still regarded as a national hero.

begriffe.erklaerung: Dense sea ice pushed together and moved by wind and currents.
The slow movement of sea ice caused by wind and ocean currents.
A research journey into a little-known area.
A document for refugees without a nationality, named after Fridtjof Nansen.
An association of states after the First World War, based in Geneva.

gewusst: The League of Nations, for which Nansen worked, had its seat in Geneva in Switzerland.
The Fram was so sturdy throughout the drift that the crew could spend the winters safely in the ice.
During their winter, Nansen and Johansen lived partly on walruses and polar bears.

teile.einleitung: Eukaryotes are all living things whose cells have a true nucleus. They include animals, plants, fungi and many single-celled organisms, and us humans too. The word literally means “true kernel”.
wichtigste: Eukaryotes have cells with a true nucleus.
Animals, plants, fungi and many single-celled organisms such as baker's yeast are eukaryotes.
Bacteria and archaea have no true nucleus.
Eukaryotic cells have organelles such as mitochondria.
A typical animal or plant cell is about 10 to 100 micrometres in size.
The chromosomes in the nucleus are long, stretched threads.
According to the endosymbiotic theory, mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from bacteria.

abschnitte.text: All living things are made of **cells**. They are divided into two large groups: cells with a true nucleus and cells without one. Living things with a true nucleus are called **eukaryotes**; the word comes from Greek and means “true kernel”. Bacteria and archaea have no such nucleus and are called prokaryotes.

Eukaryotes include all **animals**, all plants and all fungi. Many single-celled organisms also belong to them, such as the slipper animalcule, amoebas or diatoms. **Baker's yeast**, which makes bread dough rise, is a single-celled fungus and therefore also a eukaryote. From the tiny single-celled organism to the giant sequoia, they are very varied.

The **nucleus** holds the genetic information, the DNA. It is divided among several chromosomes that form long, stretched threads. A double envelope with small pores separates the nucleus from the rest of the cell. In bacteria, by contrast, the DNA usually lies free in the cell as a ring.

Eukaryotic cells have many small spaces with their own jobs, the **organelles**. The **mitochondria** are the power stations of the cell and get energy from nutrients. The Golgi apparatus packs proteins and sends them off in small bubbles. In animal cells, lysosomes use enzymes to break down waste and foreign substances, and plant cells also have chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

A typical animal or plant cell is about 10 to 100 **micrometres** in size. A micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre. Bacteria are usually only about 1 to 10 micrometres, so clearly smaller. That is why the nucleus of a plant cell can already be seen with a simple school microscope.

The first eukaryotes arose about two billion years ago, long after the first bacteria. The **endosymbiotic theory** explains how this happened. A larger cell took in smaller bacteria but did not digest them. Over time these became the mitochondria and, in plants, the chloroplasts, which still have their own small set of DNA today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest building block of a living thing that can live by itself.
The control centre of the cell, where the genetic information is found.
A small area in the cell with a particular job.
A living thing without a true nucleus, for example a bacterium.

gewusst: The human body consists of many trillions of eukaryotic cells.
Mitochondria have their own small set of DNA, a sign that they used to be bacteria.
Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.

teile.einleitung: A research diary is a notebook in which you write down observations, experiments and ideas. It helps you not to forget anything and to follow exactly later what happened. Famous naturalists such as Charles Darwin kept such notebooks.
wichtigste: A research diary is used to write down observations.
Every entry includes the date.
You write observations down at once so that you do not forget anything.
Besides text, drawings and sketches are allowed too.
With long observations it helps to make a short entry every day.
Even if an experiment fails, you honestly write down what really happened.
Charles Darwin filled many notebooks on his voyage around the world.

abschnitte.text: A **research diary** is a notebook just for your research. In it you record what you are studying, what you expect and what you observe. Unlike an ordinary diary it is not about feelings but about precise **observations**. In this way it becomes your personal store of knowledge.

Every entry begins with the **date**, often also the time, the place and the weather. Then come the research question, your idea and a description of the experiment. Measurements can be collected in small **tables**. Drawings and sketches often show more than many words, for example exactly what a leaf or a beetle looks like.

Ella wants to know how fast a bean sprouts and watches it for 14 days. Every day she makes a short entry, measures the seedling with a ruler and draws it. At the end she can see exactly in her notebook on which day the first root appeared. Without the daily notes she would have forgotten that long ago.

Not every experiment works out the way you expected. All the same, you **honestly** write down what really happened, including mistakes and mishaps. You can learn a great deal precisely from failed experiments. Anyone who wants to repeat the experiment later will find in the research diary exactly how it was done.

The English naturalist **Charles Darwin** travelled around the world on the ship Beagle from 1831 to 1836. He filled many notebooks with observations about animals, plants and rocks. These notes later helped him to develop his **theory of evolution**. Leonardo da Vinci also left behind thousands of pages of sketches and notes on nature and technology.

begriffe.erklaerung: Looking at something closely and describing what you see
A section in the diary for a particular day
A simple drawing that shows the most important things
A number you get when measuring, for example 3 centimetres

gewusst: Real researchers in laboratories keep a laboratory notebook, which works just like a research diary.
Darwin's notebooks are so valuable today that they are kept in museums and libraries.
Leonardo da Vinci wrote many of his notes in mirror writing.

teile.einleitung: In DNA sequencing, you read the order of the building blocks in DNA. This tells you what is written in the genetic material of a living thing. What used to take years can be done by modern machines in hours today.
wichtigste: Sequencing means working out the order of the four bases A, T, G and C in a piece of DNA.
In 1977 Frederick Sanger developed the chain termination method, which was the standard for decades.
In the same year, Allan Maxam and Walter Gilbert developed a chemical method.
Sanger received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry twice, which very few people have achieved.
In next generation sequencing, millions of pieces of DNA are read at the same time.
In nanopore sequencing, a strand of DNA is pulled through a tiny pore.
From many short pieces, the reads, a computer puts together the whole sequence.

abschnitte.text: DNA is like a very long book made up of only four letters: A, T, G and C. The **sequence** is the exact order of these letters. In **DNA sequencing**, this order is read letter by letter. The human genetic material contains about three billion such base pairs. Printed out, it would fill many thousands of thick books.

In 1977 Frederick Sanger presented the **chain termination method**. In it, DNA is copied in a test tube and special building blocks are mixed in, the **dideoxynucleotides**. When such a building block is inserted, the copy stops exactly at that point. This produces pieces of different lengths, which are sorted by size, and the order is read from them. Later the four bases were coloured with four different **fluorescent dyes**, so that machines could recognise the colours automatically.

From about 2005, machines for **next generation sequencing** came along. They read millions of short pieces of DNA at the same time, that is, in parallel. In **pyrosequencing**, for example, a small flash of light is produced each time a base is added. In **nanopore sequencing**, a strand of DNA is pulled through a tiny hole, and each base changes the electric current a little. Some of these nanopore devices are only as big as a mobile phone.

A sequencing machine usually does not read the whole DNA in one piece, but many short pieces. Each piece that is read is called a **read**. A computer then looks for places where the reads overlap and puts them together like a gigantic puzzle. This putting together is called **assembly**. It needs special programs and a lot of computing power, which is why biology and computer science work closely together here.

In 1977 Sanger sequenced the first complete genome, that of a small virus, the bacteriophage PhiX174. From 1990 to 2003 the **Human Genome Project** ran, in which researchers from many countries read the human genetic material. It cost about three billion US dollars. Today sequencing a human genome costs only a tiny fraction of that. This has turned the method into an everyday tool of research.

In medicine, sequencing helps to detect rare inherited diseases and to study cancer cells more closely. During the **Covid-19 pandemic**, laboratories around the world, including in Switzerland, used sequencing to track new virus variants. In biology, the genetic material of different species is compared to find out how they are related. Food inspectors and the police also use DNA analysis. Even the genetic material of extinct animals such as the mammoth has been read from old bones.

begriffe.erklaerung: The exact order of the building blocks in a piece of DNA.
One of the four letters of DNA: adenine, thymine, guanine or cytosine.
A single piece of DNA that a sequencing machine has read.
Putting together many short reads into one long complete sequence on a computer.
When a substance glows in colour itself under a certain kind of light.

gewusst: Frederick Sanger received his first Nobel Prize in 1958 for working out the structure of insulin and his second in 1980 for DNA sequencing.
Walter Gilbert shared the 1980 Nobel Prize with Sanger and Paul Berg.
The Human Genome Project took about 13 years; today one machine can do a human genome in about a day.

teile.einleitung: Fossilisation is the process by which remains or traces of living things turn into fossils over a very long time. Only very few animals and plants are so lucky, because usually everything is eaten or broken down by other living things. Thanks to fossils we know today what dinosaurs, prehistoric fish or ancient forests looked like.
wichtigste: A fossil is a remain or a trace of a living thing that lived a very long time ago.
For a fossil to form, the dead living thing must be covered quickly and sealed off from the air.
Most often, hard parts such as bones, teeth and shells are preserved.
In petrification, minerals gradually replace the original material, for example wood.
In amber, a fossil tree resin, insects are often perfectly preserved.
Footprints or feeding burrows are called trace fossils.
The science of fossils is called palaeontology.

abschnitte.text: The word **fossil** comes from the Latin word for “dug up”. Fossils are usually thousands to many millions of years old. They can be petrified bones, mussel shells, leaves or whole tree trunks. Impressions in the rock also count, when the living thing itself has long since disappeared.

When an animal dies, it is normally broken down by scavengers, bacteria and fungi. Only if it is quickly covered by mud, sand or volcanic ash is it protected from oxygen. That is why many fossils form at the bottom of seas, lakes and rivers. Over time the layers become **sedimentary rock**, and water with dissolved minerals seeps into the remains. In this way bone or wood slowly turns to stone.

In **petrification**, cavities are filled with minerals or the material is replaced entirely, as in petrified wood. If a shell dissolves, often only an impression or a **stone core** is left. In amber or in the ice of the permafrost, soft parts are sometimes preserved too, for example in mammoths from Siberia. **Trace fossils** such as dinosaur tracks show how animals moved.

**Palaeontology** studies fossils and with them the history of life on Earth. Palaeontologists dig fossils out carefully, prepare them and compare them with living things of today. From the layer of rock in which a fossil lies, its age can be estimated. Some species such as the coelacanth or the ginkgo have changed so little that they are called **living fossils**.

At Monte San Giorgio in Ticino you find famous fossils of marine reptiles and fish from the Triassic period. The mountain has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003. In Frick in the canton of Aargau, many skeletons of the dinosaur **Plateosaurus** were dug up, and they can be seen in the Dinosaur Museum in Frick. In the Jura, petrified shells and ammonites are also often found, because there was once a sea there.

begriffe.erklaerung: A remain or trace of a living thing from long ago, usually preserved in rock.
The science that studies fossils and the history of life.
Fossil tree resin that has hardened, sometimes with insects trapped in it.
A fossil that shows no body part but a trace such as a footprint or a feeding burrow.
A layer of deposited sand, mud or lime that later becomes rock.

gewusst: Only a tiny fraction of all the living things that ever existed has been preserved as fossils.
The coelacanth was thought to have died out long ago, until a living specimen was caught off South Africa in 1938.
Ammonites were sea creatures with snail-like coiled shells and are popular fossils in the Jura today.

teile.einleitung: Concordia Station is a research station in the middle of the Antarctic ice. France and Italy run it together on Dome C, one of the coldest and loneliest places on Earth. Because of the extreme conditions it is also called the “White Mars”.
wichtigste: Concordia Station is run jointly by France and Italy.
It stands on Dome C, a rise on the Antarctic ice plateau more than 3,000 metres high.
Since 2005 the station has been occupied all year round.
In winter about a dozen people live there for months completely cut off.
ESA uses the station to study the isolation of long space missions.
The EPICA ice core, containing about 800,000 years of climate history, was drilled at Dome C.
The dry, calm air and the long polar night are ideal for observing the stars.

abschnitte.text: The station stands on **Dome C**, a flat dome of the East Antarctic ice sheet. It lies about 3,200 metres above sea level and more than 1,000 kilometres from the nearest coast. Beneath the station there is ice more than three kilometres thick. Because it is so remote, it can only be reached in the short southern summer by plane or with long tractor trains pulling sledges.

On Dome C it is almost always bitterly cold; in winter the temperature drops below minus 80 degrees Celsius. The air is very dry and, because of the altitude, contains less oxygen. From about May to August there is the **polar night**, when the sun does not rise for months. Because of these conditions the station got the nickname **“White Mars”**.

The station was built jointly by France and **Italy**; its name means “harmony” in Latin. It consists of two large round buildings with several floors, connected by a walkway. Since **2005** it has also been lived in during winter. In summer many researchers work there; in winter only a small crew of about a dozen people stays.

At Dome C the European project **EPICA** drilled an **ice core** more than three kilometres long. Tiny air bubbles from earlier times are trapped in the ice. From them you can read how warm it was and how much carbon dioxide the air contained. The core covers about **800,000 years** of climate history, and researchers from the University of Bern were among those who analysed it.

The air above Dome C is extremely dry, clear and calm. That makes the place excellent for **astronomical observations**, especially during the long polar night. The European Space Agency **ESA** also studies there how people cope with cold, darkness and isolation. This helps with planning future journeys to Mars.

The people who spend the winter there cook, work and spend their free time with the same people for months. No outside help can come in winter, so there is always a doctor on site. Generators provide electricity, and water is made from melted **snow**. Many residents say that the first sunlight after the polar night is a special moment.

begriffe.erklaerung: The region around the South Pole with the continent of Antarctica, which is almost completely covered in ice.
A time in polar regions when the sun does not rise for days or months.
A long cylinder of ice drilled from deep down that gives information about the climate in the past.
The European Space Agency, of which Switzerland is also a member.

gewusst: The name Concordia is Latin and means “harmony”; it stands for the cooperation between France and Italy.
Because Concordia Station is so isolated, it serves as a practice site for future journeys to Mars.

teile.einleitung: Dual use means «two kinds of use». It refers to knowledge, technology or goods that can be used for peaceful purposes, but also for harmful purposes such as weapons. Many great inventions have these two sides, and that is why researchers and states have to be especially careful.
wichtigste: Dual use means that something can be used both peacefully and harmfully.
The chemist Fritz Haber is a classic example, because he developed ammonia synthesis and poison gas.
Around 2011 and 2012, research on how the bird flu virus H5N1 spreads caused a big debate.
Gain-of-function research deliberately gives pathogens new abilities.
The Biological Weapons Convention of 1972 bans the development and stockpiling of biological weapons.
In Switzerland, the Goods Control Act regulates the export of dual-use goods.
Spiez Laboratory is the Swiss specialist centre for protection against nuclear, biological and chemical threats.

abschnitte.text: The term means **two kinds of use**. A knife can cut bread, but it can also injure someone, and many inventions are just the same. Rockets carry satellites into space, but they can also carry weapons. Drones help to search for missing people, but they are also used in war. So dual use is not about good or bad things, but about what people use them for.

At the beginning of the 20th century, the German chemist **Fritz Haber** found out how to make ammonia from the nitrogen in the air. With the **Haber-Bosch process** developed from it, artificial fertiliser is still produced today, and it feeds billions of people. Haber received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for ammonia synthesis. In the First World War, however, he also led the development of poison gas, which was used at Ypres in Belgium in 1915. His life shows how close benefit and harm can lie in science.

Around 2011 and 2012, research groups in the Netherlands and the USA changed the bird flu virus **H5N1** so that it could spread through the air between ferrets. They wanted to understand how dangerous the virus could become for humans. Critics feared that someone could misuse the methods. An advisory board in the USA at first recommended not publishing sensitive details of the methods. Experiments like this are called **gain-of-function research**, because the pathogens gain new abilities.

The **Biological Weapons Convention** of 1972 bans the development, production and stockpiling of biological weapons. For chemical weapons there is the Chemical Weapons Convention, which came into force in 1997. The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons in The Hague checks that it is kept. Many countries also agree on which sensitive goods they only export with a permit. This is meant to stop dangerous technology from falling into the wrong hands.

In Switzerland, the **Goods Control Act** regulates when goods with two kinds of use may be sold abroad. The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs SECO is responsible for the permits. This applies, for example, to certain machine tools, chemicals or laboratory equipment. **Spiez Laboratory** in the canton of Bern is the national specialist centre for protection against nuclear, biological and chemical threats. For example, it tests samples for warfare agents on behalf of international organisations.

Researchers have to ask themselves whether their results could be misused. A typical step is a **review of sensitive method details** before publication. Some universities have their own committees for this. At the same time, open research is important, for example so that vaccines can be developed quickly. That is why people always look for a balance between freedom and safety.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something can be used for peaceful and for harmful purposes.
Research in which pathogens are deliberately given new abilities.
The state checks whether sensitive goods may be sold abroad.
A weapon that uses pathogens or poisons from living things.

gewusst: The internet and the satellite navigation system GPS were originally developed by the US military and are used peacefully by almost everyone today.
Artificial fertiliser from the Haber-Bosch process feeds roughly about half of the world's population today.

teile.einleitung: Third-party funding is money that universities and research institutes receive on top of their fixed basic funding. It comes, for example, from research funding bodies, foundations or companies. Many research projects in Switzerland would not be possible without third-party funding.
wichtigste: Third-party funding is research money from sources outside a university's basic funding.
Important funders in Switzerland are the Swiss National Science Foundation and Innosuisse.
Competitive third-party funding is awarded in a competition in which the applications are reviewed.
The overhead covers indirect costs such as infrastructure and administration.
When a company orders and pays for research, it is called contract research.
With money from private companies, there is debate about conflicts of interest and freedom of research.
The third-party funding ratio shows what share of the budget comes from third-party funding.

abschnitte.text: Universities receive money from the state so that they can carry out teaching and research; this is the **basic funding**. On top of that, researchers often get extra money from outside, the **third-party funding**. The name comes from the fact that the money comes from a “third party”, that is, neither from the university itself nor directly from the body that runs it. Third-party funding pays, for example, for the salaries of doctoral students, for equipment or for trips to research sites.

In Switzerland the **Swiss National Science Foundation** (SNSF) is the most important funder of basic research; it was founded in 1952. **Innosuisse** supports projects in which universities and companies develop something new together. Then there are foundations, international programmes such as the EU research programmes, and companies. When a company orders and pays for a project, it is called **contract research**.

abschnitte.titel: How do you get third-party funding?
abschnitte.text: Much third-party funding is **competitive**, which means you have to apply for it in a competition. Researchers write an **application** in which they explain the aim, method and costs of their project. Experts review the applications and compare them with one another. Only the best receive money; if a programme approves, for example, 300 out of 1,200 applications, the success rate is 25 per cent.

The **third-party funding ratio** shows what share of the budget comes from third-party funding. If an institute has a budget of 8 million francs, of which 3 million is third-party funding, the ratio is 3 divided by 8, that is, 37.5 per cent. If a project receives 450,000 francs for 3 years, on average 150,000 francs a year are available. Part of this often goes to the university as **overhead** to cover indirect costs such as rooms, electricity and administration.

Third-party funding makes many projects possible that could not otherwise be financed. It also shows that a research group can convince others in a competition. With money from private companies, however, there is debate about possible **conflicts of interest**. It is important that **freedom of research** is preserved and that unwelcome results may also be published.

Many universities publish who their third-party funding comes from, so that everything is transparent. Young researchers learn early on how to write good applications. School pupils can also win prizes with projects in competitions such as Swiss Youth in Science, a kind of first experience of funding. So if you want to do research, you need not only good ideas but also skill in explaining and planning.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fixed money a university regularly receives from the body that runs it.
A written request asking for money for a project.
An extra amount for indirect costs such as rooms, electricity and administration.
When personal advantages could endanger the independence of a decision.
Research that a company orders from a university and pays for.

gewusst: At some university institutes, more than half of the money comes from third-party funding.
Many doctoral students in Switzerland are paid with money from the Swiss National Science Foundation.

teile.einleitung: ETH Zurich is the federal institute of technology in Zurich and one of the best-known universities in the world. Famous researchers such as Albert Einstein studied here. ETH belongs to the federal government and trains experts in technology, the natural sciences and architecture.
wichtigste: ETH is in Zurich, and the T in the name stands for technology.
Young adults study at ETH after leaving school, for example computer science or physics.
ETH is financed mainly by the federal government.
The main building was designed by the architect Gottfried Semper.
The second large site, on the edge of the city, is called Hönggerberg.
The Polybahn runs up from Central to ETH.
Together with EPFL and four research institutes it forms the ETH Domain.

abschnitte.text: ETH Zurich is a **technical university** where you can study after finishing school. Subjects on offer include computer science, physics, chemistry, mathematics, biology, mechanical engineering, architecture and environmental sciences. Today more than twenty thousand people from many countries study there. ETH regularly takes top places in international rankings.

Shortly after the founding of the federal state, parliament decided to create a national technical school. In 1855 the **Federal Polytechnic** opened in Zurich. This is where the nickname Poly comes from, which is still used today. Since 1911 the school has been called the Federal Institute of Technology.

The splendid **main building** above the old town was designed by the German architect Gottfried Semper. From Central, the small funicular **Polybahn** runs up to ETH. Because space in the centre became tight, a second site was built at Hönggerberg on the edge of the city. Many laboratories and institutes are there today.

Albert Einstein studied at ETH and completed his studies in 1900. The physicist **Wolfgang Pauli** taught at ETH for a long time and received the Nobel Prize in 1945. Richard Ernst received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1991 for developing NMR spectroscopy further, which is now used in hospitals for images of the body. In all, ETH is linked with more than 20 Nobel Prize winners.

Together with EPFL in Lausanne and four research institutes, ETH Zurich forms the **ETH Domain**. These research institutes are the Paul Scherrer Institute, WSL, Empa and Eawag. The ETH Domain is run strategically by the **ETH Board**. It comes under the Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research.

ETH has one of the largest libraries in Switzerland. It also houses the **Thomas Mann Archive** with books, letters and belongings of the famous German writer. Thomas Mann lived his last years near Zurich. ETH also has collections on earth sciences, graphic art and art.

begriffe.erklaerung: An earlier name for a school where many technical subjects are taught.
The body that runs ETH, EPFL and the research institutes.
A famous award for outstanding achievements in science.
A railway pulled up a steep slope by a cable.
The school-leaving qualification that allows you to study at a university.

gewusst: Albert Einstein failed the ETH entrance examination at his first attempt, because he was too weak in some subjects.
The Polybahn is more than 130 years old and covers only a short but steep stretch.
From the terrace of the ETH main building you have one of the finest views over the old town of Zurich.

teile.einleitung: A research station is a permanent place where scientists live and do research, often in very remote spots. The best known are in the Antarctic and the Arctic, where it is icy cold and stays dark for months. There are also such stations high in the Alps and even in space.
wichtigste: Research stations are places where researchers live and work for longer periods.
Many countries run stations in the Antarctic, and most people work there in the Antarctic summer.
Some stations stand on stilts so that they do not sink into the snow.
The Belgian station Princess Elisabeth gets its electricity mainly from wind and sun.
Food and fuel come by ship and plane.
Researchers regularly send up weather balloons and drill ice cores out of the ice.
The Swiss Polar Institute supports Swiss polar research.

abschnitte.text: A **research station** is a building or a small settlement in which researchers live and work. It usually stands where something special can be studied, such as ice, weather, animals or stars. There are stations in deserts, in the rainforest, on islands, on mountains and on the sea floor. The best known are the **polar stations** in the Arctic and the Antarctic. The International Space Station ISS is also a research station, just in space.

In the **Antarctic**, about 30 countries run dozens of stations. Since the Antarctic Treaty of 1959, the continent may only be used peacefully and for research. The American Amundsen-Scott station stands right at the South Pole, and the German **Neumayer Station III** on hydraulic stilts so that it does not sink into the snow. The French-Italian station **Concordia** lies at more than 3,000 metres, where it can get colder than minus 70 degrees in winter. The Belgian station Princess Elisabeth gets its electricity mainly from wind and sun.

Most people work on the stations in the **Antarctic summer** from about November to February. In winter only small teams stay, who cannot leave for months because it is dark and too cold for aircraft. Food, fuel and materials come by **ship** and plane. Because people at Concordia live cut off from the world for a long time, the European Space Agency studies there how people might cope with long journeys in space. The researchers also cook, clean and make repairs themselves.

Researchers drill **ice cores** out of the ice to find out what the climate was like in the past. They regularly send **weather balloons** up into the sky, which measure temperature, wind and humidity. They observe penguins, seals and life in the ice-cold sea. Because of the clear, dry air, some stations are also very well suited to astronomy. In the Antarctic, researchers also discovered the **ozone hole** in the 1980s.

abschnitte.titel: Research in the ice of the Arctic
abschnitte.text: In the Arctic there is no continent but a frozen sea. That is why research there is often done from ships or on islands such as Svalbard, where several countries run stations. In 2019 and 2020 the German research vessel **Polarstern** let itself drift with the sea ice through the Arctic for a year on the MOSAiC expedition. On the ice, researchers from many countries set up measuring stations. Swiss researchers took part too.

Switzerland does not have its own polar station, but the **Swiss Polar Institute** has supported polar research and high mountain research since 2016. On the **Jungfraujoch**, at more than 3,400 metres, stands one of the highest research stations in Europe. There, air pollutants, greenhouse gases and radiation from space are measured, for example. The Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research in Davos also runs measuring stations in the mountains. Swiss researchers also work at many stations run by other countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: A research station in the Arctic or the Antarctic.
An agreement of 1959 that protects the Antarctic for peace and research.
A balloon filled with gas that carries instruments high into the air.
A research journey into a remote area.

gewusst: At the Russian station Vostok in 1983, minus 89.2 degrees was measured, the lowest air temperature ever observed directly on Earth.
Some Antarctic stations have greenhouses in which fresh vegetables grow without soil.
The Polarstern is an icebreaker and can push through ice more than a metre thick.

teile.einleitung: An erratic boulder is a large chunk of rock that a glacier often carried many kilometres during an ice age. When the ice melted, the stone was left lying in the middle of a strange landscape. That is why an erratic boulder usually does not match the rock around it, and that makes it a fascinating witness to the history of the Earth.
wichtigste: Erratic boulders are large stones that were carried by glaciers.
You can often recognise them because they do not match the rock around them.
In Switzerland many erratic boulders are found on the Swiss Plateau and at the southern foot of the Jura.
Erratic boulders show researchers how far the glaciers once reached.
In old legends, giants are said to have hurled the boulders through the air.
Many erratic boulders were broken up in the past, because the stone was needed for building.
Today many erratic boulders are protected.

abschnitte.text: An erratic boulder, also called an **erratic block**, is a chunk of rock lying far from where it came from. Some are as small as a football, others as big as a house and weigh many tonnes. What is typical is that the rock does not match the ground beneath it. A block of granite from the Alps lying on limestone in the Jura is a classic erratic boulder.

During the **ice ages**, large parts of Switzerland were covered by mighty glaciers. Rockfalls in the Alps dropped stones onto the ice, or the glacier tore them from the ground. The ice moved slowly down the valley and carried the stones along like a gigantic conveyor belt. When the glaciers melted away at the end of the last ice age, the boulders were left lying.

There are especially many erratic boulders on the **Swiss Plateau** and on the slopes of the Jura. In the last great glaciation the Rhone Glacier reached as far as the area around Solothurn and brought rock with it from Valais. A famous example is the **Pierre à Bot** above Neuchâtel, a huge block of granite from the Mont Blanc area. There are also many erratic boulders of Glarus and Grisons rock in the canton of Zurich and around Lake Zurich.

Because the origin of the rock can be determined, erratic boulders show the path and the extent of the glaciers of the past. In the 19th century Swiss researchers such as Ignaz Venetz and Jean de Charpentier studied the erratic boulders closely. Their observations helped to establish the idea of the **ice age**. The naturalist Louis Agassiz, who worked in Neuchâtel, later made the ice age theory known worldwide.

In the past people could not explain how the huge stones got to where they were. In many **legends** it is said that giants or the devil hurled them through the air. Many erratic boulders were broken up because the stone was needed for houses, walls or fountains. To save the last ones, conservationists and municipalities bought individual blocks in the 19th century. Today many erratic boulders are protected as **natural monuments**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A stone that a glacier carried far from where it came from.
The technical term for an erratic boulder, from the Latin word for “to wander about”.
A long cold period in which glaciers covered large areas.
A special natural object that is protected by law.

gewusst: Some erratic boulders in northern Germany come from Scandinavia and were carried across what is now the Baltic Sea.
Erratic boulders often have names like devil's stone or heathen stone, which recall old legends.
From the distribution of erratic boulders it was possible to reconstruct where the ice age glaciers reached their greatest extent.

teile.einleitung: An ensemble forecast is a weather forecast in which a computer model is run not just once but many times with slightly different starting values. This lets meteorologists see how certain or uncertain a forecast is. It also produces statements such as “70 per cent chance of rain”.
wichtigste: Small initial errors grow strongly in the chaotic atmosphere, which is why ensemble forecasts are needed.
With his research on chaos, the meteorologist Edward Lorenz coined the term “butterfly effect”.
A wide spread of the runs means that the forecast is uncertain.
The run with the unchanged best initial state is called the control run.
The ECMWF ensemble traditionally has 51 members.
If 34 of 51 runs show rain, the chance of rain is about 67 per cent.
A spaghetti diagram shows the same contour line from all the runs on top of each other.
The average of all the runs is often more accurate, because random errors partly cancel out.

abschnitte.text: Weather forecasts are calculated by **computer models** that reproduce the physics of the atmosphere. For this, the model needs a starting state from measurements by weather stations, balloons, aircraft and satellites. But these measurements are never completely precise and do not cover every place. That is why, in an **ensemble forecast**, the model is run many times with slightly different starting values. The individual calculations are called **runs** or members of the ensemble.

In the 1960s the US meteorologist **Edward Lorenz** discovered that tiny differences at the start of a weather calculation can lead to completely different weather after a few days. He once asked whether the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil could set off a tornado in Texas. From this came the term **butterfly effect**. So the atmosphere is a **chaotic system** in which small errors grow strongly. That is why the weather can only be forecast about one to two weeks ahead.

If the runs lie close together, the forecast is certain; with a wide **spread** it is uncertain. A **spaghetti diagram** shows the same line, such as a particular air pressure line, from all the runs on top of each other. If the lines run wildly apart, the picture looks like a plate of spaghetti. From the number of runs showing rain, a **probability** is calculated. If, for example, 34 of 51 runs show rain, the chance of rain is about 67 per cent.

One run is calculated with the unchanged best initial state, and it is called the **control run**. All the other runs start with small disturbances. From all the runs the **ensemble mean** is calculated. For several days ahead, this average is often more accurate than a single run, because random errors partly cancel out. For severe weather warnings, however, individual extreme runs are also looked at.

The **European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts**, or ECMWF, has been calculating ensemble forecasts regularly since 1992. Its global ensemble traditionally has 51 members: one control run and 50 altered runs. Switzerland is a member of the ECMWF and uses its data. **MeteoSwiss** also calculates its own very fine ensembles for the Alpine region, because mountains and valleys strongly affect the weather. In weather apps you often see the results as probabilities or as a range of temperatures.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of many forecast runs that are looked at together.
The run calculated with the unchanged best starting state.
A system in which tiny differences at the start have big consequences later.
A line on a map joining places with the same value, such as the same air pressure.

gewusst: Ensemble forecasts need so much computing power that they run on some of the largest supercomputers in the world.
Edward Lorenz discovered chaos by chance when he repeated a calculation with rounded starting values and got a completely different result.

teile.einleitung: Dimensional analysis is a method from physics and engineering in which you calculate with units such as metres, kilograms and seconds. It lets you check whether a formula can be right at all, and sometimes even guess new formulas. It is a simple but very powerful tool.
wichtigste: Every physical quantity has a dimension, for example length L, mass M or time T.
A force has the dimension M · L · T^-2.
The joule can be written as kg · m² · s^-2, the pascal as kg · m^-1 · s^-2.
In a correct formula both sides must have the same dimension.
For a simple pendulum, dimensional analysis gives: T is proportional to √(l/g).
The Buckingham Π theorem allows relationships to be written with dimensionless numbers.
In 1999 the NASA probe Mars Climate Orbiter was lost because units were mixed up.

abschnitte.text: In physics the **dimension** describes what kind of quantity something is. A distance is a length L, whether you measure it in metres or kilometres. Speed has the dimension length divided by time, that is, L · T^-1. The basis is formed by the **SI base units** such as the metre, kilogram and second.

An equation can only be right if the **same dimension** is on the left and the right. You cannot compare apples with metres or add seconds to kilograms. That is why only a formula like E = ½ · m · v² is possible for kinetic energy, because kg · m² · s^-2 gives exactly one **joule**. The argument of a sine or exponential function must also be dimensionless.

The period T of a **simple pendulum** depends on the length of the string l and the acceleration due to gravity g. The only combination that gives a time is the square root of l divided by g. It follows that T is proportional to √(l/g), without needing an experiment. Dimensional analysis only fails to reveal a fixed numerical factor, here 2π.

The **Buckingham Π theorem** of 1914 says: a relationship with n quantities and k basic dimensions can be written with n minus k dimensionless numbers. A famous one is the **Reynolds number**, named after the British engineer Osborne Reynolds. It compares inertial forces with viscous forces and predicts whether a flow is smooth or turbulent. Thanks to such numbers, aircraft or ships can be tested as small models in a wind tunnel or water tank.

In 1999 the NASA probe **Mars Climate Orbiter** burned up in the atmosphere of Mars. One team had calculated in pound-force seconds, while the other expected newton seconds. Because of this **mix-up of units**, the probe flew far too low. The case shows how important it is to calculate carefully with units.

begriffe.erklaerung: The kind of a physical quantity, for example length, mass or time.
The international system of units of measurement such as the metre, kilogram and second.
A number without a unit, because all the units have cancelled out.
A number that shows whether a flow is smooth or swirling.

gewusst: The British physicist G. I. Taylor estimated the explosive power of the first atomic bomb from photos and dimensional analysis alone.
If you always check the units in your calculations at school, you will find many mistakes before you even work out the numbers.
The Mach number, which gives an aircraft's speed compared with the speed of sound, is also dimensionless.

teile.einleitung: EPFL is the federal institute of technology in Lausanne, in French the École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne. Together with ETH Zurich it belongs to the federal government and is one of the best technical universities in the world. Its campus lies right on the shore of Lake Geneva.
wichtigste: EPFL is in Lausanne on Lake Geneva.
In everyday life, French is mainly spoken at EPFL.
The F in EPFL stands for fédérale, that is, federal.
Since 1969 EPFL has belonged to the federal government, like ETH Zurich.
Research and study at EPFL focus above all on technology and the natural sciences.
EPFL students built the first Swiss satellite, SwissCube.
The Rolex Learning Center with its wavy floor opened in 2010.

abschnitte.text: EPFL is a **technical university** where young adults study after leaving school. You can learn computer science, architecture, physics, mechanical engineering or life sciences there, for example. Alongside teaching, a great deal of research is done. Today more than ten thousand people from all over the world study there.

The roots of EPFL go back to 1853, when a private engineering school was founded in Lausanne. Later the school belonged to the University of Lausanne. In 1969 the **federal government** took over the institution, and since then it has been called a federal institute of technology. After that it moved to a large new campus in Ecublens, right by the lake.

The campus lies right next to the **University of Lausanne**, with which EPFL works closely. One landmark is the **Rolex Learning Center**, a library and learning centre with a wave-shaped floor and roof. It opened in 2010 and was designed by Japanese architects. EPFL also has outlying sites, for example in Sion in Valais, where research is done on energy among other things.

EPFL students built the small satellite **SwissCube**, which in 2009 became the first Swiss satellite to be launched into space. EPFL also took part in research on the aircraft Solar Impulse, which flew around the world on solar energy alone. From 2005 the Blue Brain Project tried to reproduce parts of the brain in a computer. The company ClearSpace, which came out of EPFL, wants to remove space debris from orbit.

Together with ETH Zurich and four research institutes, EPFL forms the **ETH Domain**. Both universities are financed mainly by the federal government. Many students come from abroad, which is why teaching in later years is often in English. Numerous young companies, known as start-ups, come out of EPFL every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: A school for adults where people study and do research.
The grounds on which all the buildings of a university stand.
Belonging to the Confederation, that is, to the whole of Switzerland.
A young company with a new idea.
A craft that orbits the Earth in space.

gewusst: SwissCube was a cube with sides of only about 10 centimetres and weighed about one kilogram.
In the Rolex Learning Center there are hardly any stairs; you walk over gentle hills and valleys in the floor.
EPFL has its own metro station, because line M1 of the Lausanne metro runs right to the campus.

teile.einleitung: The fly agaric is probably the best-known mushroom in the world: a red cap with white spots. It looks as if it came out of a fairy tale book, but it is poisonous. All the same, in our part of the world it is seen as a symbol of good luck.
wichtigste: The fly agaric has a red cap with white spots.
It is poisonous and must not be eaten.
The white spots are the remains of a protective covering from the mushroom's youth.
Under the cap it has white gills.
You often find it under birches and spruces, usually in autumn.
In the past it was used against flies, which probably explains its name.
In our part of the world it is a popular symbol of good luck, for example at New Year.

abschnitte.text: The cap of the fly agaric is bright red to orange-red and can grow about 5 to 20 centimetres wide. The white flakes on it are the remains of a **covering** that surrounds the young mushroom like an egg and tears open as it grows. Rain can wash the spots off, and then the cap is completely red. Under the cap there are white **gills**, and the white stalk has a ring and a bulb-like swelling at the bottom.

The fly agaric grows in the woods of Europe, Asia and North America, and it is common in Switzerland too. It lives in a close partnership with trees, above all with **birches** and **spruces**, and sometimes with pines. Its fine fungal threads wrap around the tree roots and exchange water and minerals for sugar. This cooperation is called **mycorrhiza**.

The fly agaric contains poisons such as **ibotenic acid** and muscimol, which act on the nervous system. After eating it, people can become confused and suffer nausea, dizziness and deep sleep. Deaths are rare, but poisoning is dangerous and must be treated. So you should only eat mushrooms if an expert at a **mushroom inspection point** has checked them.

In the past, pieces of the mushroom were put in a bowl with milk and sugar. Flies drank from it and were stupefied or died. That is probably where the German name **Fliegenpilz** comes from. It is similar in other languages; in English it is called “fly agaric”.

In German-speaking countries the fly agaric, together with the four-leaf clover, the horseshoe and the chimney sweep, is seen as a **bringer of luck**. At New Year it is often given as a figure made of chocolate or marzipan. It is also popular in children's books, garden gnome gardens and computer games. Its striking red colour is a **warning colour**, like those known from other poisonous living things.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thin sheets under the cap where the spores form
Tiny particles with which fungi spread
Fungi and tree roots living together for mutual benefit
A place where experts check gathered mushrooms for poisonous ones

gewusst: The actual fungus is a huge network of threads in the soil, and the red cap is only its fruiting body.
In many Swiss municipalities you can have gathered mushrooms checked free of charge at an official mushroom inspection point.
A young fly agaric looks like a white egg, and the red colour only appears as it grows.

teile.einleitung: A research vessel is a floating laboratory with which scientists study the seas. On board there are measuring instruments, cranes, winches and often diving robots. Research vessels have revealed many secrets of the deep sea and the polar regions.
wichtigste: Research vessels are floating laboratories for marine research.
With a CTD probe they measure the conductivity, temperature and depth of the water.
Steel cables kilometres long on winches lower instruments into the depths.
Cores from the sea floor reveal something about the climate of the past.
ROVs are remotely operated underwater robots.
From 1893 Fridtjof Nansen let the Fram drift in the pack ice.
In 1986 the submersible Alvin visited the wreck of the Titanic.

abschnitte.text: A **research vessel** is specially built to collect knowledge about the sea, the sea floor and the weather. On board, researchers work in **laboratories** while the crew steers the ship. Some ships are at sea for weeks or months. Icebreakers such as the German **Polarstern** can even sail through the ice of the Arctic and the Antarctic.

One of the most important instruments is the **CTD probe**, which measures conductivity, temperature and depth. From the conductivity you can work out how salty the water is. With winches and **steel cables** kilometres long, the researchers lower instruments and water bottles into the depths. With drill pipes they bring up cores from the sea floor, whose layers show what the climate was like thousands of years ago.

From many ships an **ROV** is deployed, a remotely operated underwater robot with cameras and grabbing arms. It hangs on a cable and is steered from the ship. The manned submersible **Alvin** from the USA visited the wreck of the Titanic in 1986. Today thousands of drifting **Argo floats** add to the measurements; they dive and surface by themselves and send their data via satellites.

From 1893 the Norwegian Fridtjof Nansen let the **Fram** drift in the pack ice through the Arctic Ocean. The British HMS Challenger sailed around the world from 1872 to 1876 and is regarded as the beginning of modern marine research. The Frenchman Jacques-Yves Cousteau explored the underwater world with his ship **Calypso** and showed it in films. His ship had previously been a minesweeper.

Switzerland has no sea, but Swiss people have shaped deep-sea research greatly. The physicist Auguste Piccard developed the submersible **Trieste**. In 1960 his son Jacques Piccard dived with it, together with Don Walsh, into the Mariana Trench, the deepest place in the world's oceans. On Swiss lakes too there are small research boats that measure water quality, for example.

begriffe.erklaerung: An instrument for measuring the conductivity, temperature and depth of sea water
A remotely operated underwater robot that hangs on a cable
A long cylinder of rock or mud drilled out of the ground
A drifting measuring robot that dives and surfaces by itself
Sea ice pushed together in the polar regions

gewusst: The Fram was built so that the pack ice pushed it upwards instead of crushing it.
The sea floor is less well mapped than the surface of the Moon.
A research vessel can lower instruments on cables several kilometres deep.

teile.einleitung: Electrostatics is a branch of physics that deals with electric charges at rest. You know it from everyday life: when a balloon rubs against your hair, or when you get a small shock from a door handle, electrostatics is at work. You can explore it well with simple experiments.
wichtigste: A balloon rubbed on your hair attracts the hair, so that it stands up.
A rubbed balloon sticks to the wall.
A thin stream of water bends towards a rubbed balloon.
Two balloons rubbed on your hair repel each other.
When you pull off a woollen jumper quickly, you can sometimes see tiny sparks in the dark.
The balloon experiment works best with dry hair.
You get a shock from a door handle when your body is electrically charged.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of atoms, and these contain **positive** and **negative** charges. Normally they balance out, and an object is electrically neutral. If you rub two materials against each other, tiny negative particles, the **electrons**, move from one material to the other. Then one object has too many and the other too few electrons. Because these charges are at rest and do not flow as they do in a cable, we speak of static electricity.

If you rub a balloon on your hair, the balloon takes up electrons and becomes negatively charged. Your hair becomes positive and stands up towards the balloon as you slowly pull it away. If you hold the balloon against the wall, it sticks, and little **scraps of paper** jump up to it. Even a thin stream of water from the tap bends towards the balloon. Two balloons with the same charge, on the other hand, repel each other.

A simple rule applies: **like charges repel each other, unlike charges attract.** The force becomes stronger the closer the charges are to each other. The French physicist Charles-Augustin de Coulomb measured this law precisely in 1785. Neutral objects such as paper are also attracted, because their charges shift slightly for a moment. Damp air carries the charges away quickly, which is why the experiments work best with dry hair and on dry winter days.

If you walk across a carpet with rubber soles, your body becomes charged. If you then touch a metal **door handle**, the charge is released with a small shock. When you pull off a woollen jumper quickly it crackles, and in the dark you can see tiny sparks. The spark has a voltage of several thousand volts, but very little current flows, so it is harmless. The biggest spark in nature is **lightning** in a thunderstorm.

About 2,600 years ago the Greek scholar Thales of Miletus already observed that rubbed **amber** attracts feathers. The Greek word for amber, “elektron”, gave electricity its name. Today electrostatics is used in laser printers and photocopiers, where charged toner powder sticks to the paper. In filters at power stations, dust is caught in this way, and when cars are painted the paint sticks better. In factories for computer chips, on the other hand, people have to protect against discharges, because they can destroy components.

begriffe.erklaerung: A property of particles that can be positive or negative.
A tiny, negatively charged particle in the shell of an atom.
The balancing out of charges, often with a spark.
The shifting of charges in an object when a charge comes near it.

gewusst: Tankers and aircraft are earthed while being refuelled, so that no spark can set the fuel alight.
A Van de Graaff generator can collect so much charge that the hair of a person touching it stands on end.

teile.einleitung: In genetics, dominance is the term for one inherited trait winning out over another. Every living thing has two versions of many genes, and often only one of them decides what it looks like. This version is called dominant and the weaker one recessive.
wichtigste: A dominant allele wins out in the appearance.
In a cross diagram, a dominant allele is written with a capital letter and a recessive one with a small letter.
Gregor Mendel introduced the terms “dominant” and “recessive” into genetics.
A genotype like Aa, with one dominant and one recessive allele, is called heterozygous.
In a cross between AA and aa, all the offspring show the dominant feature.
A recessive feature only shows when both alleles are recessive, for example ss.
In blood group AB, both alleles are fully expressed; this is called codominance.

abschnitte.text: Many genes are present twice in a living thing, with one version coming from each parent. The different versions of a gene are called **alleles**. When two different alleles come together, one of them often wins out in the appearance. This allele is called **dominant**, the other one **recessive**.

In the 19th century the monk **Gregor Mendel** crossed thousands of **pea plants** in the monastery in Brno. He observed features such as flower colour and the shape of the seeds. He noticed that some features disappeared in the next generation and later reappeared. He introduced the terms “dominant” and “recessive” for this and published his results in 1866.

In a **cross diagram**, dominant alleles are written with a capital letter, for example A, and recessive ones with a small letter, a. If a living thing has two identical alleles, AA or aa, it is **homozygous**. If it has two different ones, Aa, it is called **heterozygous**. If you cross AA with aa, all the offspring are Aa and show the dominant feature.

Suppose black fur S is dominant over white fur s. Animals with SS or Ss then have black fur. Only animals with **ss** have white fur, because there is no dominant allele. If you cross two heterozygous animals Ss with each other, you would expect on average three black animals for every white one.

It is not always just one allele that wins out. In **blood groups**, the alleles A and B are both dominant over the allele 0. But when A and B come together, both are fully expressed and blood group AB results; this is called **codominance**. Some plants also have in-between forms, such as pink flowers from red and white parents.

Knowing about dominance lets you predict which features are likely to appear in offspring. **Breeders** use this with plants and animals, for example for hornless cattle or particular fur colours. In medicine too, it helps to understand how some inherited diseases are passed on. The important thing is: dominant does not mean more common or better, only that the allele wins out in the appearance.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of several possible versions of a gene.
An allele that only shows when no dominant allele is present.
The combination of alleles that a living thing has.
The visible appearance of a living thing, for example its fur colour.
When two different alleles are both fully visible in the appearance.

gewusst: Mendel's work was hardly noticed during his lifetime and was only rediscovered around 1900.
A dominant feature can still be rare in a population.

teile.einleitung: Chemosynthesis is the way some living things make nutrients without needing sunlight. Instead of light, they use the energy from chemical reactions with substances such as hydrogen sulphide or methane. This allows whole communities of living things to exist in the complete darkness of the deep sea.
wichtigste: In chemosynthesis, organic substances are built up using energy from chemical reactions instead of light.
The main difference from photosynthesis is the source of energy.
At hydrothermal vents, many bacteria use hydrogen sulphide as a source of energy.
At cold seeps on the seabed, methane serves as the source of energy.
Sergei Winogradsky was the first to describe chemosynthesis, in the 19th century.
Living things that live this way and use CO2 as their source of carbon are called chemoautotrophic.
Chemosynthesis also happens on land, for example in nitrifying bacteria.

abschnitte.text: All living things need energy and building materials. Plants get their energy from sunlight; this is **photosynthesis**. In **chemosynthesis**, on the other hand, the energy comes from chemical reactions with inorganic substances. With this energy, the living things build sugar and other organic substances from **carbon dioxide**.

In the 19th century the Russian microbiologist **Sergei Winogradsky** studied sulphur bacteria. He found that they get energy from sulphur compounds, without any light at all. In this way he was the first to describe chemosynthesis. Such living things are called **chemoautotrophic**, because they feed themselves with the help of chemical energy.

In 1977 researchers in a submersible discovered hot springs on the seabed in the Pacific, known as **hydrothermal vents**. There, heated water full of **hydrogen sulphide** streams out of the ground. Bacteria use this substance for chemosynthesis and form the basis of a rich community of life. Giant tube worms, mussels and crabs live there in complete darkness.

It is not only hot vents that make chemosynthesis possible. At **cold seeps**, methane comes out of the seabed, and microbes use it as a source of energy. When a dead whale sinks to the sea floor, a special community of life also forms. As the bones break down, sulphur compounds are released, and chemosynthetic bacteria live on them.

Chemosynthesis also takes place in the soil. **Nitrifying bacteria** turn ammonium into nitrite and then into nitrate, gaining energy as they do so. Nitrate is an important nutrient for plants. These bacteria also work in sewage treatment plants and help to clean waste water.

Chemosynthesis shows that life is possible even without sunlight. Some researchers think that life on Earth might have begun at hot vents like these. That is why chemosynthesis is also of interest in the search for life in space. There might be similar vents under the ice of some moons in the solar system.

begriffe.erklaerung: Making sugar with the help of sunlight, as plants do.
A living thing that gets energy from chemical reactions and uses carbon dioxide.
A hot spring on the seabed from which mineral-rich water streams out.
A poisonous gas that smells of rotten eggs.
The conversion of ammonium into nitrate by bacteria.

gewusst: The giant tube worms at hot vents have neither a mouth nor a gut; they are fed by bacteria inside their bodies.
Some hydrothermal vents give out black water and are therefore called black smokers.
A single whale carcass on the sea floor can feed living things for many years.

teile.einleitung: An ice grotto is a tunnel or cave in the ice of a glacier. Some form naturally through meltwater, while others are dug into the glacier by people so that visitors can walk inside. Inside, the ice glows a beautiful blue.
wichtigste: An ice grotto is a tunnel or cave in the ice.
The ice glows blue because thick ice absorbs red light.
On the Jungfraujoch there is an ice palace inside the glacier at more than 3,400 metres.
The ice grotto in the Rhone Glacier has to be dug again every year, because the glacier flows and melts.
In an ice grotto it is about zero degrees.
In summer meltwater often drips from the ceiling.
A natural cave that meltwater has eaten into a glacier is called a glacier cave.

abschnitte.text: An **ice grotto** is a hollow space in glacier ice that you can walk through. Many ice grottos in the Alps are dug artificially and are meant for tourists. Natural caves in a glacier are called **glacier caves**. They form when meltwater eats a way through or under the ice. These are not to be confused with ice caves in rock, in which ice lies all year round.

Sunlight consists of all the colours of the rainbow. When light travels through thick, dense glacier ice, the **red light** is absorbed more strongly than the blue. What is left is mainly blue light, and that is why the ice glows blue. The thicker and clearer the ice, the stronger the colour. White ice, on the other hand, contains many air bubbles that scatter the light in all directions.

abschnitte.titel: The ice palace on the Jungfraujoch
abschnitte.text: On the **Jungfraujoch**, at about 3,450 metres above sea level, lies the ice palace. Mountain guides began hewing tunnels into the glacier ice in the 1930s. Today you can walk through the icy tunnels and admire ice figures, for example animals made of ice. The glacier moves here too, so the tunnels have to be repaired regularly. The Jungfraujoch can be reached with the Jungfrau Railway and is part of the Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.titel: The ice grotto in the Rhone Glacier
abschnitte.text: At the **Rhone Glacier** near the Furka Pass in the canton of Valais, a new ice grotto has been dug every spring for many decades. This is necessary because the glacier slowly flows down the valley and melts in summer. To slow the melting, part of the glacier is covered with **white sheets** in summer. The Rhone Glacier has shrunk considerably in the last 150 years, which can be clearly seen on site. Its meltwater forms the Rhone, which later flows through Lake Geneva.

In an ice grotto it is about **zero degrees** all year round, even when the sun is shining outside. So you should wear a warm jacket, a hat and good shoes. The floor can be slippery, and in summer **meltwater** drips from the ceiling. You should never enter natural glacier caves without experts, because they can collapse suddenly. The secured ice grottos for visitors, on the other hand, are well monitored.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large mass of ice from compressed snow that slowly flows down the valley.
A natural cave that meltwater has eaten into a glacier.
Water that forms when snow or ice melts.
The slow movement of glacier ice down the valley.

gewusst: A glacier can flow many metres further in a year, so ice grottos are constantly changing.
The white sheets on the Rhone Glacier reflect the sunlight, rather as a white T-shirt is cooler in summer than a black one.

teile.einleitung: An ethics committee is a group of experts and lay people that checks whether research involving people is fair and safe. Before a new medicine is tested on volunteers, for example, the committee has to look at the project and approve it. In this way the rights and the health of the participants are protected.
wichtigste: Ethics committees check research projects involving people before they begin.
They are interdisciplinary, with expert and lay members.
In Switzerland the ethics committees for human research are organised by canton.
Their umbrella organisation is called swissethics.
Clinical trials with medicines must also be approved by Swissmedic.
If dangers become known, a committee can withdraw the approval or impose conditions.
The national commissions NEK and ECNH advise politicians and the public.

abschnitte.text: The word **ethics** means thinking about what is right and good. An ethics committee is a body that examines exactly such questions in research. It looks, for example, at whether the benefit of an experiment justifies the possible risks. It also makes sure that nobody is pushed into taking part.

Before starting, researchers submit a detailed plan of their project. The committee checks whether the aim makes sense, whether the methods are scientifically sound and whether the risks are kept small. **Consent** is also important: participants must be informed in an understandable way and must agree voluntarily. Only with an **approval** may the project start.

Ethics committees are **interdisciplinary**. They include, for example, doctors, nursing professionals, lawyers and experts in statistics and ethics. Often lay members also sit on them to bring in the view of the public. In the USA such bodies are usually called Institutional Review Boards.

The basis is the **Human Research Act**, which has applied since 2014. The ethics committees are organised by canton, and their umbrella organisation is called **swissethics**. For clinical trials with medicines, the federal authority Swissmedic must also give its consent. During a project too, the committee can step in, impose conditions or withdraw the approval.

Besides the committees that approve individual projects, there are advisory bodies. The **National Advisory Commission on Biomedical Ethics** (NEK) advises politicians and the public on difficult questions in medicine. The **ECNH** deals with ethical questions of biotechnology in animals, plants and the environment. For animal experiments there are separate cantonal committees.

An important milestone was the **Declaration of Helsinki** of the World Medical Association in 1964. It states that research involving people must be reviewed independently. Since then, ethics committees have been required in many countries. They make sure that people can trust research.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thinking about what is right, good and fair.
Research involving people or data and samples from people.
Voluntary agreement after being well informed.
A study in which, for example, a new medicine is tested with volunteers.

gewusst: Anyone taking part in a study may drop out at any time without having to give a reason.
Research with children is also possible, but only under especially strict rules.
The ethics committee even checks whether the information sheets for participants are written in an understandable way.

teile.einleitung: Claude Bernard was a French doctor and physiologist, that is, a researcher who studies how the body works. He is regarded as one of the founders of experimental medicine. His idea of the body's inner balance is still a cornerstone of biology today.
wichtigste: Claude Bernard lived in France from 1813 to 1878.
He was an assistant to the physiologist François Magendie.
He coined the term milieu intérieur for the stable surroundings of the body's cells.
He discovered the storage substance glycogen in the liver.
He showed that the arrow poison curare blocks the signal from nerve to muscle.
In 1865 he published his fundamental work on experimental medicine.
Later, Walter Cannon coined the term homeostasis for his idea.

abschnitte.text: Claude Bernard was born in 1813 in a village in the Beaujolais, a wine region in France. As a young man he first wanted to write plays. But a critic advised him to study medicine. In Paris he became an assistant to **François Magendie** and later a professor at the Collège de France.

Bernard's most important idea was the **milieu intérieur**, the inner environment. By this he meant the fluid around the body's cells, which must always stay as constant as possible. The body constantly balances temperature, salt levels and sugar in the blood. The American physiologist **Walter Cannon** later called this balance **homeostasis**.

Bernard discovered that the **liver** stores sugar as **glycogen** and releases it into the blood when needed. He proved that the juice of the **pancreas** breaks down fats. He also showed that nerves control how wide the blood vessels are. This lets vessels become narrower or wider and regulate blood flow.

Bernard used poisons to understand the body better. The South American arrow poison **curare** blocks the signal from nerve to muscle, so that the muscles go limp. With **carbon monoxide**, he found out that it pushes oxygen out of the blood pigment. That is why this invisible gas is so dangerous.

In 1865 his book “Introduction à l'étude de la médecine expérimentale” was published. In it he demanded that medicine should be based on careful **experiments** and not on guesswork. You should put forward an idea, test it with experiments and reject it if it is wrong. Bernard carried out many **animal experiments**, which was already strongly criticised at the time and is still debated today.

In 1868 Bernard was elected to the famous **Académie française**. When he died in 1878, he was the first scientist in France to receive a state funeral. Claude Bernard University Lyon 1 is named after him. His way of thinking still shapes medicine and physiology today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of how the body and its organs work.
The balance that the body maintains inside.
A storage substance made of sugar in the liver and muscles.
An arrow poison from South America that paralyses muscles.

gewusst: As a young man, Claude Bernard wrote a play before he became a doctor.
In a modified form, curare is used in operations today to relax muscles.
Bernard was the first scientist to be given a state funeral by France.

teile.einleitung: Charles Babbage was an English mathematician and inventor of the 19th century. He was the first to design a programmable calculating machine, the Analytical Engine. That is why he is considered one of the fathers of the computer, even though his machines were never fully built during his lifetime.
wichtigste: Charles Babbage lived in England from 1791 to 1871.
He taught mathematics as a professor at the University of Cambridge.
His Difference Engine was meant to calculate tables of numbers without mistakes.
In 1837 he designed the Analytical Engine, a programmable calculating machine.
He took the idea of entering instructions with punched cards from the Jacquard loom.
He called the calculating unit of his machine the mill.
In 1991 his Difference Engine No. 2 was built in London from the original plans.

abschnitte.text: **Charles Babbage** was born in London in 1791 and died there in 1871. He was a mathematician, inventor and engineer. From 1828 to 1839 he was professor of **mathematics** at the University of **Cambridge**. He worked on many subjects, from railways to coding secret messages.

In Babbage's time, people calculated long tables of numbers by hand, for example for sailing ships. Many mistakes happened, and they could be dangerous. So Babbage planned the **Difference Engine**, which was meant to calculate such tables mechanically and without errors. He built part of it, but the whole machine was never finished because of costs and disputes.

In 1837 Babbage designed the **Analytical Engine**. It was meant not just to solve one task but to carry out different calculations following a program. It had a memory for numbers and a calculating unit that Babbage called the **mill**. So it already contained the most important parts of a modern computer.

The instructions were to be entered with **punched cards**. Babbage took this idea from the **Jacquard loom**, which used punched cards to weave patterns into fabric. Depending on where the holes were, the machine carried out different steps. Punched cards were still used for computers well into the 20th century.

The mathematician **Ada Lovelace** worked with Babbage and wrote detailed explanations of the Analytical Engine. In them she described a sequence of steps for how the machine could calculate certain numbers. This is often seen as the first computer program. She also realised that such machines could process more than just numbers.

The Analytical Engine was not completed during Babbage's lifetime; only parts of it were built. For Babbage's 200th birthday in 1991, the Science Museum in London built the **Difference Engine No. 2** from his plans. It worked and calculated accurately. This proved that Babbage's ideas were right.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sequence of instructions that a machine carries out step by step.
A card with holes whose pattern gives a machine instructions.
The part of a computer that carries out the calculations.
The part of a computer where numbers and data are stored.

gewusst: The rebuilt Difference Engine No. 2 consists of thousands of parts and weighs several tonnes.
Part of Babbage's brain is still kept in a London museum today.
Babbage was so annoyed by street musicians that he campaigned against them in public.

teile.einleitung: Dendrochronology is a method for working out the age of wood from the growth rings of trees. Because each year leaves its own ring with its own width, wooden beams can often be dated to the exact year. This tells you when a house was built or what the climate was like thousands of years ago.
wichtigste: Dendrochronology dates wood using the growth rings of trees.
Growth rings have different widths because the weather is different every year.
A growth ring of an oak consists of light earlywood and dark latewood.
To find the exact year a tree was felled, you need the last ring directly under the bark.
Long tree-ring calendars are made by lining up the ring patterns of overlapping pieces of wood.
Many Swiss lake-dwelling settlements can be dated to the exact year in this way.
Growth rings also reveal the climate of earlier years.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from Greek: “dendron” means **tree** and “chronos” means time. So dendrochronology is dating with trees, also called **tree-ring dating**. It is used to work out in which year a tree was felled. It is one of the most precise dating methods there is.

In regions with seasons, trees grow a new layer of wood thicker every year. In spring the tree forms light, loose **earlywood**, and in summer darker, firm **latewood**. Together they make a **growth ring**, which you can see clearly on a tree stump. In good years with enough warmth and rain the ring is wide; in dry or cold years it is narrow.

Because the weather is different every year, a sequence of wide and narrow rings forms, like a **barcode**. Researchers measure the ring widths under a microscope and compare the pattern with a known **tree-ring calendar**. By lining up overlapping pieces of wood, from today's trees through old beams to wood from bogs and rivers, such calendars reach back many thousands of years. To get the felling year exactly right, you need the last ring directly under the bark, the **waney edge**.

In Switzerland the method is especially important for the **lake dwellings** on the shores of lakes such as Lake Zurich, Lake Biel or Lake Neuchâtel.
