Their wooden posts survived in the damp ground, and thanks to the growth rings it is often known exactly in which year a village was built or rebuilt. Since 2011 the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Old farmhouses, churches and wooden bridges are also studied in this way.

The ring widths show how warm, cold, wet or dry earlier years were. In this way experts study the **climate** of past centuries, long before there were thermometers. Especially cold years after major volcanic eruptions, for example, show up as very narrow rings. The Swiss Federal Research Institute WSL in Birmensdorf is a world leader in this field.

Dendrochronology was founded at the beginning of the 20th century by the American astronomer **Andrew Ellicott Douglass**. He actually wanted to find out whether sunspots affect the weather, and studied tree rings in Arizona to do so. He noticed that the ring patterns of different trees can be compared. Later he used this to date old settlements of the indigenous peoples in the southwest of the USA.

begriffe.erklaerung: The layer of wood that a tree forms in one year.
Light, loose wood that a tree forms in spring.
Dark, firm wood that a tree forms in summer.
The last growth ring directly under the bark, which reveals the year of felling.
Working out how old something is or which year it comes from.

gewusst: The longest tree-ring calendar in Europe reaches back more than 12,000 years.
In tropical rainforests without seasons, many trees do not form clear growth rings.
You do not have to fell a tree to study it; you can pull out a thin rod of wood with a narrow drill.

teile.einleitung: A scientific journal is a publication, in print or online, in which researchers publish their new results. Before an article appears, it is usually examined by independent experts. In this way new knowledge is checked, collected and shared with the whole world.
wichtigste: Researchers publish their results in scientific journals.
In peer review, independent experts examine an article before publication.
At the beginning of a scientific article there is a short summary, the abstract.
Many references show what an article is based on.
The Philosophical Transactions of 1665 is regarded as the oldest scientific journal still published.
The journal Nature has appeared in London since 1869.
Most scientific articles in the natural sciences now appear in English.

abschnitte.text: A **scientific journal** is aimed at experts in a particular field, such as medicine, physics or history. It appears regularly, nowadays usually online. It contains new research results, review articles and discussions. Unlike a newspaper, the texts are usually written by the researchers themselves.

Before an article appears, the editors send it to independent experts. This examination is called **peer review**. The reviewers look for mistakes, gaps and unclear passages. Often an article has to be revised, and some are rejected altogether.

At the beginning there is an **abstract**, a short summary of the most important results. After that come the introduction, methods, results and discussion. At the end there is a long list of **references**. With it, every reader can check what the article is based on.

The **Philosophical Transactions** of the Royal Society in London was founded in 1665 and is regarded as the oldest scientific journal still published. **Nature** has appeared in London since 1869, and the journal Science since 1880 in the USA. Anyone who publishes there is read by many researchers. Besides these there are thousands of specialised journals on almost every field.

Many scientific articles cost money, and libraries pay for subscriptions. With **open access**, by contrast, articles can be read free of charge on the internet. The Swiss National Science Foundation requires that research it pays for becomes freely available. In this way schools, doctors and interested lay people can also read the results.

Scientific journals make mistakes too, because reviewers do not spot everything. If it later turns out that an article contains serious errors or has been faked, it is **retracted**. The article usually stays visible but with a clear note. In this way science corrects itself.

begriffe.erklaerung: The examination of a research article by independent experts.
The short summary at the beginning of a scientific article.
Free access to scientific articles on the internet at no cost.
A note saying where a piece of information or an idea comes from.

gewusst: Every year several million scientific articles appear worldwide.
The reviewers in peer review often stay anonymous to the authors.
Many researchers put drafts of their articles on the internet as so-called preprints even before review.

teile.einleitung: EPICA is a large European research project in which experts drilled deep into the ice of the Antarctic. The name stands for “European Project for Ice Coring in Antarctica”. The ice holds a climate archive that reaches back about 800,000 years.
wichtigste: EPICA means “European Project for Ice Coring in Antarctica”.
The oldest ice core comes from the place called Dome C in East Antarctica.
The ice from Dome C tells the climate history of about 800,000 years.
The core covers about eight ice age cycles.
A second drilling site was in Dronning Maud Land.
Tiny air bubbles in the ice show how much carbon dioxide there was in the air in the past.
The follow-up project “Beyond EPICA Oldest Ice” is looking for ice about 1.5 million years old.

abschnitte.text: EPICA was a project of ten European countries, including Switzerland. The aim was to bring up and study the oldest possible ice from the Antarctic **ice sheet**. For this the researchers drilled more than three kilometres deep into the ice. The drilling work took place mainly between 1996 and 2006.

The most important drilling site was **Dome C**, an ice dome high up on the plateau of East Antarctica. The French-Italian research station Concordia stands there, where it can get colder than minus 70 degrees in winter. The second drilling site was in **Dronning Maud Land** near the German Kohnen Station. This area lies closer to the Atlantic and is therefore well suited to comparison with ice cores from Greenland.

Every year a little snow falls in the Antarctic, and over time it is pressed into ice. In the process, tiny **air bubbles** are trapped that contain air from that time. The deeper you drill, the older the ice. From the make-up of the ice, researchers can read how warm or cold it was in the past.

The Dome C core shows about eight **ice age cycles**, in which long cold periods alternated with shorter warm periods. The level of **carbon dioxide** rose and fell almost in step with the temperature. In all those 800,000 years it was always clearly lower than today. The Climate and Environmental Physics division of the University of Bern made a large part of these gas measurements.

The comparison with Greenland showed an interesting pattern, the **bipolar seesaw**. During abrupt climate changes the Antarctic warmed while Greenland cooled, and the other way round. This is explained by ocean currents in the Atlantic that move heat between south and north. If this current becomes weaker, more heat stays in the south.

The follow-up project **Beyond EPICA Oldest Ice** is drilling at a place called Little Dome C, not far from Concordia. The aim is ice about 1.5 million years old. With it, researchers want to understand why the ice age cycles lengthened in the past from about 41,000 to about 100,000 years. At the beginning of 2025 the team reached the bedrock under the ice.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long rod of ice taken out of the ice with a hollow drill.
A natural store from which you can read what the climate was like in the past.
The change from a long cold period to a shorter warm period.
When it gets warmer at one pole, it gets colder at the other.

gewusst: One metre of ice core from great depth can contain thousands of years of climate history.
The ice cores are brought to Europe deep-frozen so that they do not melt.
In the Antarctic ice you even find dust that the wind carried there long ago from far-off continents.

teile.einleitung: Eawag is the water research institute of the ETH Domain and one of the most important water research institutions in the world. It studies how lakes, rivers and groundwater stay clean and how people everywhere in the world can get good drinking water. Many clean Swiss lakes owe their condition partly to its research.
wichtigste: Eawag deals with water in all its forms.
The name originally stood for the Federal Institute for Water Supply, Sewage Purification and Water Protection.
Eawag has sites in Dübendorf near Zurich and in Kastanienbaum on Lake Lucerne.
The SODIS method disinfects water in PET bottles using sunlight.
Thanks to its research, many treatment plants are adding a stage to remove micropollutants.
In the Projet Lac, Eawag studied the fish species of the large Swiss lakes.
In 1986 phosphate in laundry detergents was banned in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Like ETH Zurich and EPFL, **Eawag** belongs to the federal ETH Domain. Its roots lie in an advisory office of ETH Zurich that was founded in 1936. The name was originally an abbreviation for “Federal Institute for Water Supply, Sewage Purification and Water Protection”. Today several hundred people from biology, chemistry, engineering and the social sciences work there together. They do research, advise the authorities and train students.

The headquarters are in **Dübendorf** in the canton of Zurich. The main building there, **Forum Chriesbach**, uses very little energy and makes use of rainwater. The second site is **Kastanienbaum** near Lucerne, right on Lake Lucerne. There, experts study mainly lakes, fish and other living things in the water. The lake on their doorstep serves as an open-air laboratory.

In the 1960s and 1970s many Swiss lakes were heavily over-fertilised, algae spread and fish died. One main reason was **phosphate** from detergents and waste water. Research by Eawag helped to get phosphate banned in laundry detergents in 1986 and removed in treatment plants. In the **Projet Lac**, researchers fished systematically in the large lakes at the edge of the Alps and counted the fish species. They also found species that had not been described scientifically before.

Waste water contains tiny traces of medicines, cleaning products and pesticides, known as **micropollutants**. Even the smallest amounts can harm fish and other water animals. Eawag has tested methods for removing these substances with ozone or activated carbon. Since 2016 the Swiss water protection law has required many larger treatment plants to add such an extra cleaning stage. This makes Switzerland one of the pioneers worldwide.

abschnitte.titel: SODIS: disinfecting water with the sun
abschnitte.text: Many people in the world have no clean drinking water. The **SODIS** method (solar water disinfection), promoted by Eawag, is very simple. You fill clear water into transparent PET bottles and leave them in the sun for several hours. The UV radiation and the heat kill many germs. The method is used in numerous countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant that cleans dirty waste water before it flows into rivers and lakes.
Tiny amounts of harmful substances such as traces of medicines in water.
Too many nutrients in the water, so that algae grow strongly and oxygen is lacking.
The group of the two federal institutes of technology and four federal research institutes.

gewusst: The toilets in Forum Chriesbach separate urine so that researchers can turn it into fertiliser.
SODIS needs no electricity and no chemicals, only sunlight and bottles.

teile.einleitung: The button mushroom is the edible mushroom you find most often in shops. It is grown in large quantities, but there are also wild relatives of it in meadows and pastures. Anyone who gathers wild mushrooms has to be very careful, though.
wichtigste: The button mushroom is the mushroom that is grown and sold most often.
Button mushrooms from the shop are usually white or brown.
They are grown on compost made from manure and straw.
They are usually grown in dark, damp sheds.
The gills are pink at first and turn dark brown with age.
The field mushroom can be mistaken for the deadly poisonous death cap.
The French word “champignon” simply means mushroom.

abschnitte.text: A button mushroom has a rounded **cap** and a short, sturdy stalk. Farmed mushrooms are usually white or brown; the brown ones are often called chestnut mushrooms. Under the cap there are thin little sheets, the **gills**. In young mushrooms they are pink; with age they turn dark brown to almost black.

Fungi are neither plants nor animals but form their own kingdom of living things. The actual fungus lives as a fine network of threads in the soil, the **mycelium**. What we eat is only the fruiting body, which grows above the ground. In its gills it forms tiny **spores**, from which new fungi grow.

Button mushrooms are grown on **compost** made from horse manure, straw and other ingredients. They are usually grown in dark, damp **sheds**, because mushrooms do not need light to grow. Mushrooms were already being grown in France in the 17th century, and later also in old quarries and cellars near Paris. Button mushrooms are grown in Switzerland too.

In nature, the **field mushroom**, for example, grows in pastures and meadows, especially where cows or horses graze. It usually appears in late summer and autumn after rain. There are also other species of this family in the woods. Some wild species are edible, while others cause stomach ache.

The field mushroom can be mistaken for the **death cap**, the most dangerous poisonous mushroom in Europe. However, the death cap always has white gills and a bulb-like swelling at the base of the stalk. Even a small piece can be deadly. That is why you should always have mushrooms you have gathered checked at an official **mushroom inspection point**, which many Swiss municipalities have.

You can eat button mushrooms raw in salad, or fry, steam or bake them. They consist largely of water and contain few calories. They are popular in sauces, on pizza or in risotto. You should only clean them briefly and not leave them lying in water for long, because otherwise they soak it up.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fine network of threads in the soil, the actual body of a fungus.
The visible part of a mushroom with cap and stalk.
Thin sheets under the cap in which the spores are formed.
Tiny particles from which new fungi grow.
A place where experts check gathered mushrooms for poisonous ones.

gewusst: Shop mushrooms grow so fast that they can often be harvested just a few weeks after being planted.
Because button mushrooms used to be grown in Paris cellars, in French they are also called “champignons de Paris”.
Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.

teile.einleitung: Edward Jenner was an English country doctor. In 1796 he developed the first vaccine against a disease, namely against dangerous smallpox. He is therefore regarded as the founder of modern vaccination.
wichtigste: Edward Jenner lived in England from 1749 to 1823.
He worked as a doctor in the village of Berkeley in the county of Gloucestershire.
He noticed that milkmaids who had caught harmless cowpox did not get smallpox.
In 1796 he vaccinated a boy with cowpox and so protected him from smallpox.
With this he developed the first vaccine against a disease.
The word vaccine comes from the Latin word for cow.
In 1980 the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated.

abschnitte.text: **Edward Jenner** was born on 17 May 1749 in Berkeley in England. His father was a clergyman. At the age of 13 Jenner was apprenticed to a surgeon and afterwards studied in London. He returned to his home village and worked there as a **country doctor**. Besides medicine he was also interested in birds and nature.

**Smallpox** was one of the most dangerous diseases in human history. It caused a high fever and pus-filled blisters all over the body. About one in three people who caught it died, and survivors often had scars or went blind. At the time, people tried to protect themselves by deliberately infecting healthy people with a little pus from the sick. But this **variolation** was risky, because some people died from it.

Jenner heard that milkmaids rarely caught smallpox. They had often caught the harmless **cowpox** from cows. On 14 May 1796 Jenner took some fluid from a cowpox blister on the milkmaid Sarah Nelmes. He scratched it into the arm of eight-year-old James Phipps. It later turned out that the boy could no longer catch smallpox.

Jenner named his method after the Latin word “vacca” for cow. This is where the words **vaccination** and vaccine come from. The method spread quickly throughout Europe and beyond. Jenner asked for no money for his discovery, so that as many people as possible could be protected. Later Louis Pasteur followed his example and developed vaccines against other diseases.

Thanks to worldwide vaccination campaigns, smallpox gradually disappeared. The last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977. In 1980 the **World Health Organization** WHO, based in Geneva, officially declared smallpox eradicated. It is the first human disease to be completely defeated. Today vaccinations protect against measles, tetanus and polio, among others.

begriffe.erklaerung: A method that prepares the body to fight off a disease.
A formerly very dangerous, infectious disease with blisters on the skin.
The substance used for a vaccination.
The body's own defence against germs.

gewusst: Jenner was also elected a member of the Royal Society, because he had studied the behaviour of young cuckoos in the nest.
Smallpox is still the only human disease that has been completely eradicated.

teile.einleitung: Empa is a Swiss research institute for materials science and technology. It studies how building materials, metals, plastics and new materials can be made better, safer and more environmentally friendly. Its headquarters are in Dübendorf near Zurich.
wichtigste: The name Empa stands for the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology.
Empa belongs to the ETH Domain, together with ETH Zurich, EPFL and other research institutes.
Its headquarters are in Dübendorf, and it has further sites in St Gallen and Thun.
Empa's history began in 1880 with a testing institute for building materials.
In the NEST research building, new building techniques are tested in everyday use.
Empa runs the national air measurement network NABEL and measures greenhouse gases on the Jungfraujoch.
For authorities and companies it tests how much strain materials can take.

abschnitte.text: **Empa** is a federal research institute and belongs to the **ETH Domain**. Experts from many countries do research there on new materials and technologies. The aim is to turn findings from the laboratory into useful products for the economy and for society. Empa works closely with universities and companies to do this. Its topics include energy, health, building, the environment and nanotechnology.

Empa's history began in **1880** in Zurich as a testing institute for building materials. At that time, cement, steel and wood for bridges and houses were tested, for example. Today the headquarters are in **Dübendorf** in the canton of Zurich. Further sites are **St Gallen**, where research is done on textiles and medical materials among other things, and **Thun**.

**NEST** is a special, modular building on the site in Dübendorf. It consists of a basic framework into which individual living and working units can be slotted. Real people live and work in them while new building and timber technologies, energy systems and materials are tested in everyday use. This quickly shows whether an idea from the laboratory also works in practice.

On behalf of the Federal Office for the Environment, Empa runs **NABEL**, the national air pollution monitoring network. At measuring stations all over Switzerland, air quality is measured, for example fine dust and nitrogen oxides. At the high-alpine research station on the **Jungfraujoch**, Empa measures greenhouse gases in very clean air. These data help to follow changes in the atmosphere over many years.

Empa is also known for unusual research. Researchers treated spruce and maple wood with **wood-decaying fungi** so that violins would sound better. Together with ETH they partly removed the wood substance lignin, so that wood can be squashed and produces an electrical voltage under pressure. Empa also tests for authorities and companies how much strain materials can take, for example ropes, components or cycle helmets.

begriffe.erklaerung: Research into what things are made of and how materials can be improved.
The group of universities and research institutes that belong to the federal government.
A gas such as carbon dioxide that holds heat in the atmosphere.
A substance in wood that makes it firm and stiff.
An organisation that tests whether materials meet requirements.

gewusst: The station on the Jungfraujoch lies at about 3,500 metres above sea level and is one of the highest measuring stations in Europe.
At NEST, some living units are removed again after a few years and replaced by new experiments.
Before Empa moved to Dübendorf, it was housed in Zurich near ETH.

teile.einleitung: The hand axe is one of the oldest tools of humankind, a stone worked on both sides into the shape of a teardrop or an almond. Early humans used it for more than a million years for cutting, scraping and chopping. It was a kind of pocket knife of the Old Stone Age.
wichtigste: The hand axe is a typical tool of the Old Stone Age.
It was worked on both sides by carefully aimed blows.
A typical hand axe has the shape of a teardrop or an almond.
In Europe it was often made of flint.
It was probably used for cutting, scraping and chopping.
The culture of the early hand axes is called Acheulean, after a site in France.
The oldest hand axes come from Africa and are about 1.7 million years old.

abschnitte.text: A hand axe is a **stone tool** that is usually about the size of a hand. It is worked on **both sides** and often has a point and sharp edges. Its shape is like a teardrop or an **almond**. It is one of the best-known finds of the Stone Age.

For a hand axe you needed a hard stone that splits well, such as **flint**, quartzite or obsidian. With a hammerstone or a piece of bone or antler you struck off flakes with careful aim, which is called the **knapping technique**. You turned the stone again and again so that both sides became even. Making good hand axes took a lot of practice and planning.

With a hand axe you could probably **cut, scrape and chop**. Early humans used them to butcher animals they had killed, scrape hides clean or work wood. Some researchers think it was also used for digging up roots. Because it was good for so many things, it is sometimes called the Swiss army knife of the Stone Age.

The hand axe belongs to the **Old Stone Age**, the longest section of human history. The oldest known hand axes were found in Kenya and are about 1.7 million years old, probably made by **Homo erectus**. The culture of these tools is called the **Acheulean**, after the site of Saint-Acheul in northern France. Hand axes were made in Africa, Europe and Asia for more than a million years.

In Switzerland, finds from this early time are very rare, because the glaciers of the ice ages destroyed many traces. A famous find is the **hand axe of Pratteln** in the canton of Basel-Landschaft, which is regarded as one of the oldest tools in Switzerland. Later, Neanderthals lived in Switzerland and also made stone tools.

The hand axe shows that early humans could already **plan** and picture a shape in advance. It is important evidence for the development of thinking and skill. Today archaeologists try making hand axes themselves in order to understand the technique. In many museums, for example the National Museum in Zurich, you can admire Stone Age tools.

begriffe.erklaerung: The oldest and longest section of the Stone Age, also called the Palaeolithic.
A hard stone that forms very sharp edges when it is struck.
The name of the early culture in which hand axes were made.
An early kind of human that walked upright and made hand axes.
The science that digs up and studies old traces of people.

gewusst: Hand axes were made almost unchanged for more than a million years, longer than any other tool.
Some hand axes are so large and heavy that researchers wonder whether they were used as tools at all.

teile.einleitung: Ernest Shackleton was a British polar explorer who was born in Ireland. He became famous through the expedition with the ship Endurance, which was crushed by the pack ice in 1915. Despite cold, hunger and storms, he brought every man of his ship's crew back alive.
wichtigste: Ernest Shackleton was born in 1874 in what is now Ireland.
On the Nimrod expedition he turned back in 1909 about 180 kilometres from the South Pole.
His ship Endurance was crushed by pack ice in the Weddell Sea in 1915.
In 1916 the men saved themselves by reaching Elephant Island in lifeboats.
Shackleton sailed in the small boat James Caird to South Georgia to get help.
Not one man of the Endurance's ship's crew lost his life.
The wreck of the Endurance was found in 2022 at a depth of about 3,000 metres.

abschnitte.text: Ernest Shackleton was born on 15 February 1874 in Ireland and later grew up in London. As a young man he went to sea. From 1901 to 1904 he took part in Robert Falcon Scott's **Discovery expedition** to the Antarctic. He died on 5 January 1922 on another expedition and was buried on South Georgia.

abschnitte.titel: Just short of the South Pole
abschnitte.text: With the **Nimrod expedition** from 1907 to 1909, Shackleton wanted to be the first to reach the South Pole. In January 1909 he and three companions were only about 180 kilometres from their goal. Because their supplies were running too low, he decided to turn back. In this way he saved himself and his men, and he was celebrated as a hero in Britain for it.

In 1914 Shackleton set out with 28 men to cross the Antarctic on foot. But in the **Weddell Sea** the Endurance became stuck in the pack ice at the beginning of 1915. For months the ship drifted with the ice until it was crushed and sank in November 1915. After that the men lived in tents on the drifting ice.

In April 1916 all the men reached the bare **Elephant Island** in three lifeboats. Shackleton then sailed with five companions in the open boat **James Caird** about 1,300 kilometres through stormy seas to South Georgia. There they crossed the unknown, glaciated mountains on foot to reach a whaling station. In August 1916 Shackleton picked up the remaining men from Elephant Island with a Chilean ship.

For a long time nobody knew exactly where the Endurance lay. In March 2022 the Endurance22 expedition found the wreck in the Weddell Sea at a depth of about 3,000 metres. Underwater robots filmed the ship, which is astonishingly well preserved and even shows its name on the stern. The wreck is protected as a monument and may not be touched.

Today Shackleton is regarded as a model of good **leadership** in difficult situations. He made sure that his men stuck together and did not lose heart. The photos taken by the expedition photographer Frank Hurley still give a striking picture of life in the ice. Many books and films tell the story of the Endurance.

begriffe.erklaerung: Drifting floes of ice pushed tightly together on the sea.
A long, planned research journey into an unknown area.
The region around the South Pole, which is almost completely covered in ice.
The remains of a sunken or destroyed ship.

gewusst: The boat journey in the James Caird took about 16 days through one of the stormiest seas in the world.
On Elephant Island, 22 men had to hold out for more than four months under two upturned boats.
The name Endurance means the ability to keep going.

teile.einleitung: The Great Wall of China is the longest structure in the world and stretches across mountains, deserts and valleys in northern China. Many stories surround it, for example the claim that you can see it from space. That is not true, and it shows exactly why it is important to test claims scientifically.
wichtigste: With all its sections, the Great Wall of China is more than 20,000 kilometres long.
It was built to protect against attacks from the north.
It was built from stone, bricks and rammed earth.
The towers were used for keeping watch and sending signals.
You cannot see the wall from space with the naked eye.
It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.
It is easy to visit near the capital, Beijing.

abschnitte.titel: What is the Great Wall of China?
abschnitte.text: The Great Wall of China is not a single wall but a network of many **sections of wall**, ditches and towers. Chinese experts measured all the parts and came to more than **20,000 kilometres**. That is about half the distance around the whole Earth. Many sections have now crumbled or can only be recognised as earth banks.

More than 2,500 years ago, Chinese principalities were already building the first protective walls. In the 3rd century BC the first emperor, **Qin Shi Huang**, had many of these walls joined up. The well-known sections of stone and brick mostly date from the time of the **Ming dynasty**, roughly from 1368 to 1644. They were meant to protect the empire from horse-riding peoples from the north, such as the Mongols.

Depending on the area, the workers built with whatever was available: **stone**, fired **bricks**, rammed earth or even wood and reeds. **Watchtowers** stood at intervals along the wall. From there, soldiers kept a lookout and passed on signals with smoke by day and fire by night. In this way a warning could travel quickly over long distances.

You often hear that the wall is the only structure that can be seen from **space**. That is wrong. The wall is usually only a few metres wide and is almost the same colour as its surroundings. The first Chinese astronaut, **Yang Liwei**, reported in 2003 that he could not see it.

Since 1987 the Great Wall of China has been on the list of **UNESCO World Heritage Sites**. Especially well-known sections such as **Badaling** and Mutianyu are near **Beijing**. Every year millions of people walk up and down the steep steps there. But wind, rain and people take their toll on the structure, so it is protected and restored in many places.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ruling family that governs a country for a long time.
A tower from which soldiers watch the surrounding area.
A list of especially valuable places in the world that are meant to be protected.
A widespread story that is not true.

gewusst: For the mortar of some sections of the wall, sticky rice was mixed into the lime.
From low Earth orbit you are more likely to see cities, roads and airports than the narrow wall.
The Great Wall of China was not built in one go but was extended again and again over about 2,000 years.

teile.einleitung: Emmy Noether was a German mathematician and is regarded as one of the most important women mathematicians in history. She shaped abstract algebra and, with Noether's theorem, found one of the most important connections in physics. All her life she had to fight against obstacles because she was a woman.
wichtigste: Emmy Noether became famous in mathematics.
Noether's theorem links symmetries with conservation laws.
Because the laws of nature apply tomorrow just as they do today, the theorem says that energy is conserved.
David Hilbert and Felix Klein brought her to the University of Göttingen in 1915.
At first her lectures were announced under the name of a professor.
Only in 1919 was she allowed to qualify as a university teacher.
After being dismissed by the Nazis in 1933, she emigrated to the USA.

abschnitte.text: Emmy Noether was born on 23 March 1882 in **Erlangen** in Bavaria. Her father Max Noether was a professor of mathematics at the university there. At that time women in Germany were usually not allowed to study properly, so at first she attended lectures only as a guest. Later she was able to enrol after all and completed her **doctoral thesis** in 1907. After that she worked for years at the University of Erlangen without pay.

In 1915 the famous mathematicians **David Hilbert** and **Felix Klein** brought her to the University of Göttingen, at that time a centre of mathematics. Many professors were against a woman teaching. Hilbert is said to have replied that a university is not a public bath, where sex should matter. At first her lectures were announced under Hilbert's name. Only in 1919 was she allowed to **qualify as a university teacher**, that is, to gain the right to teach.

In 1918 Emmy Noether proved a theorem that is now called **Noether's theorem**. It says: for every symmetry of a physical system there is a quantity that is conserved. Because the laws of nature apply tomorrow just as they do today, for example, **energy** is conserved. Because they apply in the same way everywhere, momentum is conserved. This theorem is still a cornerstone of modern physics.

Even more important for mathematics was her work in **abstract algebra**. Instead of calculating with individual numbers, she studied general structures such as rings and ideals. Noetherian rings, for example, are named after her. A group of young researchers formed around her in Göttingen, who were called the “Noether boys”. In 1932 she gave a major plenary lecture at the **International Congress of Mathematicians in Zurich**.

In 1933 the Nazis dismissed Emmy Noether because she was Jewish. She emigrated to the **USA** and taught at the women's college **Bryn Mawr** in Pennsylvania and gave lectures in Princeton. She died as early as 14 April 1935 after an operation. Albert Einstein paid tribute to her in an obituary as a great mathematical genius. Today prizes, research programmes and a crater on the Moon bear her name.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mathematical statement that has been proved.
A property that stays the same when you move or turn something, or look at it later.
A law of nature saying that a quantity such as energy stays the same.
An examination that gives you permission to teach at a university.

gewusst: For years Emmy Noether received no regular salary in Göttingen, although she was one of the most influential researchers there.
On walks she discussed mathematics so enthusiastically that her students could hardly keep up.

teile.einleitung: A result is what you have found out at the end of an investigation, an experiment or a calculation. In research, the result answers the question you asked at the beginning. So that others can learn from it, you have to write it down and present it well.
wichtigste: A result is what you have found out.
The result of an experiment answers the research question.
At the end you compare the result with the idea you had at the beginning.
A measurement is a number you have measured; a result often comes from many measurements.
A bar chart shows numbers as bars of different heights.
Surprising results should be written down especially carefully.
Researchers publish their results so that others learn about them.

abschnitte.text: Every investigation begins with a **research question**, for example: does cress grow in the dark? Then you put forward an **idea**, also called a hypothesis. After that you carry out an experiment, observe and measure. What comes out at the end is the **result**. In mathematics too, the solution of a calculation is called a result, for example 3 plus 5 gives 8.

A **measurement** is a number you have measured, for example the height of a plant in centimetres. If Kim counts 3 ladybirds on Monday and 5 on Tuesday, that makes 8 altogether. For results to be reliable, you measure as precisely as possible and often several times. You write all the values down straight away in a **table**, so that nothing is forgotten. The important thing is to write down honestly what you really saw.

Numbers are often easier to understand if you show them as a picture. A **bar chart** shows numbers as bars of different heights, so you can see at a glance which is bigger. A line chart shows well how something changes over time, such as the temperature. To show a result to others, a **poster** with the question, the method, the result and photos works well. A short talk or a presentation are also good options.

At the end you compare the result with the idea you had at the beginning. Sometimes the idea is right, sometimes it is not, and both are genuine results. If a result is surprising, you should write it down especially carefully and, if possible, repeat the experiment. Many important discoveries began with an unexpected result. In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould killed bacteria, and in this way he discovered **penicillin**.

Researchers **publish** their results in scientific journals or present them at conferences. Before an article appears, other experts examine the work closely, which is called **peer review**. In this way others can repeat the experiments and check whether they get the same result. A result only counts as well established when it can be repeated. In this way the knowledge of the whole world grows step by step.

begriffe.erklaerung: The question you want to answer with an investigation.
An idea about what might come out of an experiment, before you know.
A number you have obtained with a measuring device.
A picture that shows numbers clearly, for example with bars or lines.

gewusst: An experiment in which your idea turns out to be wrong also gives a valuable result.
Every year several million scientific articles with new results appear worldwide.
The glue on yellow sticky notes was actually a failed result in the search for an especially strong adhesive.

teile.einleitung: An iceberg is a large piece of ice that has broken off a glacier or an ice shelf and drifts in the sea. Only a small part sticks out of the water, and the largest part lies hidden below the surface. Icebergs can be enormous and have been dangerous for many ships.
wichtigste: About nine tenths of an iceberg lies under water.
The ice of an iceberg is fresh water, not salt water.
When an iceberg breaks off a glacier into the sea, it is called calving.
The Titanic sank in 1912 after colliding with an iceberg.
Many icebergs in the North Atlantic come from Greenland.
Flat icebergs with straight sides are called tabular icebergs and are common in the Antarctic.
The largest icebergs can be bigger than the canton of Zurich.

abschnitte.text: In Greenland and in the Antarctic there are huge ice sheets of snow that has been pressed into ice over thousands of years. The ice flows slowly to the sea as a glacier. There, pieces break off and crash into the water, which is called **calving**. Because the ice formed from snow, an iceberg consists of **fresh water**. So you could drink melted iceberg ice.

Ice is a little lighter than sea water and therefore floats. But only just: about **nine tenths** of an iceberg lies under water. That is why people say “that is only the tip of the iceberg” when they can see only a small part of a problem. Under water an iceberg can be much wider than above, which is dangerous for ships. When an iceberg melts underneath, it can suddenly tip over.

In the Antarctic, flat, huge **tabular icebergs** with straight, steep sides often break off the ice shelf. In the North Atlantic the icebergs are usually smaller and have jagged points, peaks and arches. The iceberg B-15, which broke off in the Antarctic in 2000, was about 11,000 square kilometres in size. That is more than six times the area of the canton of Zurich. Small lumps of ice are called **growlers**, because they make growling noises as they roll in the water.

On the night of 14 to 15 April 1912, the **Titanic** collided with an iceberg in the North Atlantic. The ship, thought to be unsinkable, was on its first voyage from England to New York. It sank in less than three hours, and about 1,500 people died. After the disaster, several countries founded the **International Ice Patrol**, which watches icebergs and warns ships. Today satellites and radar also help to spot icebergs early.

Many icebergs in the North Atlantic come from glaciers on the west coast of Greenland, for example from the **Ilulissat Icefjord**, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. From there they drift south with the ocean current as far as Newfoundland. Because of global warming, the ice sheets are melting faster and more icebergs are breaking off. This contributes to the rise in sea level. At the same time icebergs are a habitat: along their edges, algae, krill and seabirds find food.

begriffe.erklaerung: The breaking off of pieces of ice from a glacier into the water.
A huge sheet of ice that extends from the land and floats on the sea.
A flat iceberg with straight sides, typical of the Antarctic.
A small lump of ice that barely sticks out of the water.

gewusst: Icebergs can drift through the sea for years before they have melted completely.
Because tiny air bubbles are trapped in the ice, iceberg ice crackles and hisses as it melts in water.

teile.einleitung: Empiricism is a school of philosophy that says: everything we know comes from our experience through the senses. Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling and tasting are, according to it, the source of our knowledge. This idea strongly shaped modern natural science.
wichtigste: Empiricism says that all knowledge comes from experience through the senses.
The name comes from the Greek word empeiria, which means experience.
John Locke compared the mind at birth with a blank sheet, the tabula rasa.
In his 1620 work Novum Organum, Francis Bacon called for a science based on experience and experiments.
George Berkeley coined the phrase “esse est percipi”, to be is to be perceived.
David Hume distinguished vivid impressions from weaker ideas.
The opponent of empiricism is rationalism, which sees thinking as the most important source of knowledge.

abschnitte.text: **Empiricism** is a doctrine from **epistemology**, the part of philosophy that asks how we can know anything at all. Empiricists believe that there is nothing in our mind that did not first come in through the senses. In Latin this principle reads “Nihil est in intellectu, quod non prius fuerit in sensu”. A child who has never seen snow, for example, cannot picture exactly what it feels like. Only experience fills the mind with knowledge.

The Englishman **Francis Bacon** lived from 1561 to 1626 and was a politician and philosopher. In his work **Novum Organum** of 1620 he called for a new science that observes carefully and carries out experiments. He warned against prejudices that deceive the mind, which he called **idols**. These include, for example, errors caused by imprecise language or by blind belief in old authorities. Bacon is therefore seen as a pioneer of modern natural science.

The Englishman **John Locke** published his main work “An Essay Concerning Human Understanding” in 1689. In it he described the mind of a newborn as a **tabula rasa**, a blank sheet. He distinguished primary qualities such as shape and size, which lie in the object itself, from **secondary qualities** such as colour, taste and smell. According to Locke, these only arise in our perception. Locke was also an important thinker on freedom and human rights.

The Irish bishop **George Berkeley** went even further and said: things exist only insofar as they are perceived. He summed this up in the phrase “esse est percipi”. The Scot **David Hume** lived from 1711 to 1776 and distinguished vivid impressions from weaker ideas, such as the memory of a taste. Hume also asked why we may be sure that the sun will rise again tomorrow. This is called the **problem of induction**.

Opposed to empiricism stands the **rationalism** of René Descartes, Baruch de Spinoza and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Rationalists believe that some truths can be recognised by thinking alone, for example in mathematics. In 1781 the German philosopher Immanuel Kant tried to combine both sides in his “Critique of Pure Reason”. He argued that knowledge begins with experience, but that the mind gives it an order. This debate still shapes philosophy today.

Empiricism strongly influenced the **natural sciences**. Researchers put forward an idea and test it with observations, measurements and experiments. What is confirmed in many experiments counts as well established. The word **empirical** is used today for anything based on data and experience. At school too you learn empirically when you carry out an experiment and observe the result.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of philosophy that asks where our knowledge comes from and how certain it is.
Latin for blank sheet, an image for a mind with no prior knowledge.
A school of philosophy that sees thinking and reason as the most important source of knowledge.
Based on observation, experience and measurement.

gewusst: Francis Bacon is said to have died after an experiment in which he stuffed a chicken with snow to test whether cold keeps meat fresh.
The Californian city of Berkeley is named after George Berkeley.
John Locke was also a doctor and worked on medicine.

teile.einleitung: The noble gases are a group of chemical elements that includes helium and neon. They hardly take part in chemical reactions and prefer to keep to themselves. You know them from balloons and brightly glowing advertising signs.
wichtigste: The noble gases are in the last column of the periodic table, group 18.
They include helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon.
They hardly react with other substances, because their outer electron shell is full.
At normal temperatures all noble gases are colourless, odourless gases.
Argon is the most common noble gas in our air.
Helium is lighter than air and is used for balloons.
Radon is radioactive and can build up in cellars.

abschnitte.text: The **noble gases** form a family of elements in the periodic table. They are called that because, like grand nobles, they hardly mix with other substances. Chemists say they are **unreactive**. They include helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and the radioactive radon. All of them are invisible gases without smell at room temperature.

Atoms form bonds in order to fill up their outer electron shell. In the noble gases this **outer shell** is already completely filled. So they have hardly any reason to react with other atoms. Other elements aim for exactly this state, which is called the **noble gas configuration**. It was only in 1962 that a first compound with xenon was made.

Helium was discovered in 1868 in the light of the sun, even before it was found on Earth. Its name comes from the Greek word “helios” for sun. In 1894 Lord Rayleigh and **William Ramsay** discovered argon in the air. In the following years Ramsay also found neon, krypton and xenon. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1904.

**Helium** fills balloons and airships, because it is light and not flammable. Liquid helium cools the magnets in hospitals for magnetic resonance scans. **Neon** glows red-orange in glass tubes when electricity passes through it and is used for illuminated signs. Argon protects hot metal from the oxygen in the air during welding. Xenon is found in very bright car headlights.

**Radon** forms in the ground when natural uranium in the rock decays. It can get into cellars and living rooms through cracks. Because it is radioactive, over time it can cause lung cancer. In Switzerland, parts of the Alps and the Jura are especially affected. The Federal Office of Public Health recommends measuring radon levels in buildings and airing rooms well.

begriffe.erklaerung: An element of group 18 that hardly takes part in chemical reactions.
The word for substances that react only with great difficulty with others.
A path around the nucleus of an atom on which electrons are found.
A substance that decays by itself and gives off radiation as it does so.

gewusst: Anyone who breathes in helium speaks briefly in a squeaky voice, but this can be dangerous and should not be copied.
After hydrogen, helium is the second most common element in the whole universe, but it is rare on Earth.

teile.einleitung: Florence Nightingale was a British nurse who founded modern nursing. She became famous in the Crimean War as “the lady with the lamp”, who went to see wounded soldiers at night. But she was also a clever statistician who fought for better hospitals with figures and diagrams.
wichtigste: Florence Nightingale was born in Florence in 1820 and was named after that city.
In the Crimean War she nursed wounded British soldiers in the military hospital at Scutari.
Because she walked through the wards at night, she was called “the lady with the lamp”.
Most soldiers did not die of their wounds but of infectious diseases.
With cleanliness, fresh air and good food she lowered the death rate.
She showed the causes of death in a rose diagram and became the first woman member of the Royal Statistical Society.
In 1860 she founded a nursing school at St Thomas' Hospital in London.

abschnitte.text: **Florence Nightingale** was born on 12 May 1820 in **Florence** in Italy, where her wealthy English parents happened to be travelling. She grew up in England and received a very good education from her father, including in mathematics. At that time it was unusual for a woman from a rich family to take up a profession. But Florence was determined to nurse the sick and got her way against her family. Among other places she trained at a deaconess institution in Kaiserswerth in Germany.

From 1853 to 1856, Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire fought Russia in the **Crimean War**. In 1854 Florence Nightingale travelled with 38 nurses to the British **military hospital at Scutari**, which is now part of Istanbul. Conditions there were dreadful, with dirt, rats and too little food. Most soldiers died not of their injuries but of diseases such as cholera and typhus. At night she walked through the wards with a lamp, which is why she was called **“the lady with the lamp”**.

Nightingale made sure there was **cleanliness**, washed linen, fresh air and good food. Together with a commission that had the hospital's sewers cleaned, the death rate then fell sharply. After the war she wanted to prove that poor **hygiene** had killed many soldiers. In 1859 she wrote down her experiences in the book “Notes on Nursing”, which was very successful. It is regarded as one of the first textbooks of modern nursing.

Nightingale collected precise figures on what soldiers had died of. To show them clearly, she drew a special **rose diagram**, which looks like a flower made of sectors of a circle. From it, everyone could see at once how many deaths could have been avoided. In this way she persuaded politicians to improve hospitals and barracks. In 1858 she became the first woman to be elected to the **Royal Statistical Society**.

In 1860 Nightingale founded a **nursing school** at St Thomas' Hospital in London, which became a model for many others. Nursing thus became a respected profession with proper training. In 1907 she was the first woman to receive the British Order of Merit. She died on 13 August 1910 in London. On her birthday, 12 May, the **International Day of Nurses** is celebrated worldwide today.

The Genevan **Henry Dunant** witnessed the Battle of Solferino in 1859 and afterwards founded the Red Cross. He named Florence Nightingale as a model for his idea of helping wounded soldiers. In Switzerland too, nursing training was built up on her model in the 19th and 20th centuries. Today nursing professionals in Switzerland train at higher technical colleges and universities of applied sciences. The Nightingale Medal of the Red Cross still honours especially deserving nurses today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hospital for wounded and sick soldiers.
All the measures for cleanliness that protect against disease.
The collecting, ordering and analysing of figures.
A round diagram made of sectors of a circle that looks like a flower.

gewusst: Her older sister Parthenope was named after the ancient Greek name of the city of Naples, where she was born.
After the war Florence Nightingale was often ill and went on working from her bed for many years.
Many hospitals in Britain bear her name today.

teile.einleitung: The Denisovans are an extinct group of humans who were closely related to the Neanderthals. They were not discovered from a skeleton but from the DNA in a tiny finger bone. Many people in Asia and Oceania still carry traces of their genetic material today.
wichtigste: The Denisovans are named after Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains in Siberia.
A small finger bone led to their discovery.
By studying its DNA, researchers realised that they were a separate group of humans.
People in Papua New Guinea carry an especially large amount of Denisovan genetic material.
Many Tibetans probably inherited their ability to live well at high altitude from Denisovans.
A lower jaw that is attributed to the Denisovans was found on the Tibetan Plateau.
Because there are very few bones, little is known about what they looked like.

abschnitte.text: **Denisova Cave** lies in the **Altai Mountains** in Siberia, near the borders with Kazakhstan, Mongolia and China. People lived in it again and again over a very long time. Researchers found tools, jewellery and bones there from many thousands of years. In 2008 they discovered a tiny **finger bone** of a child there.

The team led by the Swedish researcher **Svante Pääbo** in Leipzig studied the **DNA** from the finger bone. In 2010 they found that it matched neither modern humans nor Neanderthals. It was a previously unknown group of humans. For the first time, a form of human had been discovered from its genetic material alone; Pääbo received the Nobel Prize for his research in 2022.

To this day only very few **fossils** of Denisovans are known, mainly teeth and pieces of bone. That is why little is known about what they looked like. The large molars suggest a powerful jaw. A lower jaw that is attributed to the Denisovans was found on the **Tibetan Plateau**.

The Denisovans were closely related to the **Neanderthals**. In the cave, bones of a girl whom the researchers called “Denny” were also found. Her DNA showed that her mother was a Neanderthal and her father a Denisovan. So different groups of humans met one another and at times lived in the same area.

Modern humans also met Denisovans, which is why a small part of their genetic material is found in people today. People in **Papua New Guinea** and on neighbouring islands carry an especially large amount of it. Many **Tibetans** have a gene variant that helps them to live well at high altitude with little oxygen. They probably inherited this from Denisovans.

Exactly what the Denisovans looked like and how they lived is not yet fully understood. Nor is it known exactly how widely they were spread across Asia. Researchers are therefore searching caves for more bones and even for traces of DNA in the **cave floor**. Every new find can change our picture of human history.

begriffe.erklaerung: The molecule in which the genetic information of all living things is stored.
The remains of a living thing from long ago, for example a bone that has turned to stone.
An extinct form of human that lived in Europe and western Asia.
All the genetic information of a living thing.

gewusst: The famous finger bone with which everything began came from a young girl.
The genetic material of the Denisovans was known before anyone knew what they looked like.

teile.einleitung: Ernest Rutherford was a physicist from New Zealand who is regarded as the father of nuclear physics. With the famous gold foil experiment he discovered that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus. He was also the first to change one element artificially into another.
wichtigste: Ernest Rutherford lived from 1871 to 1937.
He was born in New Zealand and later worked in Canada and England.
He distinguished the radioactive kinds of radiation alpha and beta.
In 1908 he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
With the gold foil experiment he discovered the atomic nucleus.
In 1919 he was the first to change one element artificially into another.
The element rutherfordium is named after him.

abschnitte.text: **Ernest Rutherford** was born on 30 August 1871 in Brightwater in New Zealand. He grew up as one of twelve children on a farm. Thanks to a scholarship he was able to do research at the University of Cambridge in England. Later he was a professor in Montreal in Canada, in Manchester and finally in Cambridge again. He died on 19 October 1937 in Cambridge.

Rutherford studied the radiation of radioactive substances. He found that there are different kinds and called them **alpha radiation** and **beta radiation**. He showed that radioactive elements turn into other elements as they decay. For this he received the **Nobel Prize** in Chemistry in 1908. He is said to have joked that he himself had now been transformed into a chemist.

From 1909 his colleagues Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at an extremely thin sheet of **gold foil**. Most of the particles simply flew through. But a few bounced off strongly, and some even came back. Rutherford compared this to a cannonball bouncing back off a sheet of tissue paper. In 1911 he explained: in the atom there is a tiny, heavy **nucleus**, and the rest is almost empty space.

abschnitte.titel: A new picture of the atom
abschnitte.text: Before this, people pictured the atom like a cake with raisins, in which the charges are spread out evenly. Rutherford showed that almost all the mass is in the nucleus. The nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller than the whole atom. If an atom were as big as a football stadium, the nucleus would only be the size of a pinhead. From this his colleague **Niels Bohr** developed the shell model in 1913.

In 1919 Rutherford bombarded nitrogen with alpha particles and obtained oxygen. This was the first artificial **transformation of a nucleus**, an old dream of the alchemists. In these experiments he also detected the **proton**, the positively charged building block of the nucleus. He also predicted a neutral particle in the nucleus, which was discovered as the neutron in 1932. Element 104 is called rutherfordium in his honour.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny, heavy centre of an atom.
A particle given off by some radioactive substances.
The decay of certain atoms, which produces radiation.
A positively charged building block of the atomic nucleus.

gewusst: Rutherford received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, even though he always saw himself as a physicist.
His portrait appears on the New Zealand 100 dollar note.

teile.einleitung: An echo is a sound that comes back. If you shout loudly in the mountains, a rock face reflects the sound and you hear your own voice a second time. Animals such as bats and dolphins even use echoes to find their way.
wichtigste: An echo is created when sound is reflected off a wall.
Sound travels through air at about 340 metres per second.
You only hear a clear echo if the wall is at least about 17 metres away.
From the time it takes the echo to come back, you can work out the distance to the wall.
Bats and dolphins find their way with the help of echoes.
Ships measure the depth of the water with echo sounders.
The name comes from the nymph Echo in Greek legend.

abschnitte.text: **Sound** consists of vibrations that travel through the air as waves. When these waves hit a hard, large surface such as a rock face, they bounce off. This is called **reflection**. The reflected sound then reaches us again a little later. We hear this returning sound as an **echo**.

abschnitte.titel: When do you hear an echo?
abschnitte.text: Our ears can only tell two sounds apart if there is about a tenth of a second between them. In that time sound travels about 34 metres, that is, 17 metres there and 17 metres back. If the wall is closer, the echo merges with your own shout. In large rooms such as churches the sound then carries on for longer, which is called **reverberation**. Soft materials such as curtains and carpets absorb sound and prevent echoes.

With an echo you can measure how far away something is. Sound takes about three seconds to travel one kilometre. If you hear the echo after three seconds, the sound travelled one kilometre, so the wall is about 500 metres away. The **echo sounder** on ships works on the same principle. It sends sounds to the sea floor and measures how long the echo takes.

**Bats** give out very high calls that humans cannot hear. From the echoes they recognise obstacles and flying insects in the dark. This ability is called **echolocation**. Dolphins and toothed whales also locate fish with clicking sounds in the water. About 30 species of bat live in Switzerland, and all of them are protected.

abschnitte.titel: Echoes in the mountains and in technology
abschnitte.text: In the Alps there are many places where a shout echoes back several times from rock faces. Some hiking trails even advertise an especially fine echo. In medicine, **ultrasound** is used, and its echoes create a picture of the inside of the body. Submarines and ships use sonar to find other objects in the water. Parking sensors on cars also work with echoes.

The name comes from Greek mythology. There, **Echo** was a mountain nymph who was punished by the goddess Hera. She could only repeat the last words that others said to her. Echo fell in love with the handsome young man Narcissus, who rejected her. In the end, only her voice is said to have been left.

begriffe.erklaerung: Vibrations of the air that we hear with our ears.
The bouncing back of sound or light off a surface.
The ability of animals to find their way with the help of echoes.
A device that uses sound to measure the depth of water.

gewusst: An echo is always a little quieter than the original shout, because part of the sound is absorbed.
The calls of some bats are very loud; we just do not hear them because they are too high for our ears.

teile.einleitung: Joy is a pleasant feeling that we have when something nice happens. You can often see it at once in a person's face, in a smile or in shining eyes. Researchers study how joy arises in the brain and why it is so important for us.
wichtigste: Joy is one of the basic feelings of human beings.
In the face you usually show joy with a smile.
Someone who is overjoyed often jumps about or leaps for joy.
Loud, overflowing joy in a group is called cheering.
If you make someone else happy, you usually feel happy yourself too.
Exercise in the fresh air makes many people cheerful.
You can write down or draw happy moments so that you remember them later.

abschnitte.text: Joy is a **feeling**, that is, an inner reaction to something we experience. It arises, for example, at a birthday party, at a reunion or after a game that went well. Experts count joy among the **basic feelings** that people all over the world know. A person who feels joy seems **cheerful**.

You recognise joy most clearly in a **smile**. In a genuine smile the corners of the mouth lift and small wrinkles form around the eyes. Many children jump about for joy, clap their hands or **leap for joy**. When many people are loudly happy together, for example in a football stadium, it is called **cheering**.

When we feel joy, the brain releases certain messenger substances, for example **dopamine**. These substances belong to what is known as the brain's **reward system**. The heart then often beats faster, and you feel full of energy. Laughing and exercise can also strengthen such pleasant feelings.

Joy is catching; if you see others laughing, you often laugh too. If you give someone a present or help them, you usually feel happy yourself. Shared joy strengthens **friendships** and the bonds in families and classes. That is why people like to celebrate together.

Exercise in the **fresh air** makes many people cheerful. Enough sleep, music, playing and time with friends are also good for you. You can write down or draw happy moments in a **diary**. Looking through it later lets you experience the joy a second time.

Many songs, pictures and poems are about joy. A famous poem is “Ode to Joy” by Friedrich **Schiller**, which Ludwig van **Beethoven** set to music in his Ninth Symphony. This melody is now the anthem of the European Union. Festivals such as Christmas, birthdays or carnival are also occasions for expressing joy.

begriffe.erklaerung: An inner reaction to an experience, for example joy, fear or anger.
A messenger substance in the brain that plays an important part in joy and reward.
Loud, shared joy, for example after a goal.
A jump into the air that you make out of sheer joy.

gewusst: Even babies smile in their first weeks of life when they see familiar faces.
People all over the world recognise a cheerful face, whatever language they speak.
Smiling can sometimes lift your own mood a little.

teile.einleitung: The “Elements” of the Greek mathematician Euclid is one of the most famous textbooks of all time. Euclid wrote it around 300 BC in Alexandria, and for more than 2,000 years pupils learned geometry from it. What is special about it: everything is proved step by step from a few basic principles.
wichtigste: Euclid worked around 300 BC in the city of Alexandria in Egypt.
The “Elements” consists of 13 books.
It is mainly about geometry, but also about numbers.
Euclid proved theorems from a few basic principles, the axioms and postulates.
The parallel postulate was disputed for a long time.
It also contains a method for working out the greatest common divisor.
The “Elements” is one of the most printed books in the world.

abschnitte.text: The “Elements” is a collection of the mathematical knowledge of the ancient Greeks. It consists of **13 books**, which should be thought of more like chapters. The first books deal with **geometry** in the plane, that is, points, straight lines, triangles and circles. Later books deal with numbers, ratios and finally solids such as cubes and pyramids.

Very little is known about Euclid's life. He taught around 300 BC in **Alexandria**, a city founded by Alexander the Great on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt. There was a huge library there and the Museion, a kind of research centre. Many of the theorems in the “Elements” were already known to earlier mathematicians, but Euclid arranged them into one great complete work.

Euclid begins with **definitions**, such as “A point is that which has no parts”. Then he sets out a few **postulates** and axioms, that is, basic principles accepted without proof. One example is that you can always draw a straight line between two points. From these principles he derives theorem after theorem by strict logic. This method of **proof** still shapes mathematics today.

The “Elements” contains a proof of Pythagoras' theorem. Euclid also shows that there are **infinitely many prime numbers**. Also well known is the **Euclidean algorithm**, with which you find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. For 48 and 18 you calculate: 48 divided by 18 leaves a remainder of 12, 18 divided by 12 leaves a remainder of 6, and 12 divided by 6 leaves none. So the greatest common divisor is 6.

Put simply, the fifth postulate says that through a point outside a straight line there is exactly one **parallel** to it. Many mathematicians found it too complicated and tried for more than 2,000 years to prove it from the other principles. Only in the 19th century did Carl Friedrich Gauss, János Bolyai and Nikolai Lobachevsky realise that a consistent geometry can also be built without this postulate. This led to **non-Euclidean geometry**, which later became important for Einstein's theory of relativity too.

The “Elements” was translated into Arabic and into Latin and so passed on in the Middle Ages. In 1482 one of the first printed editions appeared in Venice. Until the 20th century the work was the most important geometry book in many schools. That is why what we learn at school today about triangles, angles and circles is often called **Euclidean geometry**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic principle accepted as true without proof.
A basic requirement on which further proofs are built.
A complete logical argument showing why a statement is true.
A straight line that never crosses another.
The largest number by which two numbers can be divided without a remainder.

gewusst: According to legend, Euclid told a king that there is no easy royal road to geometry.
A fragment of papyrus from Egypt with an illustration from the “Elements” is almost 2,000 years old.
On a sphere such as the Earth, Euclidean geometry does not apply: there a triangle can have three right angles.

teile.einleitung: “Egg in salt water” is a simple and exciting experiment to do at home. A raw egg sinks in ordinary water, but if you stir in enough salt, it suddenly floats on top. The experiment shows how density and buoyancy work.
wichtigste: A raw egg sinks to the bottom in tap water.
If you stir a lot of salt into the water, the egg floats on top.
Salt water carries things better than fresh water, because it is denser.
With salt water at the bottom and tap water on top, the egg hovers in the middle.
In the very salty Dead Sea you can lie in the water almost without swimming.
A very fresh egg lies flat on the bottom in water, while an old one rises to the top.
Once salt has dissolved, you can no longer see it in the water.

abschnitte.text: You need a tall glass, tap water, a raw egg, plenty of table salt and a spoon. First you carefully put the egg into the water, and it **sinks** to the bottom. Then you take the egg out and stir several tablespoons of salt into the water until no more will dissolve. If you now put the egg back in, it floats on top. The dissolved salt has become invisible, but it is still there, and you can even taste it.

Whether something floats depends on its **density**, that is, on how heavy a certain volume of a substance is. An egg is a little denser than tap water and therefore sinks. If you dissolve salt in water, the water becomes heavier without taking up much more space. If the salt water is denser than the egg, its **buoyancy** pushes the egg upwards. The Greek scholar Archimedes worked out this connection more than 2,000 years ago.

You can make the experiment even more amazing. First you fill the glass halfway with strong salt water. Then you very slowly pour tap water on top, for example over a spoon, so that the two do not mix. The egg sinks through the light tap water and comes to rest on the heavy salt water, **hovering** in the middle. If you colour one layer with food colouring, you can see the boundary especially well.

You can also use water to check how fresh an egg is. Inside the egg there is a small **air bubble** at the blunt end. Over time, water evaporates through the fine pores of the shell, and the air bubble gets bigger. That is why a very fresh egg lies flat on the bottom. An older egg stands up, and a very old egg even rises to the top and should not be eaten.

The **Dead Sea** between Israel, the West Bank and Jordan is one of the saltiest lakes on Earth. Its water contains almost ten times as much salt as ordinary sea water. That is why it carries people so well that you can lie in it and read a newspaper. In the Mediterranean too you swim a little more easily than in Lake Zurich, because sea water is salty. However, there are no fish in the Dead Sea because of all the salt.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much mass there is in a certain space, that is, how heavy a substance is for its size.
The force with which a liquid pushes an object upwards.
A liquid in which a substance such as salt has completely spread out.
Water with very little salt, as in streams, lakes and tap water.

gewusst: Ships sit a little higher in the salty sea than in a freshwater lake, which is why large ships have different markings on their hulls.
The Dead Sea lies more than 400 metres below sea level and is therefore the lowest point on land.

teile.einleitung: The Dartmouth Conference was a research meeting in the summer of 1956 in the USA. Experts met there to find out whether machines can think and learn. It is regarded as the birth of research into artificial intelligence, or AI for short.
wichtigste: The Dartmouth Conference took place in 1956 at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire.
The proposal was submitted by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon.
The term “artificial intelligence” appeared for the first time in the proposal.
The idea was that every aspect of learning can be described so precisely that a machine can simulate it.
The Rockefeller Foundation paid for the meeting.
It was organised as a summer research project lasting several weeks.
John McCarthy later developed the programming language Lisp, for a long time the standard language of AI.

abschnitte.text: The meeting took place in the **summer of 1956** at **Dartmouth College** in the town of Hanover in the US state of **New Hampshire**. It lasted several weeks and was intended as a **summer research project**. The participants came and went at different times. They discussed, calculated and presented their ideas to each other.

The proposal was written in 1955 by four experts. **John McCarthy** was a young mathematician at Dartmouth College, and **Marvin Minsky** did research at Harvard University. Nathaniel Rochester worked at the computer company IBM. **Claude Shannon** of Bell Labs is regarded as the founder of information theory.

The proposal contained a bold claim: every aspect of learning and intelligence could be described so precisely that a **machine** could **simulate** it. The researchers wanted to find out how computers could use language, form concepts and solve problems. For this new field of research, McCarthy chose the name **“artificial intelligence”**. The Rockefeller Foundation provided the money for the meeting.

The participants did not answer all the questions that summer, as they had hoped. But Allen Newell and Herbert Simon presented the **Logic Theorist**, a program that could prove mathematical theorems. Many ideas discussed there shaped research in the following decades. The conversations led to new research groups at universities such as MIT and Stanford University.

After 1956 **artificial intelligence** became a research subject of its own. In 1958 McCarthy developed the programming language **Lisp**, which was long regarded as the standard language of AI research. Chess computers, speech recognition and learning programs followed later. Today's AI applications such as translation programs or chatbots go back to the questions asked at Dartmouth.

begriffe.erklaerung: A field in which computers are taught abilities such as learning, understanding and solving problems.
To imitate something, for example a thought process in a computer program.
The study of how information is measured, transmitted and stored.
An artificial language used to give a computer instructions.

gewusst: The researchers believed that ten people could make great progress on thinking machines in one summer.
The term “artificial intelligence” was coined for this meeting and is now known worldwide.

teile.einleitung: Feathers are the mark of birds, because no other animals alive today have them. They help with flying, keep birds warm, protect them from wet and make them colourful or inconspicuous. They are made of horn, rather like your fingernails.
wichtigste: Only birds have feathers.
Feathers are made of horn, the substance keratin, like hair and fingernails.
A bird needs the flight feathers on its wings in order to fly.
The soft, fluffy down feathers keep it warm.
When feathers are changed, in the moult, a bird loses old feathers and gets new ones.
Ducks oil their feathers and so stay dry in the water.
In the past people often wrote with a goose quill.

abschnitte.text: A feather is made of **horn**, more precisely of the protein keratin. Down the middle runs the **shaft**, a firm, hollow stem. On both sides many fine branches grow that together form the vane. On the branches there are even finer barbules with tiny **hooks** that hook into one another like a hook-and-loop fastener. If the vane comes apart, the bird can smooth it again with its beak.

The long **flight feathers** on the wings carry the bird through the air. The tail feathers help with steering and braking. The **contour feathers** cover the body and give the bird its shape and colour. Underneath lie the soft **down feathers**, which trap a lot of air and so keep it very warm. That is why duvets and winter jackets are filled with down.

Birds spend a lot of time arranging and cleaning their **plumage** with their beaks. Many birds have a gland at the base of the tail that produces an oily substance. Ducks, for example, use it to oil their feathers, so that water runs off. Because feathers wear out over time, birds replace them regularly, usually once a year. This change of feathers is called the **moult**.

Some feather colours come from pigments, others from the fine structure of the feather, which bends the light. The glowing blue of the **kingfisher**, for example, is such a structural colour. Many male birds are splendidly coloured, like the peacock or the goldfinch. The feathers of many females, by contrast, are rather brown and inconspicuous, so that they are well **camouflaged** while sitting on the nest. The ptarmigan in the Swiss Alps has white plumage in winter and brown-speckled plumage in summer.

Feathers existed long before today's birds. Researchers have found many fossils of **dinosaurs** with feathers, above all from China. The famous **Archaeopteryx**, which lived about 150 million years ago, had both feathers and teeth. Today we know that birds descend from small meat-eating dinosaurs. The first feathers probably served for warmth rather than for flying.

Until the 19th century people in Europe wrote with **quills**, usually from geese. The tip was cut at an angle and dipped in ink. That is why in German a pen with a metal nib is still called a Füllfeder. Feathers were also used as decoration on hats and clothes, which meant some bird species were heavily hunted in the past. Today many birds and their feathers are protected in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A firm protein that feathers, hair, nails and horns are made of.
A soft, fluffy feather without a firm shaft that keeps a bird warm.
The regular replacing of old feathers with new ones.
All the feathers of a bird together.

gewusst: A swan can have more than 25,000 feathers, while a hummingbird has only about 1,000.
A bird's feathers often weigh more than its whole skeleton.
Owls have especially soft feather edges and so fly almost silently.

teile.einleitung: Deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA for short, is the molecule in which the genetic information of all living things is stored. It is like a long set of building instructions that decides how a living thing is built and how it works. Its shape is like a twisted rope ladder, the double helix.
wichtigste: DNA is short for deoxyribonucleic acid.
The DNA molecule has the shape of a double helix.
