The sides of the DNA ladder are made of the sugar deoxyribose and phosphate.
DNA contains four different bases: adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine.
Adenine always pairs with thymine, and guanine always with cytosine.
Most of the DNA of a human cell is in the cell nucleus.
The Basel researcher Friedrich Miescher discovered DNA in 1869.

abschnitte.text: **Deoxyribonucleic acid** is a very long molecule in the cells of all living things. It stores the **genetic information**, that is, the instructions for building the body and for how it works. Particular sections of DNA are called **genes**. Each gene contains, for example, the instructions for a particular protein.

DNA looks like a rope ladder that is twisted around itself; this is called a **double helix**. The two sides are made alternately of the sugar **deoxyribose** and of phosphate. The rungs are each formed by two bases that meet in the middle. **Adenine** always fits with thymine and **guanine** always with cytosine, like two puzzle pieces.

With just four bases, nature writes all its building plans, rather like the way you can form countless words from a few letters. What matters is the **order** of the bases. The cell reads them in groups of three and uses them to build proteins. The human genetic material contains about three billion base pairs.

In humans, most of the DNA is in the **cell nucleus**. There it is tightly coiled and divided among 46 **chromosomes**. If you unrolled the DNA of a single cell, it would be about two metres long. A small part of the DNA is found in the mitochondria, the power stations of the cell.

In 1869 the Basel doctor **Friedrich Miescher**, working in Tübingen, discovered a new substance in cell nuclei, which he called nuclein. For a long time nobody knew that this substance carries the genetic information. In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick described the **double helix**, helped by X-ray images taken by Rosalind Franklin. In 2003 the human genetic material was almost completely decoded in the Human Genome Project.

abschnitte.titel: Why is knowledge of DNA important?
abschnitte.text: With DNA analysis the police can link traces to a person, because almost every person has unique DNA. In medicine, DNA tests help to detect inherited diseases and improve treatments. Researchers compare DNA to work out how animals and plants are related. Old bones also reveal a great deal about human history through their DNA.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of DNA with the instructions for a particular feature or protein.
One of the four building blocks of DNA, abbreviated as the letters A, T, G and C.
A coiled package of DNA in the cell nucleus.
The part of a cell where most of the genetic information is stored.

gewusst: The DNA of all the cells of one person put together would be many billions of kilometres long if unrolled.
The DNA of any two people is more than 99 per cent the same.

teile.einleitung: Single-celled organisms are living things that consist of only one cell. Most are so tiny that you can only see them under a microscope. All the same, they eat, move and reproduce, and they are found everywhere: in water, in the soil and even in our bodies.
wichtigste: A single-celled organism is a living thing made of just one cell.
The slipper animalcule is covered in tiny hairs and has the shape of a shoe sole.
With a cyst, many single-celled organisms survive dry conditions.
The green eyespot flagellate has a red eyespot and a flagellum.
The single-celled organism Plasmodium causes malaria.
The single-celled fungus yeast makes bread dough rise.
Diatoms have shells of silica, and foraminifera often have shells of chalk.

abschnitte.text: In a **single-celled organism**, one single cell does everything that is needed for life. This includes bacteria and archaea, which have no cell nucleus. Other single-celled organisms do have a nucleus, for example amoebas, slipper animalcules, yeasts and many algae. Most are only a few thousandths of a millimetre in size. The first person to see them was the Dutchman Antoni van Leeuwenhoek in the 17th century, with a **microscope** he had built himself.

The **slipper animalcule** lives in ponds, has the shape of a shoe sole and rows along with thousands of fine hairs. The **amoeba** constantly changes its shape and creeps forward with false feet. The green **eyespot flagellate** (Euglena) has a red eyespot with which it detects light, and swims with a flagellum. It can carry out photosynthesis like a plant but can also take in food. At about a fifth of a millimetre, slipper animalcules can just be seen with the naked eye as little dots.

In the sea, huge numbers of single-celled algae float in the **plankton**. **Diatoms** build beautiful shells of silica that look like little jewellery boxes. Through photosynthesis they produce a large part of the Earth's oxygen. **Foraminifera** often form shells of chalk with many chambers. Over millions of years, whole layers of rock have formed from their shells.

Many single-celled organisms are very useful to us. **Yeast** makes bread dough rise and is needed for brewing beer. Bacteria in the gut help with digestion, and in sewage treatment plants single-celled organisms clean the waste water. But some of them cause illness: **Plasmodium** causes malaria and is passed on by mosquitoes. In tropical countries malaria is one of the most dangerous diseases.

Most single-celled organisms reproduce by simply dividing into two cells. Under good conditions this can happen very quickly, in some bacteria every 20 minutes. If it gets too dry or too cold, many single-celled organisms form a **cyst**. This is a tough covering in which they can rest for a long time. When water comes again, they hatch out of it and carry on living.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest unit of a living thing that can live on its own.
A firm protective covering in which a single-celled organism survives bad times.
A long, whip-like thread with which some cells move about.
Tiny living things that float in the water and are carried by the current.

gewusst: There are giant single-celled organisms: some foraminifera grow to several centimetres.
You too started out as a single cell before it became trillions of cells.

teile.einleitung: A codon is a three-letter word made of building blocks of genetic information. Each codon tells the cell which amino acid it should add to a protein next, or where it has to stop. All the codons together make up the genetic code, the language of life.
wichtigste: A codon consists of three nucleotides, that is, three bases in a row.
There are 64 different codons, which stand for 20 amino acids and the stop signal.
The most common start codon is AUG; it also stands for the amino acid methionine.
The stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA end the building of a protein.
Many amino acids have several codons; leucine, for example, has six, but tryptophan has only one, UGG.
A change in a codon is called a mutation and may or may not change the protein.
The genetic code is the same in almost all living things.

abschnitte.text: Genetic information is stored in **DNA** and in the **mRNA** copied from it as a sequence of bases. In mRNA they are called A, U, G and C. The cell always reads this sequence in groups of three, the **codons**. You can imagine it like an alphabet with four letters in which every word has exactly three letters.

Proteins are built in the **ribosomes**, the cell's small protein factories. The ribosome reads the mRNA codon by codon. Matching transport molecules, the **tRNA**, each bring the right amino acid. This creates a chain that folds into a finished protein.

Reading usually begins at the **start codon AUG**, which also stands for the amino acid methionine. Then it carries on codon by codon until a **stop codon** comes. In the standard code these are UAA, UAG and UGA. There is no matching amino acid for them, so the protein chain ends there.

With four bases in groups of three, there are 4 times 4 times 4, that is **64**, combinations. But there are only 20 amino acids in proteins. That is why many amino acids are coded by several codons, **leucine** for example by six. **Tryptophan**, on the other hand, has only a single codon, UGG.

If one base changes, this is called a **point mutation**. If the amino acid still stays the same, it is a **silent mutation** with no consequences. If a codon turns into a stop codon, the protein breaks off too early and often no longer works. If a single base is inserted or removed, the whole **reading frame** shifts and all the following codons are read wrongly.

In the early 1960s, Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei found out that the codon UUU stands for the amino acid phenylalanine. In the following years the whole **genetic code** was cracked. In 1968 Nirenberg and two other researchers received the Nobel Prize for this. Today this knowledge is used in medicine and biotechnology.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building block of genetic information that contains one of the four bases.
A small building block from which proteins are made.
A tiny protein factory in the cell that makes proteins.
The division of the base sequence into groups of three when it is read.
A change in the genetic information.

gewusst: A bacterium, a fir tree and a human use almost exactly the same genetic code.
In the mitochondria, the power stations of the cell, there are small exceptions to the standard code.

teile.einleitung: The paper clip is a small, bent piece of wire used to hold sheets of paper together. It is simple, cheap and can be used again and again. Even so, there is a lot of technology and history in it.
wichtigste: A paper clip is used to hold sheets of paper together.
A simple paper clip consists of bent wire.
Unlike with a stapler, the paper does not get holes.
If you bend a paper clip open and shut again and again, it breaks.
Steel paper clips are attracted by a magnet.
In Norway a giant paper clip stands as a monument.
The best-known shape with two loops is called the Gem clip.

abschnitte.text: A **paper clip** is a piece of wire bent so that it clamps several sheets together. The wire is **elastic**: after being pushed on, it springs back and presses the paper together. Unlike with a stapler, which in Switzerland is called a **“Bostitch”**, the paper does not get holes. The clip can therefore be removed easily and used again.

Most paper clips are made of **steel wire**, which is often galvanised or nickel-plated so that it does not rust. There are also coloured clips with a plastic coating. Machines bend the wire into the right shape in fractions of a second. Because steel contains iron, such a clip is attracted by a **magnet**.

Before there were paper clips, sheets were pinned together with pins or tied with string. Towards the end of the 19th century the first bent wire clips appeared. The best-known shape with two oval loops is called the **Gem clip**, after an English company. Around 1900 the Norwegian **Johan Vaaler** also patented a paper clip, but in a different shape.

In Norway the paper clip is regarded as a symbol. In the Second World War some people wore paper clips on their clothes to show that they stood together and to show their resistance to the occupation. In Sandvika near Oslo there is a **giant paper clip** several metres high as a monument. It is a reminder of Johan Vaaler.

If you bend a paper clip open and shut again and again, it breaks at some point. This is because of **metal fatigue**: every bend creates tiny cracks in the metal. The spot also gets a little warm. After many movements the cracks become so large that the wire breaks through.

You can make a long **chain** out of many paper clips. They are often kept in a small box or a magnetic tin. Some people use a straightened clip to press a small button on a device or to change a SIM card. If you place a paper clip carefully on water, it can even float thanks to surface tension.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material is elastic if it springs back into its shape after being bent.
The weakening of a material through many repeated loads.
The right to be the only one to use an invention for a certain time.
Swiss word for an office stapler that pushes staples through paper.

gewusst: From 2005 a Canadian swapped a red paper clip in many steps for more and more valuable things and finally got a house.
A metal paper clip can stay lying on the water, although steel is much heavier than water.
A well-known computer program used to have a talking paper clip as a help figure.

teile.einleitung: A chloroplast is a tiny green body in the cells of plants and algae. Photosynthesis takes place inside it, turning light, water and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen. Without chloroplasts there would be hardly any oxygen to breathe and no food for animals and people.
wichtigste: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts.
The pigment chlorophyll makes chloroplasts green.
Chloroplasts are found in the cells of the green parts of plants.
For photosynthesis the chloroplast needs water, carbon dioxide and light.
Oxygen is released in the process.
Inside there are stacked membrane discs, the thylakoids.
Chloroplasts probably descend from bacteria that were taken into other cells a very long time ago.

abschnitte.text: A **chloroplast** is a small part of a plant cell, known as an **organelle**. It is usually lens-shaped and only a few thousandths of a millimetre in size. A single leaf cell can contain dozens of chloroplasts. They are found in the cells of the green parts of plants, above all in the leaves.

Chloroplasts are green because they contain the pigment **chlorophyll**. Chlorophyll mainly captures red and blue light. Green light is reflected, which is why leaves look green. In autumn many trees break down their chlorophyll, and then yellow and orange pigments become visible.

**Photosynthesis** takes place in the chloroplast. Using the energy of light, it turns water and carbon dioxide into sugar. This releases **oxygen**, which animals and people need to breathe. Chloroplasts store the sugar for a while as grains of **starch**.

A chloroplast is surrounded by two envelopes. Inside there are flat membrane discs, the **thylakoids**, stacked like coins. The chlorophyll sits in their membranes, and that is where the light is captured. Around the stacks there is a fluid, the **stroma**, in which the sugar is built up.

Chloroplasts have their own small set of **DNA** and multiply by dividing. Researchers believe that they descend from **cyanobacteria**. A very long time ago, such bacteria were taken in by another cell and went on living inside it. This idea is called the **endosymbiotic theory**.

Not all plant cells have chloroplasts. They are missing in roots and in the white layers of an onion. These parts grow without light and do not carry out photosynthesis. At school, you can see chloroplasts well under the microscope in the small leaves of waterweed or of mosses.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small part of a cell with a particular job.
A green pigment that captures light.
Making sugar and oxygen with the help of light.
A flat membrane disc in the chloroplast in which light is captured.
A storage substance made of many sugar building blocks.

gewusst: Chloroplasts can move around in the cell and line themselves up differently depending on how bright the light is.
Almost all the oxygen in our air comes from the photosynthesis of plants, algae and cyanobacteria.
A sea slug can take chloroplasts from the algae it eats into its body and use them for a while.

teile.einleitung: The European mole is a small mammal that spends almost its whole life underground. With its shovel-like front paws it digs long tunnels and hunts earthworms and insect larvae there. Almost every child knows its heaps of earth, the molehills.
wichtigste: The mole lives almost entirely underground.
It digs its tunnels with shovel-like front paws.
It does not eat plant roots but small animals such as earthworms.
It senses its prey above all with its sensitive nose.
Molehills are made of earth that it pushes out of its tunnels.
The mole does not hibernate.
The water vole is often mistaken for it, but it eats roots.

abschnitte.text: The mole is about 12 to 16 centimetres long and has a short tail. Its body is cylindrical and covered with velvety, blackish-grey **fur**. The fur can be stroked in any direction, which is why it can also run backwards in its tunnel. Its eyes are tiny and can mainly tell light from dark, and it has no outer ears.

The front paws are broad like **shovels** and turned outwards. An extra bone at the thumb makes them even broader. With them the mole digs a whole network of tunnels that can be many dozens of metres long. It pushes the surplus earth upwards, and this creates the **molehills**.

The mole eats mainly **earthworms**, but also insect larvae, snails and millipedes. It senses its prey with its sensitive nose, the tip of which carries many fine touch organs. Because it needs a great deal of energy, it has to eat every few hours. In a **store chamber** it keeps paralysed earthworms, which stay alive there but cannot move.

The European mole lives in large parts of Europe as far as western Asia. It likes loose, damp soil in meadows, pastures, fields and gardens. In Switzerland it is widespread, from the Swiss Plateau to the mountain valleys. It lives as a **loner** and is active all year round, including in winter, when it uses deeper tunnels.

In the garden the mole is often mistaken for the **water vole**. The water vole is a rodent and nibbles roots, tubers and flower bulbs. Its heaps of earth are flatter and more irregular, often with bits of root in them. Molehills, on the other hand, are round and usually lie in a row.

The mole loosens and airs the soil with its tunnels. It also eats many insect larvae that can harm plants. For farmers, however, the heaps in meadows can be a nuisance, because earth gets into the fodder. Anyone who does not want the mole in their garden should drive it away gently rather than harm it.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal with fur whose young are fed with milk.
A heap made of the earth that the mole pushes out of its tunnels.
An animal that lives alone most of the time.
A rodent that lives underground and eats roots.

gewusst: The German name Maulwurf has nothing to do with the mouth; older forms of the word meant something like “heap thrower” or “earth thrower”.
For its size, a mole can move an astonishing amount of earth and is a real strongman.
With the touch organs on the tip of its nose, the mole senses the tiniest movements in the soil.

teile.einleitung: A mistake is something that did not work out as planned. In science, mistakes are not just annoying but often very instructive. Some of the most important discoveries in history even came about from mistakes or chance.
wichtigste: Researchers often say: you can learn from mistakes.
If an experiment does not work, you look for the reason and try again.
An experiment with an unexpected result shows something new about the subject.
You write mistakes in your research diary so that you do not repeat them.
A measurement error means that you have measured something imprecisely.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin on a forgotten dish.
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895 more or less by chance.

abschnitte.text: A **mistake** is a departure from what was right or planned. It can be a wrong calculation, a forgotten step or an imprecise measurement. All people make mistakes, including famous researchers. What matters is how you deal with them.

With a **measurement error** you have measured something imprecisely. That can be due to the measuring device, to the way you read it off, or to small disturbances. That is why researchers repeat measurements several times and work out an average. In this way random errors become smaller, and you can see how accurate a result is.

In 1928 **Alexander Fleming** came back from holiday and found a mould on a forgotten dish of bacteria. Around the mould no bacteria were growing any more. In this way he discovered **penicillin**, the first antibiotic, which later saved millions of lives. In 1895 Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen noticed a glow more or less by chance and so discovered X-rays.

The inventor **Thomas Edison** needed a great many attempts before he had a good light bulb. He tested countless materials for the filament. Every failed attempt showed him what does not work. If an experiment does not work, you find out why and try again.

Good researchers write everything in a **research diary** or laboratory notebook. The mistakes are written there too, so that they are not repeated. In this way others can follow what was done. Sometimes, when reading back later, you discover something important that you overlooked at first.

In 1999 NASA's space probe **Mars Climate Orbiter** was lost. One team had calculated in American units, the other in metric ones. Nobody noticed the difference in time, and the probe flew too close to Mars. Since then even more care is taken over checks and clear agreements.

begriffe.erklaerung: A difference between the measured value and the real value.
A planned test with which you check a question.
A medicine that fights bacteria.
The way a group deals with mistakes, for example talking about them openly.

gewusst: The microwave oven was also invented by chance, when a chocolate bar melted in an engineer's pocket while he was working on radar devices.
In 1492 Christopher Columbus believed he had arrived in India, when in fact he had reached a continent unknown to him.
Fleming received the Nobel Prize in 1945 together with two colleagues for discovering penicillin.

teile.einleitung: Darwin's finches are a group of small birds that live almost only on the Galápagos Islands in the Pacific. Charles Darwin observed them on his voyage around the world, and today they are seen as a textbook example of how new species arise. Their beaks are as different as the tools in a toolbox.
wichtigste: There are about 15 species of Darwin's finches.
They live on the Galápagos Islands; one species lives on Cocos Island.
Their common ancestor probably came from the American mainland.
From one species, many species with different ways of life developed; this is called adaptive radiation.
The woodpecker finch uses a cactus spine as a tool to get insects out of holes.
Peter and Rosemary Grant studied Darwin's finches for decades on the island of Daphne Major.
According to current knowledge, Darwin's finches belong to the tanager family.

abschnitte.text: Darwin's finches are small birds, usually black, grey or brownish. They differ above all in their **beaks**. Some have thick, strong beaks for cracking hard seeds; others have fine, pointed beaks for catching insects. Each beak suits a particular kind of **food**.

The **Galápagos Islands** lie in the Pacific, about 1,000 kilometres off the coast of Ecuador. They are volcanic in origin and were never joined to the mainland. Probably a few finches came there long ago from the **American mainland**. Because the islands are separated from one another and offer different food, different species developed.

There are **ground finches**, which eat seeds on the ground, tree finches, and cactus finches, which feed on cactus flowers and fruit. The **woodpecker finch** holds a cactus spine or a small twig in its beak and uses it to poke insect larvae out of the bark. Only a few bird species use tools in this way. On some remote islands, finches even peck at seabirds to drink a little blood.

Charles Darwin visited the islands in **1835** on the ship HMS Beagle. Only later did people realise that the different finches are closely related to one another. From one ancestral species, many species with different ways of life developed; this is called **adaptive radiation**. In this way Darwin's finches helped to support Darwin's theory of **evolution** by natural selection.

From 1973 the research couple **Peter and Rosemary Grant** measured the finches on the small island of **Daphne Major** for decades. After a severe drought in 1977, almost only large, hard seeds were left. Mainly finches with larger beaks survived. Their offspring had larger beaks on average, so evolution could be measured within just a few years.

The Galápagos Islands are a **national park** and a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site. Even so, some finch species are threatened, for example the rare **mangrove finch**. Introduced animals such as rats, cats and a kind of fly whose larvae weaken the young birds cause them problems. Conservation programmes are trying to save the threatened species.

begriffe.erklaerung: The development of many species from one ancestral species, which adapt to different habitats.
The slow change of living things over many generations.
Living things that are better adapted to their environment survive more often and have more offspring.
A family of small, mostly colourful songbirds from the Americas.

gewusst: Although they are called finches, according to current knowledge Darwin's finches are not true finches but tanagers.
Darwin himself did not label his finches by island, which he later regretted very much.
The so-called vampire finch pecks at large seabirds and drinks their blood.

teile.einleitung: An honorary doctorate is a doctor's title that a university awards as a mark of distinction, without you having written a doctoral thesis. With it, the university honours people for outstanding achievements in science, culture, sport or society. The title is followed by the abbreviation h. c., which means “for the sake of honour”.
wichtigste: An honorary doctorate is a title awarded as a distinction, without a doctoral thesis.
It is awarded by a university.
It is written as Dr h. c., and the abbreviation stands for “honoris causa”.
Honoris causa means “for the sake of honour”.
People without a university education can also receive an honorary doctorate for outstanding achievements.
At the ceremony, professors at some universities wear a long gown.
One person can hold several, even very many, honorary doctorates.

abschnitte.text: Normally you get a **doctor's title** by writing a major piece of research after your studies, the **dissertation**. An honorary doctorate, on the other hand, is a **distinction** for which you do not have to write such a piece of work. With it, the university honours people who have achieved something special. In Latin the title is Doctor honoris causa, that is, doctor for the sake of honour.

Only **universities** and equivalent institutions may award honorary doctorates. In Switzerland these include, for example, the universities of Zurich, Bern, Basel and Geneva, or ETH Zurich. Usually a faculty, such as the medical or the arts faculty, proposes a person. Many universities award the titles once a year at their formal **Dies academicus**, the anniversary of the institution.

The title is followed by the abbreviation **h. c.**, for example “Dr h. c. Anna Muster”. Someone with several honorary doctorates sometimes writes **Dr h. c. mult.**, where “mult.” stands for “multiple”. An honorary doctorate is not an academic qualification and does not, for example, entitle someone to work as a doctor of medicine. But it may be used as part of the name.

Albert Einstein received his first honorary doctorate in 1909 from the **University of Geneva**, and many more followed later. The tennis player **Roger Federer** was made an honorary doctor by the University of Basel in 2017, partly for his work with his foundation. Politicians, artists, businesspeople and people from aid organisations are also honoured. Some well-known figures hold dozens of such titles.

The award is usually a formal ceremony in a large hall. At some universities the professors wear a long **gown** for it, a wide robe, sometimes with a hat. The person being honoured receives a **certificate** stating what they are being honoured for. Afterwards they often give a short speech.

begriffe.erklaerung: A high academic title that you receive after a piece of research.
The major piece of research you write for an ordinary doctor's title.
Latin for “for the sake of honour”.
A long, wide robe worn on formal occasions.
A large division of a university, for example medicine or law.

gewusst: Some people have collected more than a hundred honorary doctorates.
People without school qualifications or a university education can also receive an honorary doctorate if their achievement is outstanding.
Honorary titles from universities have existed since the late Middle Ages.

tyyc1g2.t: Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property, or IPI for short, is the Swiss authority for inventions, trade marks and designs. Here companies and inventors can have their ideas protected so that nobody simply copies them. The institute is based in Bern.
wichtigste: The IPI is based in the federal city of Bern.
It is an independent public institution of the federal government.
At the IPI you can register patents, trade marks and designs.
Copyright arises automatically and is not registered with the IPI.
A trade mark is valid for 10 years and can then be renewed.
In the online database Swissreg, anyone can look up Swiss protection rights.
The IPI also prepares laws on intellectual property.

abschnitte.text: It is not only a bicycle or a house that can belong to someone, but also an idea. This is called **intellectual property**. It includes inventions, brand names, the appearance of products, and books, songs and films. Anyone who creates something new should be rewarded for it and be able to decide who uses it. For this to work, there are protection rights that a state grants.

The **IPI** is an independent public institution of the federal government and belongs to the Federal Department of Justice and Police. It is largely financed from fees, not from taxes. The IPI checks applications and enters patents, trade marks and designs in registers. It also prepares laws on intellectual property and represents Switzerland in international negotiations. This includes working with the World Intellectual Property Organization in Geneva.

A **patent** protects a technical invention, for example a new tool, for at most 20 years. A **trade mark** protects a name or a logo so that customers can recognise a product. It is valid for 10 years and can be renewed again and again. A **design** protects the appearance of an object, such as the shape of a watch, for at most 25 years in total. All registered protection rights can be found in the public database Swissreg.

Anyone who paints a picture, writes a story or composes a song automatically holds the **copyright** to it. You do not have to register it anywhere, which is why it is not entered with the IPI either. In Switzerland the protection usually lasts until 70 years after the death of the author. So anyone who simply copies other people's works on the internet and passes them on can be infringing rights. The IPI does prepare the laws on this and informs the public.

The name “Switzerland” and the Swiss cross make products more valuable in the eyes of many people. That is why the **Swissness** rules have applied since 2017. For industrial products such as watches or machines, at least 60 per cent of the manufacturing costs must arise in Switzerland. For foods, as a rule 80 per cent of the raw materials must come from Switzerland. The IPI also works abroad to make sure that the origin label “Swiss” is not misused.

begriffe.erklaerung: A right stating that only the holder may use an idea or a name.
Protection for a technical invention for at most 20 years.
A protected name or sign by which you recognise a product.
The online database with all Swiss patents, trade marks and designs.

gewusst: Albert Einstein worked as a technical expert at the patent office in Bern, the forerunner of the IPI, from 1902 to 1909.
In Bern, alongside his work at the patent office, Einstein developed the special theory of relativity.
